/content/bbe90db5-64ac-441d-87e4-e984c5e.title: Rising bond yields add tens of billions to G7 countries’ debt costs
articleContent: The increase in global bond yields since the US war with Iran began in February has driven up the cost of borrowing for the world’s biggest developed economies by tens of billions of dollars, according to FT research.

G7 nations have locked in an additional $16bn of sovereign debt financing costs due to the rise in bond yields since the war began, according to an analysis of governments’ bond issuance data conducted by the FT. If the rise in yields persists then they could pay an estimated additional $34bn in extra financing costs by the end of the first quarter of next year.

Nearly every issue of government bonds at every maturity for all G7 countries is trading at a higher rate today than it was in February, pushing up the amount that governments must pay to sell new debt.

The US is paying the lion’s share of the increase in costs to date — an estimated $10.6bn — as it is by far the largest G7 economy and the biggest sovereign bond market in the world. It is set to pay a further $21.7bn in additional interest costs if the rise in yields persists until the end of the first quarter of 2027.

US bond yields have risen sharply in recent weeks as investors’ concerns mount about its growing public debt burden and whether policymakers will be able to contain the eruption of inflation triggered by President Donald Trump’s war in Iran. The rise in yields has persisted despite US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s attempts to keep them down by increasing the government’s purchases of longer-dated bonds.

Countries such as the UK, Italy, Germany and Japan that are big energy importers are also affected, driven by rising inflation expectations in the wake of the energy supply crisis triggered by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Other G7 countries have paid just over a third of the overall increase to date, according to the FT’s calculations.

The $16bn calculation compares actual borrowing costs to prewar rates. The $34bn estimate is made with reference to issuance plans released by each country’s treasury to predict future debt-raising needs, and each country’s pattern of issuance at different maturities.
While the increases are relatively small in comparison to overall public spending commitments, they threaten to pile additional pressure on already stretched government balance sheets.

Mohit Kumar, chief European economist at Jefferies, cautioned: “Rising rates are one of the biggest risks to equity and credit markets . . . We are entering the area where further rises in rates would be negative for both equity and credit.”

If rates were to rise, with the crucial US 10-year Treasury yield moving above 5 per cent, then “we should see a negative reaction to equity markets”, he added, as the higher bond yields would erode the relative appeal of equities while higher borrowing costs would squeeze profits.

“Deficits are rising globally as we see expansionary policies from governments . . . In addition, we are likely to see populist policies as we head into the midterms in the US and a number of parliamentary elections in Europe.”
He added that slashing deficits would be “even more difficult” in a higher-rates environment.
Economists warned that several factors were likely to add further upward pressure to yields.

“Beyond inflation risks, you’ve got real risks to political stability in the US, France, Japan, intermittently the UK, and possibly Germany,” said Adam Posen, president of the Peterson Institute. “Throw in geopolitics and that’s [another] real risk.”
Posen added: “The rise in defence spending, the rise in demographic needs, the rise of infrastructure spending and the rise in green spending outside the US all put upward pressure on real rates.”

AI build-out could also be crowding out investment in other instruments such as sovereign debt, putting upward pressure on yields. Higher government yields can also reflect investors’ higher growth expectations.

James Knightley, chief global economist at ING, said rising borrowing costs were “not only an issue for fiscal sustainability, but in the US they are already acting as a brake on economic activity via higher household and corporate borrowing costs”.
“The US housing market is already stalled and the steepening yield curve means we should be braced for mortgage rates rising above 7 per cent,” he said.

He added that the solid growth outlook was supporting the pricing of riskier assets such as equities, reducing demand for haven assets like Treasuries at the same time as these were under pressure from fiscal concerns and heavy corporate issuance, particularly from the so-called AI hyperscalers.
Michel Martinez, chief European economist at Société Générale, said the trend reflected “a repricing of a world in which capital is less abundant”.

“Sovereign borrowing is increasingly competing for savings with an AI-driven investment boom and other structural spending needs, including defence, the energy transition and re-industrialisation,” he said.
But yields were not high relative to nominal GDP growth in the US, Germany and Japan, he said.

Gianluca Salford, head of European rates strategy at Morgan Stanley, said the trend was moving matters “closer to the world we got used to” before the low-growth, low-inflation and low-rate environment of the 2010s.

“There are some challenges but to imagine that this is a structural phenomenon, it’s not obvious to me,” he said. “It doesn’t strike me in itself as something that is impossible to handle . . . Sometimes it takes a bit of a crisis. But often countries do the right thing to stay on the right track because basically there is no plausible alternative.”
Additional reporting by Claire Jones in Washington

/content/63311687-676b-4548-9bd8-3d7ad96.title: Alphaville. What’s the fiscal hit from higher yields?
articleContent: Since Operation Epic Fury was launched, bond yields have risen. There are a lot of arguments swirling around as to why.

Maybe they’re higher because oil prices surged, pushing up inflation expectations. Maybe they’re up because investors are questioning the credibility of the Fed and/or the soundness of US debt. Or maybe — as Stephen Miran wrote last week — it’s because the invasion of Iran marked the moment that investors began ratcheting up their long-run economic growth expectations. Who can tell?

What we can say is that higher bond yields mean that governments now have to cough up more when they sell bonds than they did before the shooting began. How much more? Around $50bn this year, Alphaville reckons. But it’s an annoyingly fiddly thing to estimate.

Because Alphaville was stupid enough to stick up our hands and volunteer to crunch the numbers when kind MainFT colleagues came calling, we thought it would be only fair to make you suffer the workings.
It’s not that hard, right? Just take total bonds issued and multiply by the amount that yields have risen? Sadly not.

To work out how much more governments have locked in as additional annual interest costs, we need to run a counterfactual analysis, comparing the interest cost each new bond issued locked in against the interest rate they could’ve locked in, if yields had not risen (like they have).

And given that some bonds are issued with a term of two years, some three years, some 40 years, we’re going to have to match their coulda-woulda-should issuance costs against the appropriate point for each sovereign yield curve. Actually, for most G7 countries, we need two yield curves: a nominal one and an inflation-linked one. So the calculations are not at all complicated, but there’s quite a lot of data to collect.

We first downloaded details of every bond auction, syndication and other meanderings into primary markets we could find from each of the G7. Reader, this was a lot more complicated than you might assume.

For sensible countries like the UK, the US, Germany, Canada, France and Japan, this is straightforward enough, if a bit time-consuming. Sure, different debt management offices have their esoteric rinky-dinks. The UK’s DMO has separate downloads for outright auctions, syndications and tenders. The French separate syndications, while the Canadians separate green bond issuance. And they all have their own formatting conventions. But they each look like they’re at least trying to make their data accessible.
Then there’s Italy.

You’d think that this Banca d’Italia link to download results to current-year auctions might be just the ticket. But it omits not only syndications, but also their chunky retail issuance programme. So we went pleading to friend-of-Alphaville and Italian bond guru Gus Baratta, who pinged us some more comprehensive data.

Next, we compared actual yields at which governments sold their debt to secondary market levels at the end of February. Here are some of the intermediate bits of data for the US, UK and Italy (just their non-inflation-linked bits though):
All we then needed to do was multiply the gap between each bubble and each country’s prewar yield curve as of end-February by the size of bond issued, and tot up the totals.
Ta da: $16.25bn.

Interestingly, at least for us, the country with the proportionately biggest hit to issuance costs so far has been the UK — where issuance-weighted rates of interest locked in so far are a full 71 bps higher than prewar levels. This compares to a lowly 21 bps bump in issuance-weighted rates of interest so far locked in for Japan.

And, to be clear, we’ve excluded bills from our calculations, and focused entirely on fixed and inflation-linked coupon bonds. We thought that this might be because the UK skewed its issuance longer out the curve than Japan, but the average maturity of non-bill issuance is almost identical for the two sovereigns.
Moreover, the rise in 10-year Japanese government bond yields is not a million miles away from the rise in 10-year gilt yields since Operation Epic Fury was launched:

Instead, what looks to have happened is that bond markets flipped quickly from pricing Bank of England interest rate cuts to pricing hikes in the UK, and this pushed the cost of issuing short-dated bonds up both quickly and sharply. Japanese bond markets have, much to the chagrin of punters who are desperate for the yen to rally, refused to price an equivalently sharp hiking cycle for the Bank of Japan.

And the remaining $34bn — our estimate for the extra 2026 financing costs if yields stay at this level — which takes the total up to $50bn? Simples. Take each G7 annual coupon gross issuance estimate, subtract bond issuance since the end of March, and multiply the answer by the issuance-weighted change in yields since the end of February.

Sure, this assumes that gross coupon issuance in the Q1 to Q1 period will match the fiscal year estimates provided by different G7 governments (when only the UK, Japan and Canada actually run a Q1 to Q1 fiscal year), but this doesn’t seem an unreasonable assumption.

The total $50bn annual additional cost of debt is split pretty much two-thirds to the US, with the rest of the G7 sharing the other third. And this is largely because it’s the US that issues a ton of debt.

And yes, $50bn in the context of ca $7tn collective gross bond market issuance this year is not the hugest number, but it’s not nothing. By our reckoning, the American share of the total works out at around $200 per US taxpayer.

With a bit of luck, economic growth really will accelerate massively, just as Miran claims bond markets are now pricing. In this world, not only will debt/GDP shrink rapidly, but finance ministries across the world will fund themselves with plentiful tax receipts that more than offset the rise in interest costs.
We can but hope.

/content/4f9bd1ed-f783-45c9-8542-addd8b5.title: FT Magazine. What the Indiana state fair reveals about Trump’s America
articleContent: The geography of class is visible from the sky. Flying into Indiana, my home state in the heart of the American Midwest, on a sweltering summer day in August, I can see the political history of the region from several thousand feet up. There are huge, four-mile squares of black dirt from which spring lush corn and soybeans, each evenly divided into the “country miles” that make up some of the world’s richest farmland. North of Indianapolis, the thriving state capital that is home to pharma giants like Eli Lilly, McMansions bordered by pools and lush landscaping appear. As we near the city, there are the factories and manufactured housing developments, dubbed “trailer parks” in less politically correct days. Some of my high-school friends lived in them, particularly as the farm business consolidated and the factories began closing.

I was long gone by 2016, when the small-c conservatism of my youth, which was defined by thrift, industry and local communitarianism (farmers ploughed snow-covered roads, churches ran food pantries) gave way to the rise of the insurgent wing of the American right, which became Donald Trump’s “Make America Great Again” politics. Thanks to an ambitious mother, I’d left Frankfort — where the German immigrants who settled here must have made that “o” their concession to the New World — for the Ivy League. But recently my home state has again emerged as a litmus test for where the Maga crowd, and the country in general, may be going.

The question posed by pundits and political analysts ahead of the US midterm elections in November is whether the Midwest is starting to turn against Trumpism. There have been signs this year, including the rise of rightwing alternatives to Trump, including Senator Josh Hawley in Missouri, who is planning a 2028 presidential run and has been willing to challenge the president on everything from the abuse of executive power to abortion rights and support for Big Tech.

Indiana, too, is pushing back against Maga. In December, 21 Republican state senators joined all 10 Indiana Democrats in standing up to Trump’s efforts to redistrict in advance of the midterms. The gerrymandering would have given the GOP a further advantage in Indiana, but was nonetheless antithetical to traditional conservative sentiment, which privileges states’ rights over federal intervention. Thanks to moderate Republicans’ refusal to cave to Trump’s pressure, the proposal was voted down in the state senate.

Retribution was swift. Railing against the Republicans who had voted against gerrymandering, the president declared: “Every one of these people should be ‘primaried’ and I will be there to help.” In due course, Maga Super Pacs poured millions of dollars into state senate races. The money in the primary season reached $13.5mn, compared with less than $300,000 two years earlier. Six out of eight conservative incumbents who had stood up to the president lost their primary. As one of them, state senator Travis Holdman, put it, “Welcome to DC politics in Indiana because this means that’s what’s coming.”

There was polling showing some of those districts might have gone Maga anyway. But it seems clear that big money and gerrymandering at the national level, along with the Republican leadership’s cult-like focus on Trump, has become a hugely distorting force in politics. “I’m a glass-half-full guy,” says former Indianapolis mayor Stephen Goldsmith, a moderate Republican who now teaches at Harvard. “But I think the combination of out-of-state big finance and gerrymandering is making it very hard for average people’s voices to be heard.”

What do folk from Indiana, we Hoosiers who are constitutionally suspicious of power and independently minded, think about this? Are they angry? Are an affordability crisis, an unpopular war in Iran and a sense that Republican Super Pacs bought out local senate races going to help the Democrats running on an anti-corruption message in the midterm? Are people even paying attention? This summer there was one very obvious place to take the temperature of this political moment: the Indiana State Fair.

State fairs are iconic in the Midwest. They are huge, month-long extravaganzas of commerce and culture. I get a taste of it immediately upon entering the fairgrounds in downtown Indianapolis. I arrive on the opening day, August 7, and the big event is the cheerleading competition, a fan favourite. I pass the carnival rides, the barns where prized sheep, goats and pigs are displayed, a group of middle-aged cloggers (performing a modernised version of Yorkshire clog dances that made their way to the US over the past 200 years) huffing it to an unexpected mix of hip-hop music, as well as something called the “dog dunk”, which involves canines jumping 20ft or more into a giant swimming pool, and a display of pioneer culture.

Eventually, I reach the grandstand in the centre of the fairgrounds. Squads of teenage girls in ribbons and colour-coordinated uniforms have already begun a practice session, cartwheeling and backflipping to the sounds of Fleetwood Mac, Led Zeppelin and Otis Redding. Parents mill about looking for seats, some carrying corn dogs and lemon slushies in containers as large as sand pails. Heftier girls lift twig-like ones into precarious mounts, then fling them up in the air. Toes are touched. Girls are dropped. “Dang, they are struggling more than last year,” one onlooker comments.

I corner a dance mom, Andrea, who looks like she may have been able to do a cartwheel or two in her day. Her 14-year-old daughter, Ashland, who cheers for the Jay County Junior-Senior High Patriots, is here with her comrade in pleats, Brenna. Both are extremely blonde, wearing red, white and blue uniforms and bright red lipstick.
“They did a round-off into a back handspring and then a back aerial,” says Andrea, proudly.
“Up a hill,” adds Ashland. “That was the hardest part.”
Andrea is wearing denim cut-off shorts and a “We Are Patriots” T-shirt — which, as it turns out, represents not only the squad but her politics.
She tells me she’s “a total Trump girl”, but her daughter has forbidden her to wear Maga gear today, since they are in Indianapolis “and they don’t like that kind of thing here”.

Andrea is 56, and has an enormous, blended family of 12 children that ranges in age from 38 to two. The smallest, a pair of blonde twins, are also in “We Are Patriots” shirts. They live in a rural area in the east of the state, 13 miles from the nearest store. Her family have been in the area for generations. Andrea ran a daycare centre until recently, and her husband now does construction. He’s doing well, thanks to a relatively robust state economy (Indiana outperforms the 11 other Midwestern states in terms of both GDP and a low unemployment rate, at 3.3 per cent). A strong state budget, low cost of living and good blend of manufacturing, services and agriculture have helped the state weather tougher times and higher prices. The steel, biotech and defence industries have benefited from re-industrialisation efforts at the national level.

That’s one reason Andrea and her family still support Trump. But there are others. “He’s strong,” she said, when I ask why she likes the president, “and he’s a very good leader. And he isn’t a politician — he’s a businessman. Also, he’s making decisions that are going to be good for the future, that will benefit our kids. We’ve got a strong military again. We’re bringing back patriotism and pride. We’re not taking down statues. I want our history to stay . . . OK, some of it has been ugly, but we learn from it. I want kids to know the truth, to learn respect.”

Cops and the military, she believes, should be held in higher regard. This reflects a larger cultural notion I’ve heard from others in many parts of rural America: that those in big cities or on the coasts don’t understand their values. As the speaker of the Indiana House of Representatives, Todd Huston, put it to me: “Faith, public safety, a simpler way of living — there’s a perceived lack of respect for those things.”
Recommended

Andrea is the sort of voter we hear a lot about, but people like her don’t represent the whole state. Indiana is three states, really, and each of them reflects a key element of recent American political experience. The northern half, where I was raised and my father ran factories, is a manufacturing powerhouse that was decimated by the China shock — that massive outsourcing of rust-belt industrial jobs to Asia over the last several decades. While Indiana is still the biggest manufacturing state in the union as a percentage of state GDP, most of the highly paid union jobs are gone, and the labour-left Democrats here swung hard for Trump in 2016.

Then there’s the south of the state which is, well, the South — more Appalachia than rust-belt. Indiana still has active Ku Klux Klan members and a strong strain of anti-immigrant populism. You could draw a direct line from the nativist Know-Nothings of the 19th century, to the Klan, the McCarthyites, the Tea Party and Trumpism in my home state.

Finally there’s Indianapolis, a diverse, affordable knowledge economy, with plenty of culture and entertainment. But “Indy”, which like many big American cities has a large Black population, exists in an orbit detached from (and resented by) much of the rest of the state. In that sense, the state capital and the surrounding county seats are emblematic of the national rural-urban divide that arguably defines American politics as much as the red-blue divide. Which party will be able to bridge that gap? The answer will decide the midterms, and perhaps the 2028 presidential election.

After a couple of hours of cheerleading, I move on to the Weaver Popcorn Youth Pavilion to watch the youth riding and showing competition. Teens in chaps, jeans, Western-style shirts and boots nervously show their horses. Parents and grandparents wearing muddy work boots and T-shirts cheer them on. A middle-aged woman shouts to one of the girls, “Look like you’re having fun, Piper!” Contestants are told by an announcer and judge wearing a cowboy hat, pinkish plaid jacket and boots to “Lean forward, gallop!” And they do.
I spot an especially attentive couple in the back row. The man has a tan, sandy hair, bright blue eyes. He wears jeans and cowboy boots.

The woman has an interesting face — very alert and full of feeling. It turns out Sheila Blake is a grandmother, aged 60. Her 14-year-old grandson, Tray, has just won a ribbon. “He’s worked hard, and this is the first year he’s done it all on his own,” she says proudly. That means Tray woke in the early hours of the morning to feed and care for the horse, saddle it, exercise it and so on. “Dealing with a 1,200lb animal, getting it to do what you want it to do, that’s really empowering to a child,” Blake says. “Life doesn’t happen inside four walls — showing here teaches them about work, about money.” This push for self-sufficiency stands in sharp contrast to the helicopter parents I see in my own Brooklyn neighbourhood.
Tray looks proud and a little nervous. He’s small, but sits tall on his horse, in a bright aqua cowboy shirt with white piping, as the ribbons are given.

“I was afraid I’d fall off,” he says to me later, though I doubt that was a real possibility. He’s been doing shows at the fair his whole life. “Most of the kids just spend a lot of time on their phones,” he says, when I ask about his friends at school. Then his grandmother tells him to “scratch out”, meaning sign out of the competition, and go wash down his horse, which he obligingly runs off to do.

Blake is from Brown County in the southern part of the state, and from a line of farmers. She and her husband still raise animals and crops, and they are self-sufficient in terms of food. But they both need other jobs to make ends meet — agriculture is a $35bn economy in Indiana, which is the ninth-largest farm region in the country, but farming is a tight-margin business, and only a handful of industrial farmers can afford to do it full time. Blake is a schoolteacher; her topic is Earth science. Like many people I interview, she wishes more people could spend a day on a farm. “If they did, they’d understand why the price of food is what it is. People need to get back into understanding where their food comes from and what it takes to get it to the plate. Water costs money, fuel costs money.”

Blake’s daughter works at the Department of Agriculture as a programme specialist, and both women feel that neither political party cares much about farmers — that politicians are completely out of touch with how people here live daily.
Blake worries about the war in Iran and the unsustainability of fossil-fuel usage in general.

Voting-wise, she calls herself an independent, and as I start to ask her whether Trump’s war might shift how she votes in the midterms and presidential election, she’s nodding before I finish the sentence. “It might. Yes, it just might. I’ll have to see the candidates, but it’s something I’m thinking about.”

Blake’s willingness to consider voting across party lines reflects not only Republican own goals like the war on Iran, but also the fact that Democrats are trying harder to meet rural voters where they are, talking more about values and religion. Across the Midwest, primary elections in recent weeks are being won not so much by party affiliation but by trust — does the candidate see me? Does he or she know who I am and where I live?

The conservative pollster Frank Luntz calls this trend the “politics of respect” and says that it could favour Democrats, particularly Democratic Socialists, in the midterms, and particularly in states like Michigan and Ohio, where union voters are turning against Trump. “Whoever shows up and makes people feel heard, regardless of their platform, will win,” he says. At a national level, Republicans aren’t doing so well on this score. Trump’s claims that the affordability crisis is a “hoax” and that data centres won’t take jobs don’t play with voters who have existential anxiety about AI.

The topic of data centres comes up, unexpectedly, in the swine barn, which I can smell before I arrive. The loudspeakers are blasting Eddie Money’s “Take Me Home Tonight” and Hoosier John Cougar Mellencamp’s “Jack and Diane”. It’s as though music stopped in the 1980s, but I like it. It reminds me of high-school dances.

A little girl with a giant red hair bow, who looks to be no older than 10, is shepherding a pig that must be more than 10 times her weight. The fair queen is there, in jeans and a plastic crown with paste gems, handing out award ribbons.
A horde of children waiting to show their animals to judges play football in an empty show pit covered in sawdust.

Nearby, in another pit, there is a 30-something man asking questions of about 150 children and teens gathered around, learning how to be livestock judges. They are blonde and freckled, and the girls have tight, perfectly woven French braids, or even the more complicated fishtail braids that the Amish girls in high school wore. Boys have crew cuts and caps. Everyone is in jeans and T-shirts that say things like “Purdue Ag” or “Blackhawk Livestock Judging”. The announcer quizzes them: “Question 15. When you get behind ’em, which animal has wrinkly skin?” The students scribble quietly. The announcer says, “You all over there talking, you aren’t helping yourselves by cheating.” A few of the teenage boys look abashed. “Question 16. Which is the animal with the heaviest weight?” More scribbles.

I move to the cubicles, which are shared by the pigs (many of them asleep on their sides, feet up and snoring like old men) and their owners, who are chilling in lawn chairs. I chat with a couple of farmers and, in a two-degrees-of-Indiana moment, discover that one of them works at Keystone Cooperative, a farmers’ collective now run by a boy I had a crush on in fifth grade. The farmer, Jason Hine, works multiple jobs like all the others.
He and another farmer, Melanie Bush, say that everyone here is talking about fuel prices — and data centres. “We’re following the news more closely these days, particularly at a national level.”

Bush says in her part of northern Indiana, data centres are coming into the area, driving up land prices and making it tougher to buy or lease. “Then there’s the traffic, the water consumption, all of it,” she says. Both she and Hine want people in Washington to better understand how hard it is to make a living. “It’s been hard since the 1970s really,” Hine says. Bush’s husband, a quiet man, nods knowingly. They all acknowledge the Iran war and Big Tech have added fuel to the fire of inflation. Would that make them vote Democrat? They make uncertain faces. As Hine says, “I’m thinking more about my school district rather than the midterms or the presidential election. The federal government should worry about national security, and we can worry about things like education here. There ought to be less government, not more.”
Recommended

This idea that the “government is the problem, not the answer” still runs deep here and favours conservatives, who polls predict will win the state, but by a far narrower margin than in 2024. While Democrats did well in the state between 2006 and 2010, thanks to the antipathy towards the Iraq war, in which many Indiana National Guardsmen fought — the state has historically sent a high number of soldiers to battle — and the financial crisis, Barack Obama’s victory here in 2008 was narrow. Even with all the Republican errors under Trump, it still feels as if Democrats have an uphill battle to win back this part of the country.

As I walk out of the barn I ask Brandon Smiley about the politics of race in the state. Smiley, 35, works for a party company that does the catering set-up for the fair. His family, like many in the area, came to Indiana three generations ago during the Great Migration, when many Black migrants left the South and came north for economic opportunity and to escape racism. This state hasn’t been that escape for his family — Smiley says he experiences racism “all day long”. Indiana “thinks in black and white”, he tells me, but job opportunities are good, and to him that’s what matters.

I’ve heard much the same from other Black Hoosiers on my visit. We chat for a bit, and I ask him what he makes of Trump 2. “Well, my kids are in Catholic school and the funding cuts in education have been tough. It’s $470 a month to keep both my seven- and four-year-old in school,” a significant bump from previous years. “The grocery bill has gone from $700 to $1,200 a month.” Will his community come out for Democrats the way they did for Obama in 2008? “Maybe. People don’t care until things [like prices] hit home,” and now they are. Still, Smiley says he would never move to a place like Chicago, a more diverse and inclusive city with a strong Black community, because it’s so much more expensive.

It’s almost evening, and I make my way back to the grandstand, this time for the all-important marching band competition. (A confession: I was a flag girl in the 1988 band competition. Thank God there was no social media back then.)

I don’t know whether I’m having a Sunset Boulevard moment, but the bands seem so much smaller than I remember. There is also a Cirque du Soleil quality now that feels strange — lots of costumes, theatrics, props. We just marched, threw flags and played our instruments with gusto. But the kids do seem as nervous and excited as I once was. I can see them silently counting steps, with that deer-caught-in-the-headlights look.

Technicians working the sound system chat as the kids play. “How ya doin?” one asks another. “Too early to tell — too late to care!” says another, and they both laugh. Band directors yell from the sidelines, urging the kids to hit their marks: “Go to the right, no, not that sharply!” Dozens of teenagers do a precise step formation as they blow their horns at the same time.

The West Lafayette High School is about to perform. West Lafayette is a dot of blue in a red state, the home of Purdue University, an engineering powerhouse. The band girls wear sailor caps and have something of an interpretive dance quality, almost tai chi, with some sort of ocean theme set to Debussy. The flag girls are not on their game, and as they spin and toss their props in the air, several end up in the gravel. I blame iPhones. Surely, they aren’t practising as hard as we were in the 1980s, when there was truly nothing to do all summer but detassel corn, babysit, work at the local ice-cream shop and twirl flags. Behind me, in the peanut gallery, onlookers offer colour commentary. “Oh boy, are they doing the Wizard of Oz?” “No, it’s Wicked.” “Oh, that’s better.” As a French-braided Salome dances to something vaguely Middle Eastern-sounding: “She’s beautiful — and I like her hair too.” “Yeah. That dance was badass . . . want some Kettle Korn?” That’s heavy-duty caramel popcorn for the uninitiated.

One could make a small study of food at a state fair. Fat, sugar and salt are the primary ingredients, with corn and pork coming in a close second. Corn dogs appear to come in sizes large, extra-large and obscene. Anything can be deep-fried — pickles, tomatoes, Snickers bars, ice cream, Oreos. I spot two women eating something that looks like a potato version of the fungi that explodes from the bodies of infected insects in the rainforest. I’m told it’s the “sweet and salty spiralled potato chip”, created by dunking a whole sliced potato into a deep fryer, and they can confirm it is “delicious”. As a child, I would have swooned over all this and begged my parents for a hub-cap-sized “elephant ear” of fried dough dipped in powdered sugar. Now, in the 90F heat, the thought makes me nauseous.

I gravitate to the line outside the pork tent, which is the longest, and with good reason — you can smell the salty goodness of the pulled pork half a mile away. Standing in line, the prairie sun starts to burn the back of my neck.

In the pork tent, I chat with an older couple from Montgomery County, an hour west of Indianapolis on the Illinois border. The husband, aged 66, is a retired AT&T technician and the wife won’t speak to me (“We’ve had trouble with reporters before”) even when I tell her I grew up in Clinton County, something that usually softens the Hoosiers sceptical of curious outsiders. Nonetheless, I learn they have two grown-up sons who work for the State Farm Insurance agency. They feel happy with their lot, particularly compared with how things were in the 1970s, when they were starting a family. “When we bought our first house, interest rates were 18 per cent,” says the husband, “and we’re about to pay it off soon.” The husband voted three times for Trump. “I like his policies — we need deregulation — but I don’t like the rhetoric. It’s not necessary.” What about the hoopla over redistricting, I ask? Did he pay attention? Does he care? He shakes his head, mirroring what I’ve heard all day. “It’s a game going on since politics started.” Still, he says, “I don’t love this war.” He’s convinced that “big companies are playing a game with prices”, using the war as an opportunity to drive them up.

This idea of corporate power and corruption is something that Democrats have been trying to make hay with for years now, mostly unsuccessfully. But Trump’s blatant use of executive power for self-enrichment has provided new fodder. There is research to show that candidates who refuse Pac contributions are perceived as more trustworthy. But this tends to work more at a primary level, when voters are less likely to simply pull the lever for a single party. Voters say corruption matters to them, and they want solutions to it. But how deeply they consider that in a general election is less certain. What is certain is that the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee has made Indiana a target state; Democrats need just four Indiana House seats to break the Republican supermajority. Certainly, they’ll campaign on corruption, but also on the rollback of Medicaid benefits, the failed Trump promises around manufacturing jobs and the rising costs for things like healthcare and housing.

It’s dinner time, and my eyeballs are burning from hours spent in the sun. It’s time to head back to the hotel. As I walk past the watermelon-spitting contest (the marker is set for 22ft — could anyone ever spit that far?) to the midway, I wonder who in God’s name would stand in line for “Hot Wisconsin Cheese” on a day like this. (Answer: many people.)

I don’t do fairground rides — I once put my neck out riding the Cyclone rollercoaster on Coney Island and needed a month of chiropractic treatment. But I’m fascinated by the scene. As the late writer David Foster Wallace put it in a piece about the Illinois State Fair, getting on these rides is like “paying to be in a car accident”. I pass something called the Sky Scream, in which a three-storey-tall steel lever with baskets at the end hoists eager fairgoers into the sky at high velocity, spinning them around in the baskets as the giant lever itself rotates to the sounds of fast-paced dance music. The carney pushes the handle to go, and a timid redhead grimaces and clutches the sides of his basket as the ride starts. I can’t help thinking of it as a metaphor for what’s ahead — in the midterms, the 2028 presidential elections and beyond.
Rana Foroohar is global business columnist and associate editor at the Financial Times

Summer might be ending, but we can hold on to some of its magic
articleContent: A new season, if you follow the meteorological calendar, is upon us. Even if you prefer the astronomical system (as I do) and view the equinox, in just over three weeks’ time, as the proper start to autumn, there is nevertheless a definite end-of-summer energy in the air; a palpable sense that after the long, languid, juicy days of August, things are suddenly about to get exhaustingly, painfully real again.

The French have long packaged up the resumption of regularly scheduled programming as la rentrée, or “the return” — to school, in particular, but also to the cities, to the office, to productivity. This heavily commercialised annual reset provides an important microeconomic boost to retailers of cahiers and cartables all over the country, as well as an (equally important) emotional one to those grieving the fact they have just blown the majority of their annual leave allowance in a single month.

As a child of economising parents growing up on the outskirts of Paris, I found the annual prospect of setting off to the hypermarché to buy a load of shiny new things quite thrilling. As an adult, I am struck by the consumerism and excess of the whole thing. What I do appreciate, however, is the way the ritual of the rentrée makes something out of the otherwise unacknowledged sadness and anxiety that some of us (though not necessarily all of us) feel at summer being over. Giving a name to this sudden lurch back into reality allows it to be understood as a collective experience, helping take some of the sting out of it.

I also like the way the rentrée creates a sense of new beginnings, bringing with it new chances to finally do that thing you want to do. I get a burst of energy and enthusiasm at this time of year, and must confess to even rather enjoying getting back to business, to routines and more focused work. I am not the only one feeling productive: a 2017 study from project management firm Redbooth of some 28mn tasks created by users of its platform found that September, October and November are the months with the highest completion rates.

And beyond mere productivity, there is much loveliness in what is to come. Having a sister who has lived in the tropics for the past decade and who misses the colder months has made me extra appreciative of the seasons, and autumn is a particularly delightful one. I love watching the leaves turn yellow and red and golden before falling off the trees for me to crunch underfoot; I love the abundance of root vegetables and the opportunity to make delicious warming soups; I even love the longer nights and the excuse they give me to spend my evenings curled up on the sofa with no pressure to be out gallivanting somewhere.

Yet while I do want to embrace the changing seasons, there is something about the energy of summertime that I increasingly find myself wanting to hold on to. For me, the joy of summer is not the opportunity to do nothing, but to have the time to do things slowly. To go the long way round; to spend an entire afternoon preparing a melanzane alla parmigiana; to hang out the laundry on the line; to sit down with some complicated text that usually feels like too much effort.

These things are not obvious leisure activities; in fact, they feel a lot more like chores when I don’t have the time to do them slowly and mindfully. And the fact is that in a normal working week (particularly if you have young children) that feeling of having all the time in the world is probably not going to be available. But it is still possible — optimal, I would argue — in our world of hyper-convenience and automation to realise that joy often comes not from the task being completed, but in the effort of doing the task itself.

This week, a furore broke out after it emerged the billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller had used AI to write a column on the bond market for The Wall Street Journal. Druckenmiller said he was “kind of proud” of using AI at the age of 73, and “not embarrassed” by it. I was struck less by Druckenmiller’s audacity, and more by the thought of what he had missed out on in not going through the joy, pain and ultimate satisfaction (sometimes) of the writing process.

The more AI encroaches on our lives, the more I feel myself wanting to return to doing more effortful things. I saw a couple struggling with a huge map in a car recently and it made me smile. I am about to invest in a CD-cassette-record player HiFi stack. I intend to follow through very soon on my commitment to get a dumbphone, at least for the weekends (iPhone addiction is proving sticky). Some people might call it “friction-maxxing”. I think of it as remembering how to live, not just for the summer.
jemima.kelly@ft.com

Friends with fiscal benefits
articleContent: This article is an on-site version of the Free Lunch newsletter. Premium subscribers can sign up here to get the newsletter delivered every Thursday and Sunday. Standard subscribers can upgrade to Premium here, or explore all FT newsletters
Think of your unlikeliest friend. The one you unexpectedly crossed paths with, despite being as different as chalk and cheese. How did you meet? And what have you learnt from them?

An economic literature on the power of unlikely friendships is taking shape. Researchers have long known that one’s social network is important for a range of economic outcomes, from the job search to the marriage market. But recent research suggests it might also be central to social mobility. In fact, having pals across class boundaries appears to be one of the strongest predictors of upward mobility for people in low socio-economic groups.

Raj Chetty, economics professor at Harvard University, pioneered this area of study with a 2022 paper using data on 72mn active US Facebook users and their 21bn friendships on the platform. Combining that data with US census and tax records, he and his colleagues mapped American counties based on their “economic connectedness”. That is, a measure of the prevalence of friendships between high- and low-income residents, relative to a baseline where people chum up randomly.

Cross-class friendships, they found, are much more likely to feature in Midwest and east coast social worlds than in those of the Southwest and Deep South. (Note: throughout, I’ve converted the economic connectedness variable into a percentage of low-income residents’ friends who are high-income. Low- and high-socio-economic individuals refer to those with below- and above-median incomes, respectively.)

What’s more, children who grow up in areas with more cross-class mixing go on to earn more on average, controlling for parents’ income. To isolate the effect of the county itself, the researchers tracked families who moved. Assuming those moves were not related to their children’s future prospects — a reasonable assumption — the analysis found that people who spent a larger portion of their childhood in a better-connected county went on to earn more.

David Forte, director of research translation and strategic initiatives at Opportunity Insights, a Harvard-based think-tank led by Chetty, told me that a county’s economic connectedness is shaped by two key factors: “the extent to which people from different income backgrounds interact in shared settings” and “the extent to which those interactions become friendships”.

Proximity is a key driver of friendship formation. For most of us, a large section of our social world is formed at school, university and work, though there are differences in the settings in which low- and high-income people pick up friends. Based on the connections the researchers could trace, low socio-economic groups make four times as many of their friends in their neighbourhoods as their richer peers, for example.

Moreover, environments such as churches and sports clubs are particularly effective for integrating people beyond class lines. That said, even in mixed-class settings a “friending bias” pervades, which describes people within socio-economic groups flocking to each other at a higher-than-random rate. In other words, if you put a rich and poor person in the same room, other factors can keep them apart.

Universities, especially elite ones, can transform low socio-economic individuals’ social worlds (of course, conditional on getting in). They are a setting at which people mix much closer to randomly, whether in halls of residence, seminars or extracurricular groups. And though barriers still exist on income lines — such as in fraternities and sororities, whose high-cost barrier to entry can shut out some students — rarely will someone from a low-income background ever again be surrounded by such a concentration of high-income peers.

While college benefits student outcomes through multiple channels — such as upskilling and knowledge formation — “the relationships formed there are likely part of the reason it has such lasting effects”, says Forte. Admission creates “opportunities to build relationships that can provide information, mentorship, shape aspirations and open doors to future educational and career opportunities”, he adds.

This is certainly true of my experience. On my first day in undergrad, a Finn and a Singaporean, now among my closest friends, had asked me which spring internships I was applying for. I did not know what a “spring” was, nor that I should have already started applying. Amid a feeble graduate jobs market and sinking degree wage premium, this “peer learning” may very well be among the strongest arguments for going to university today.

The UK’s Behavioural Insights Team (BIT), Meta and the Royal Society of Arts (RSA) deployed a similar methodology to Chetty to map economic connectedness across Britain. Again, they found that low-income children from the most economically connected areas go on to outearn their peers in the least connected regions.

Nonetheless, there is a geographic divide. “Deprived areas across the country tend to have fewer connections across economic lines,” said Martin Wessel, senior adviser at BIT’s home affairs and social cohesion team. The south-east stands out for its cross-class connections, while communities such as the north-east and south Wales are “rich in bonding social capital, but thin in bridging”, he added.

There are some signs that mixing is getting more rigid. For instance, UK schools are becoming “increasingly income-segregated”, Wessel tells me, with “shrinking catchment areas and rising house prices [creating] wealth barriers to entry”. Most people establish the elemental contours of their social networks in school, which means that whatever inequalities exist there can trail us throughout our lives.

But policymaker efforts to better distribute children between schools could reverse this. One example comes from Brighton and Hove, whose council prioritises free school meal-eligible children across the city over other children in a school catchment area to get a more even distribution of incomes across the region’s secondary education institutions.

Beyond school, “small, practical changes could turn routine encounters into opportunities for cross-class connection,” continues Wessel. This might look like a “family hub class that brings new parents together regardless of income, a youth programme that mixes teenagers from different schools, or a leisure centre that prices activities to reward mixed sign-ups,” he says. In that vein, the American Academy of Arts & Sciences chronicles a list of programmes boosting economic connectedness in the US.
So who knows? Maybe your next unlikely friendship could be engineered by a policymaker.

/content/458940e7-0754-42e3-aa33-f1f9e3e.title: Controversial Venezuelan executive courts investors after Trump oil deal
articleContent: The controversial Venezuelan energy executive who is now the Trump administration’s business partner has begun talking to potential investors in the oilfields they will jointly control.

As part of the unusual energy agreement between Washington and Caracas announced on Friday, Alejandro Betancourt, who owns the second-largest private oil business in Venezuela, is the administration’s minority partner in a company that will control more than 65bn barrels of the country’s reserves.

The new company will seek to award licences or establish joint ventures with US energy groups and other investors in some or all of the 17 different oilfields it has access to, according to people briefed on the agreement. Some of those oilfields have previously been held by Chinese and Russian companies.

Betancourt is a highly polarising figure in Venezuela because of his close connections to the socialist government that has been in power since Hugo Chávez took office in 1999. He is the most prominent Bolichico, a term for the class of politically connected magnates who emerged under Chávez.
Betancourt, the White House and the US state department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The agreement, which was announced on Friday evening by Donald Trump, is an attempt to generate confidence in Venezuela’s struggling oil sector, which collapsed over the past decade due to mismanagement and sanctions.
Following the January military operation to seize and capture former president Nicolás Maduro, the US had hoped to spur an investment boom in the country’s oil sector.

However, to the administration’s frustration, few major companies have been willing to invest in Venezuela because of what they see as the political and legal risks under the government now led by interim president Delcy Rodríguez.

ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips, which both had billions of dollars of assets expropriated in Venezuela over recent decades, have for the moment decided not to invest. Several companies with existing operations in the country — Chevron, Repsol and Eni — have made agreements with Venezuela’s government this year.

In a televised address on Saturday night, Rodríguez said the deal included the development of eight greenfield blocks in Venezuela’s Orinoco Oil Belt, with minimum royalties of 16 per cent and income tax of 34 per cent. The interim president did not mention Betancourt or his company, North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP).

As part of the agreement, the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital will provide guarantees to the oil companies that take on the planned licences in order to cover some of the financial and political risks they face in Venezuela.

The OSC was set up under Joe Biden’s administration to boost investment in technologies deemed critical for national security and has the capacity to lend up to $200bn. One person briefed on the deal said the OSC provided a means of offering guarantees to potential investors without asking Congress for funding.

Betancourt’s company NABEP produces about 200,000 barrels of oil a day. The private investors it is negotiating with on potential oilfield licences or joint ventures include Lionheart Holdings, according to people briefed on the talks. Lionheart Holdings is sponsored by Lionheart Capital, a Miami-based investment firm founded by Ophir Sternberg. Lionheart Capital did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

Apart from the guarantees, the US government will not provide any money upfront to the companies taking on the licences. However, according to people briefed on the structure, it could be awarded warrants that could result in it taking equity stakes in the future and would give it the right of first refusal on the oil flows.

Betancourt built his fortune in Venezuela’s electricity sector through no-bid contracts awarded by the Chávez government, later expanding into dealings tied to the state oil company Petróleos de Venezuela (PDVSA).

He and his companies have been investigated in jurisdictions including Spain and Switzerland over allegations of involvement in embezzlement and money laundering. Betancourt has not been charged in either country. His lawyers have long denied any wrongdoing and maintain that his wealth is legitimate.

Brian Naranjo, former deputy chief of mission in the US embassy in Caracas, said the announcement of the deal created “far more questions than answers”. Naranjo suggested Trump needed to signal a victory in Venezuela ahead of US midterm elections in November.

“I’m not sure it’s going to be the panacea that they claim,” he said. “I mean, how many times have we declared victory in the Gulf with Iran? Now, how many times are we going to have these giant success stories in Venezuela?”

Imdat Oner, a former Turkish diplomat who served in Caracas, said the announcement could be seen as a “face-saving move”, giving the administration an economic and strategic story to point to ahead of midterms.

However, Oner said the deal faced a real issue of legitimacy — especially given the 100-year concession announced by Trump — since Rodríguez had not been elected. Rodríguez said on Saturday the deal would remain in place for 25 years.

“A future elected government could have strong reasons to challenge or renegotiate the agreement, particularly if it believes the current government did not have the authority to commit the country for a century,” Oner said.

“The size of the deal, the speed at which it is moving, the unusual structure, the choice of partners and the legal framework on the Venezuelan side all raise real questions about whether it can actually hold up,” he said.
Recommended

Elias Ferrer, who heads Orinoco Research, an advisory firm, said the US deal could increase rather than reduce the uncertainty and risk for international investors, as it relied on the Trump administration.

“If the Democrats win the midterm elections in November they will undoubtedly go after these deals,” Ferrer said. “They’re already accusing Trump of ‘changing one dictator for another’ and favouring a Venezuelan oilman with a controversial background.”

/content/b3c98ca2-fe67-459d-89ff-4728993.title: US oil deal denounced by both sides of Venezuelan politics
articleContent: The Trump administration’s deal to take control of 65bn barrels of Venezuela’s oil has been heavily criticised by both members of the country’s opposition and some supporters of the government.

President Donald Trump on Friday evening announced an agreement granting a US-led company 100-year concessions over 17 oilfields, which account for more than a fifth of Venezuela’s reserves, the biggest in the world.
Trump called the agreement the “biggest oil deal in world history”. Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodríguez said it would bring more than $100bn of investment to the country.

The two governments have made few details available about how the arrangement would work, and have yet to explain where the new investment would come from. It is also unclear what role Petróleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), Venezuela’s sanctioned state-owned oil company, would play.

Juan Pablo Guanipá, one of the most prominent members of the opposition who is currently in Venezuela, said that foreign investment was vital to reviving the country’s oil industry following years of mismanagement, and that the deal had some “potential” to help boost activity.

But, referring to Rodríguez’s government, he added that “as long as we have the same people who destroyed the country and PDVSA handling the money that comes from this agreement, we are building a skyscraper on clay”.
Henrique Capriles, a lawmaker who leads a moderate opposition faction, said there were many doubts about the agreement because of the “opacity and corruption” of the government.

“Those who destroyed PDVSA are the same ones who remain in power and who are not going to rebuild anything,” he said on X. He said the government needed to explain the legal basis for the agreement under the constitution and the benefits to the Venezuelan people.

Earlier this month, the Venezuelan government and opposition began talks designed to lay the foundations for new elections. In the last poll in 2024, former president Nicolás Maduro declared himself the winner despite strong evidence that he lost to an opposition candidate.
Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores were seized by US forces in a night-time raid on Caracas on January 3, and are currently in a New York jail awaiting trial on drug trafficking charges.
In the wake of the capture, the Trump administration swiftly backed Rodríguez, Maduro’s deputy, who has passed laws opening up the country’s oil and mining sectors to foreign investment.

Opposition politicians fear the Trump administration will now be more reluctant to push for elections because it relies on Rodríguez to implement the new oil deal. “They don’t want an election where this will be one of the main debates,” said a prominent opposition figure.

Some of the strongest criticisms of the deal came from figures associated with the Chavismo political movement, which has held sway in Venezuela since the late revolutionary socialist Hugo Chávez, Maduro’s predecessor, took office in 1999.
Rafael Ramírez, who was president of PDVSA from 2004 to 2014, and energy minister from 2002 to 2014, said that the deal represented “the greatest looting in our country’s history”.
“It signals the end of PDVSA,” said Ramírez, who broke with Maduro in 2017 and now lives in Europe. “Now it’ll just be a contract administrator.”

William Rodríguez, a former member of Congress for the ruling United Socialist Party, said the agreement was “the greatest oil betrayal in the history of the country”, given that it had not been discussed in parliament and violated the constitution.
On Saturday, leftwing groups took to the streets of Caracas to reject the “guardianship” of Venezuela by the US, with many holding signs saying “Yankees out of Venezuela”.
“They [the US] attacked the Venezuelan homeland on January 3 and today they are trying to subjugate us,” said Fernando Berroterán, a member of the Popular Anti-imperialist Front.
Recommended

Venezuela’s oil production has fallen, partly as a result of mismanagement and partly because of US sanctions, from a high of about 3mn barrels a day to about 1.12mn, less than one-tenth of US production.

Enrique Novoa, the head of the Venezuelan petroleum chamber, said that while local oil companies have not yet seen the details of the agreement, “there is optimism in the sector for anything that supports the industry’s development”.
But Francisco Monaldi, an expert on the Venezuelan oil industry at Rice University, predicted little immediate impact on Venezuela’s oil output.

“In the short term, there’s very little that can be done to increase production quickly, so this year will likely see an increase of less than 200,000 barrels,” he said. Next year could see a somewhat higher increase, he added.

/content/53b5abd8-2919-4dc6-8dd6-81fc054.title: Iceland rejects reopening talks on EU entry
articleContent: Icelanders have rejected reopening negotiations on joining the EU despite Donald Trump’s threats against neighbouring Greenland, dealing a blow to Brussels’ efforts to draw the strategically important Arctic state closer.

Results early on Sunday showed that “No” received 52.8 per cent of the vote, according to public broadcaster RÚV, comfortably surpassing the 47.2 per cent for “Yes”. A total of 225,031 votes were recorded, a turnout of 82.5 per cent, the broadcaster said.

The vote on Saturday exposed a sharp geographic divide, with the capital Reykjavík backing renewed negotiations, while voters in rural constituencies rejected them, some by margins of nearly three to two.
The decision means the Nordic island of about 400,000 people will not, for now, revive an accession process it abandoned more than a decade ago after a clash with Brussels over fishing rights.
The US president’s repeated threats to annex Greenland, which he has on several occasions confused with Iceland, helped persuade the government to bring forward the referendum.
But the upheaval around Greenland failed to overcome a deeply rooted belief among many Icelanders that the country’s prosperity and security depended on retaining independence.
Many voters were also unconvinced that EU membership would offer meaningful protection from Trump, not least because Iceland is already a Nato member.

Control over the country’s lucrative fishing grounds has been another politically sensitive issue. Marine products account for almost 40 per cent of Iceland’s goods exports, and fisheries derailed its previous accession attempt.
“For Iceland, fisheries are like the automotive industry for Germany,” foreign minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir told the FT ahead of the vote.

Gunnarsdóttir had sought to reassure sceptical voters that Iceland’s growing strategic importance and stronger economy would allow Reykjavík to negotiate favourable terms with Brussels, demanding “sovereign control over all fisheries” in any eventual membership deal.

The vote comes as enlargement has returned to the centre of the EU’s agenda following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine and Moldova are negotiating to join alongside western Balkan states such as Albania and Montenegro.

But unlike most of the bloc’s existing candidates, Iceland already implements much of EU law through its membership of the European Economic Area and completed roughly one-third of the accession process during its previous attempt to join.

The vote also underscored the difficulty of making the case for EU membership for one of the wealthiest countries in the world. Brussels has intensified its outreach in the Arctic in response to Trump’s threats against Greenland, which have raised the strategic importance to the bloc of “like-minded” countries such as Iceland and Norway.

One senior EU diplomat said a rejection from Iceland would “tarnish the pitch that [the EU] is also a serious defence and security partner and not just an economic golden ticket for poorer eastern European states”.

The rejection is significant because Icelanders were not being asked to join the EU outright — a successful “Yes” vote would only have reopened negotiations with Brussels, with any eventual accession agreement requiring approval in a second referendum.
Recommended

It follows a knife-edge campaign in which supporters argued that households were paying the price for remaining outside the Eurozone through a volatile krona and some of Europe’s highest borrowing costs.

Icelanders’ confidence that they can prosper outside the EU was reinforced by the country’s rapid recovery from the 2008 financial crisis, with a banking collapse and IMF bailout that prompted its previous bid to join the bloc.
But Iceland rebounded with the help of a weaker króna and a tourism boom, strengthening the case of those who argued that economic independence has served the island well.
Additional reporting by Henry Foy in Brussels. Data visualisation by Aditi Bhandari

/content/3dd189e1-1af6-45a5-8993-0973af7.title: Burnham tightens prisoner release scheme and insists he is ‘tough on crime’
articleContent: Andy Burnham has moved to stop hundreds more criminals from being released early from prison, in an effort to see off one of the first major controversies of his administration and demonstrate his commitment to tough law-and-order policies.

Offenders sentenced for manslaughter, historic child sex offences, or death by drunk or dangerous driving will no longer be eligible for the early release scheme in England and Wales, which is being implemented because of a shortage of prison places.

The UK prime minister told the BBC’s Breakfast programme that he had been “tough on crime” throughout his career, and was opposed to releasing prisoners who had not served full sentences, but “there’s no easy answers here”.
“There is no more I could have done. I couldn’t have pushed the system any further without risking a significant crisis in our prisons,” he said on Sunday.

Campaigns against the policy had centred on the potential release of two men jailed for the manslaughter of PC Andrew Harper, an on-duty police officer, in 2019. The two have been blocked from eligibility under the new changes.
Luke Tryl, director of think-tank More in Common, said the prime minister’s response would be “hugely popular” but also significant in the longer term.

“Burnham has given a demonstration you don’t have to accept ‘politics of can’t’ and the government actually has agency to act on issues the public care about,” he said on X, noting this was “a riposte to the ‘politics of can’t’ under Starmerism”.
Harper’s mother, Debbie Adlam, told the BBC she was “glad and really grateful” at the news, but “immensely” worried about some of the offenders still eligible for release.
Under the early-release scheme, offenders qualify for automatic release after serving half their sentences instead of two-thirds, so long as they have not seriously breached prison rules.
It has been one of the thorniest issues on the political agenda, since it was first introduced in Rishi Sunak’s Conservative government and then expanded by Labour’s Sir Keir Starmer in 2024.
Burnham’s announcement comes ahead of parliament’s return from its summer recess on Tuesday, when he will face MPs for the first time as prime minister.

Adult male prisons in England and Wales are currently 98 per cent full. On Saturday, women and equalities minister Bridget Phillipson warned that without early releases, the network could run out of cells to hold people arrested for serious offences.
Recommended

The hundreds of additional offenders blocked from the scheme under the new changes come on top of the 1,000 serious sex offenders whom Burnham’s government blocked from eligibility for the scheme four weeks ago.

The prime minister said the extra places would be freed up by introducing a cross-party group to oversee the release of those serving indefinite Imprisonment for Public Protection sentences, and deporting foreign criminals.
UN experts warned last month that more than 2,000 prisoners were still serving IPP sentences, which could “amount to psychological torture”.
The indefinite sentences, introduced in 2005 but abolished in 2012, were given to offenders considered dangerous but not deserving of a life sentence.

On Wednesday, the Ministry of Justice announced new restrictions on serious sexual and violent offenders after their release, to prevent contact with victims, including “restriction zones” confining them to specific areas and GPS tracking.

/content/43718673-5c3f-46cc-a459-b0334e8.title: Burnham’s summer of quietly backing away from radical pledges
articleContent: Before Andy Burnham became prime minister, he promised to deliver “the most significant change moment in our politics for 40 years”.
He said he felt “uncomfortable” that some politicians backed certain causes but then got into government and “didn’t do anything”.
But in his first six weeks in charge, even some of Burnham’s supporters have noted an apparent tendency to make bold promises that do not quite materialise.
Burnham’s team deny any such charges and say that he will officially set out a more comprehensive 10-year plan for Britain later this year.
Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, has called him a “people pleaser” with “airy-fairy” plans.
Burnham wavered on compensation for the ‘Waspi women’ pension campaigners in June before he took office.
Since then, in at least six other areas, he has backed away from his original position.
One of Burnham’s signature policy pledges was to carry out “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar period”.
At the launch of his campaign to be MP for Makerfield, he said the existing £39bn fund for affordable and social housing “should be dedicated to council homes. Let’s not be coy any more”.
But last Monday the government set out plans to allocate £10bn to 33 organisations that — while including some councils — were primarily housing associations.

The allocation was broadly similar to that being finalised under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer. Government figures said Burnham had decided tearing up previous plans would have caused unacceptable delays.
Meanwhile the overall proportion of the “social rent” homes being built through the programme will remain static at 60 per cent.

Burnham emailed a campaigner earlier this year saying he would support a cap of £500,000 on political donations, saying it would “guard against the perception of any one party being unduly influenced”.
But the prime minister has decided not to back amendments to the Elections Bill that would cap the amount a person or organisation can give in a single donation.
Burnham dropped his previous support for the idea after trade union leaders warned that it could damage their ability to keep the Labour Party afloat.
Shaun Bowler, the electoral reform campaigner whom Burnham emailed in May, said the prime minister had “broken the promise he made to me”.
Burnham’s team has denied that the quasi-nationalisation of troubled utility Thames Water has been “shelved”, insisting he has never made any such commitment.
The prime minister raised expectations in June, saying: “Public ownership is absolutely an option. I would say for Thames Water that is what should be done.”

But since entering Number 10 he has been briefed on the technical challenges of pushing Thames Water into a “special administration scheme”. Officials are drawing up a menu of options and Burnham is expected to make a decision in the autumn.
Burnham hinted in July that he could increase the tax-free personal allowance.
The allowance has been frozen at £12,570 since 2021 — dragging more and more people into paying income tax as their pay rises.
He said “frustration about the personal allowance” that he heard while campaigning in the Makerfield by-election was “lodged in my mind”.
Subsequently he seemed to pour cold water on the idea, warning that any such change would be pricey and “difficult given the financial circumstances in which we find ourselves”.
While the policy change was not part of Burnham’s recent cost-of-living package, it could still in theory feature in his first Budget in late October.
But he would have to find £9bn a year by the third year of the policy if he restored the link between the allowance and inflation.

The prime minister subsequently complained that his musings about the allowance had been over-interpreted: “It’s funny these days you can’t answer a question honestly without people then reading everything else into it.”
Burnham has long backed electoral reform, arguing since 2022 that it was time for Labour to back proportional representation.
At the party’s conference last autumn he declared: “There is nothing more unstoppable than an idea whose time has come, and PR’s time has come.”
But this summer he said that any such policy was still at least three years away, saying: “I support it . . . but it would require it to be in a manifesto and endorsed at a general election.”

Burnham said in 2023 that the Parthenon Sculptures housed at the British Museum should be sent back to Greece with “no strings attached”. As far back as 2002, he supported a change to the law to facilitate the move.
He has now retreated from that position over the sculptures, also known as the Elgin Marbles.
“Ultimately it’s an issue for the British Museum, isn’t it?” he told the FT last week.

/content/32978145-d33e-4ee3-957b-39fcc72.title: Nepal rescue effort intensifies as death toll passes 700
articleContent: Nepal is “intensifying” a daunting rescue effort in a race against rising water levels as the death toll from a catastrophic landslide last week along the border with China passed 700, with more than 3,000 missing.

The government of Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Sunday it had dispatched almost 20,000 security personnel and rescued more than 8,000 people, including 270 who were trapped in various hydropower projects, despite adverse weather conditions.
Chinese authorities said on Sunday that more than 2,000 rescue workers had been mobilised and relocated 499 people from villages at further risk.

Recovery efforts continued over the weekend following a violent flash flood on Wednesday that swept away bridges, roads and buildings, leaving 734 dead and 2,498 missing in the small Himalayan nation. China has confirmed 16 deaths and 546 missing people.
The flood, which Shah described as an “unexpected thunderbolt of a natural disaster”, occurred on the Bhote Koshi river in Nepal’s mountainous Rasuwa district bordering Tibet.
Nepal’s disaster management agency on Sunday warned that water levels in the river had “increased further” and urged security personnel to “exercise utmost caution”.
“The government is intensifying rescue, search and relief operations in the affected areas overnight, leaving no stone unturned,” Shah said in a Facebook post late on Saturday.
He added that Indian and Chinese experts were “engaged” in rescue efforts in co-ordination with the Nepali army.
Recommended

Rescue teams and local officials in China’s Tibet Autonomous Region said at a press conference on Sunday that efforts had been hampered by damaged roads and communication lines, while the risk of additional flooding had caused delays.

Chinese authorities also said they believed that the landslide had been caused by an unstable glacier on the Nepal side of a river basin between the two countries. They said the glacier had come loose due to “the long-term effect of climate change”, raising a “new and distinctive feature of cryosphere disasters” in the region.

Nepal is situated on an active Himalayan fault and is home to mountains and glacial lakes, which results in its rivers frequently being flooded during heavy rains and leaves the country exposed to the risk of earthquakes, mudslides and floods.
