/content/7dbc5c59-c13b-4f2d-afd6-14e3033.title: Norway vs the world’s favourite chicken
articleContent: Tove Hellesvik’s family has farmed in central Norway for more than 500 years, and they are not always quick to embrace change.
They were “very sceptical”, Hellesvik said, when the company that buys their chickens told her and her husband to switch to a slower-growing bird.

For more than a decade until 2018, they had raised the Ross 308 chicken, one of the dominant breeds in global poultry production. Each bird was slaughtered on their farm after just 30 days. Instead, Norsk Kylling, the second-biggest chicken producer in Norway, wanted them to use a Hubbard strain, which lives for more than two weeks longer.
“Farmers are conservative. We were very sceptical. How would it work financially because you need to keep them so much longer?” said Hellesvik.
Poultry farmers across the world are beginning to ask themselves the same question.

The global poultry industry raises about 76bn birds a year for slaughter — but it rests on a narrow genetic base. Three companies dominate the breeds cultivated in commercial chicken farms across the world: Cobb, Hubbard and Aviagen, the latter two owned by the same parent company.

In recent decades, Aviagen’s proprietary Ross 308 breed has become one of the most widely used broiler chickens because it grows so fast; analysts say it accounts for tens of billions of birds eaten each year. The chunky bird reaches slaughter weight quickly, converts feed efficiently into meat and produces the uniform products demanded by supermarkets, processors and restaurant chains.

That efficiency has helped make chicken the world’s most widely consumed meat. But it has also made fast-growing broilers highly controversial. Animal welfare campaigners argue they are more prone to heart problems, lameness and legs that struggle to support their body weight. In several countries, campaigners have found evidence of overcrowding, poor litter, low light and birds struggling to walk in intensive broiler sheds.

Hellesvik’s farm was not one of those. Even so, she said, the effect of changing breed was almost immediate. Heart and leg problems dropped sharply. With Hubbard, only about 1 per cent of birds die, compared with 6 to 7 per cent for Ross 308, she added.

Her husband, Snorre, said the change was obvious. “They were livelier. They weren’t just lazy, sleeping and eating, but were curious. They went everywhere — up the steps, they followed us around. It was fun to come into the barn.”
Profitability improved. The new breed lives longer and needs more space, but the birds could be sold for higher prices.
“We use no antibiotics or probiotics. And we can concentrate on farm management, rather than going around picking up dead chicken,” said Snorre.

The debate goes to the heart of how modern chicken became so cheap. Martin Zuidhof, a poultry scientist at the University of Alberta, and colleagues found in a study that modern broilers were more than four times heavier at the same age as the 1957 strain and needed roughly half the feed to produce the same amount of meat.
Since feed accounts for about two-thirds of the cost of growing chickens, “the efficiency has everything to do with the cheapness of food”, Zuidhof told the FT.

But the same genetic progress created tensions. Zuidhof said the industry faced serious problems in the 1980s and 1990s, when birds selected for growth and yield suffered metabolic disease, heart problems, ascites — a build-up of fluid in the abdomen — and leg issues.

Breeders have since broadened the traits they select for, including welfare-related measures, according to Zuidhof, but more recently, the pressure has shown up at the reproductive end. He said heavier hens produced fewer and lower-quality offspring, while males selected for large breast muscles could struggle to mate efficiently.

Brian Earnest, lead animal protein economist at CoBank, said hatchability had become a weak spot in US production data. Producers “just weren’t producing enough baby chicks out of the breeder flock”, he said.

Commercial broiler strains, such as Ross 308, are owned by breeding companies, which keep elite pedigree lines in closed breeding programmes. The genetics are multiplied through a pyramid: pedigree birds produce great-grandparent and grandparent stock, which in turn produce parent flocks for hatcheries that deliver day-old chicks to farms.
Norway is now leading the world in trying to phase out fast-growing chickens such as Ross 308, in a move that is being closely watched globally.

Some efforts elsewhere have faltered. In the UK, several restaurant groups including the owners of KFC, Nando’s and Burger King withdrew this year from the Better Chicken Commitment, which included a pledge to move away from fast-growing breeds. In the Netherlands, the entirety of the retail market uses slower-growing breeds from Hubbard, said the company — but this does not apply to restaurants.

When supermarket chain Rema 1000 took over Norsk Kylling more than a decade ago, the quality of its chicken was poor and death rates high, said chief executive Hilde Talseth. The new owners realised drastic action was needed, so they moved away from Ross 308.
“Norsk Kylling was not best in class, in any way,” Talseth said. “We understood quickly that we had to improve the quality of our production.”
Now the rest of the Norwegian industry is following, committing in January to phase out the Ross 308 by the end of 2027.

Nortura, Norway’s leading chicken producer, is shifting towards the slower-growing Rustic Gold, another Aviagen bird; it expects them to account for more than 60 per cent of its birds by the end of the year.
“We saw that if we wanted to go further with animal welfare, then we needed to go for a slower-growing chicken,” said Kjersti Sørby, Nortura’s project manager for the transition.
“Farmers were sceptical [about] this in the beginning, and that is completely understandable. They didn’t know what price they would get.
“But now they are very satisfied. They say it’s a more robust chicken. It’s got thicker feathers, more colours than just white, and it’s pretty,” she added.
Sørby said Nortura’s farmers on average earned a little more from Rustic Gold than from Ross. But the transition requires more than 20 per cent more space and consumer prices are gradually rising.
Talseth said Norsk Kylling’s farms had more than 3,000 visitors a year, many from abroad, to see how they had managed the transition.
This is the third in a series on how chicken became the world’s favourite protein and the tension between keeping costs low and animal welfare

Part 2: The cult rotisserie chicken in a race against US inflation
Part 3: Norway vs the world’s favourite chicken
Part 4: The man who built Europe’s chicken factory
Part 5: The chicken farms that become ‘pathogen sponges’ for superbugs

But there are questions about how easy it is to replicate Norway’s move. The rich Scandinavian country imposes high agricultural tariffs to protect farmers, meaning almost all chicken consumed domestically is produced in Norway. Farmers are capped at 280,000 chickens.
“There is no doubt that import duties make it easier for us than most other countries,” said Sørby.
Zuidhof is blunter. “Norway is a rich country, so they can afford more expensive chicken,” he said. “I think welfare is very important, but so is efficiency.”

Richard Griffiths, president of the International Poultry Council, an industry group, argued concerns about fast-growing birds were “overblown”. Longer-living birds, he said, had about 30 per cent more environmental impact.
Sørby said one question was whether producers could secure enough parent eggs for slower-growing birds as the transition expanded.

Aviagen said it had broadened its breeding goals to include health, welfare and robustness, and that the Ross 308 offered “the optimum balance” between sustainable poultry production and European welfare standards.

Slower-growing breeds came with financial and environmental costs, the company said. “Any nation seeking to increase the proportion of slower-growing poultry must accept the risk that cheaper, imported poultry will reach its market to fill gaps in demand for affordable-price chicken. These imports may come from countries with lower welfare standards,” it said.

Back at Voll Gård in central Norway, Snorre Hellesvik is in no doubt about the wisdom of the move to slower-growing chickens. He said that farming chickens was not previously a source of public pride.
“We didn’t speak very loudly that we produced chicken. We had barns without windows, it was dark. The chickens were collected at night, when it was dark,” he said.
Now, he shows visitors a bright barn full of lively chickens. “Financially, we are doing better than before.”

Talseth said the transition had even helped solve one of the biggest fears of farmers worldwide: recruitment. “The discussion before was that nobody in the next generation wanted to take over the farm,” said the Norsk Kylling chief executive. “Now, it is different.”

/content/38a05881-ebfc-47ac-b326-96142ed.title: FT stock picking game results: the unexpected triumph of fundamentals
articleContent: The stock market is a cruel, capricious animal. Consider the example of Woody 5.0, a player in the FT’s new stock picking game.

In week three of the nine-week competition, they had the best-performing portfolio in the game. A week later they topped the leaderboard. And that’s pretty much where they stayed. They traded regularly but kept ahead of the pack, seemingly uncatchable.
Until about ten days before the end of the contest.

A couple of trades didn’t pay off and they slipped to fifth, then seventh. They made more changes. They rose a few spots. They brought in some investment trusts, then took them out again. They brought in airlines Wizz Air and British Airways owner IAG, and took them out too. They started to slide again.
They went back into microchips, buying shares in SanDisk, Advanced Micro, Intel and the SK Hynix ADRs (American depositary receipts) that they had sold off the week before.
Then they took their final roll of the dice: they kept SanDisk, sold the other three and bought Western Digital, Novo Nordisk, Mercado Libre and eBay. And they sank to 16th.
In the final 72 hours of the competition they lost 15,135 virtual pounds and, when the game ended at midnight on August 7, they finished in 387th place.
In his 40-year career in investing, fund manager Simon Edelsten has seen this kind of thing many times.

“It’s the sort of behaviour that bankrupted Barings,” he jokes, referring to the City of London’s oldest merchant bank, which collapsed in 1995 after rogue trader Nick Leeson chased mounting losses that ultimately hit £827mn.

“It’s the gambler’s illusion,” he says. “It’s that if you stay for one more spin at the roulette wheel, you’ve had so much bad luck it must be your turn now. Unfortunately, the gods of probability are not there listening.”
Thankfully, in our game, no one lost a penny. It was just a bit of fun — and heroic, reckless speculation was enthusiastically encouraged.
After all, no one ever won a stock picking game by buying good companies at good prices. Or did they?
Nearly 13,000 readers signed up to play the new game, which, unlike previous versions, allowed participants to trade stocks as often as they liked during the competition’s run.
And what a run it was.

“This nine weeks happened to encapsulate quite a significant turning point in the market,” says Edelsten. “I wouldn’t say the market’s quite gone from greed to fear — I think actually the equity market’s still quite greedy . . . but there was a beginning, middle and end.”

In the beginning was the SpaceX IPO, with its mind-bogglingly optimistic valuation. By the end, we were dealing with significant wobbles about the financing of AI linked to concerns about the bond market and inflation.
In the opening weeks of the competition, players ploughed their virtual money into Nvidia, Micron and Advanced Micro Devices, as the semiconductor boom reached its peak.
Then, at the end of June, Micron posted third-quarter earnings that some investors could scarcely believe: a 15-fold increase in profits and an adjusted gross margin that hit 84.9 per cent.

In the hours after the report dropped, Micron shares were trading at over $1,200 and chief executive Sanjay Mehrotra told investors that AI spelt the end of the boom-and-bust cycle that the memory chip sector is famed for.
The market was not convinced.

From that point, shares in leading memory-chip makers tumbled like a ball bouncing down a flight of stairs. By the time the competition ended, Micron’s share price was 28 per cent off its June peak, Samsung was down 32 per cent, and SanDisk was down 48 per cent.

And in the closing weeks of the game, with fears growing over the amount of money tech giants were spending on AI infrastructure, the market started the process of what Edelsten calls “separating the sheep from the goats”.
At no time was this more apparent than on July 29, when both Meta and Microsoft posted earnings reports.

With investors concerned over the Facebook owner’s high capital spending, its share price dropped 8 per cent the next day to its lowest point in four months. Not so with Microsoft. Owing to strong cloud and Copilot metrics, its shares surged by more than 15 per cent, increasing the company’s market cap by nearly half a trillion dollars in a single trading session — the largest one-day gain in US history.

And all the while, quietly at first, software-as-a-service stocks such as Adobe and Salesforce that the market had seemingly written off in the so-called SaaS-pocalypse slowly started to climb in value.

Some players embraced the ability to trade to great effect. A player called DeviT nearly won the grand prize when, in the last week of the competition, they bought Palantir the morning before its share price shot up 30 per cent. They were catapulted into the top slot — but faded in the last 48 hours to finish fourth.
When Mikey K, a retired civil engineer in his mid-sixties, noticed he was approaching the final week of the game in the top 20, he went hell-for-leather to finish as high as he could.
Until this point, his portfolio mostly consisted of insurance and construction firms. In came AstraZeneca, BP and McDonald’s.
“Then I had a wild punt in the last two days,” he says.

After releasing earnings on August 4, SpaceX shares dropped to $108 — 20 per cent lower than the company’s IPO price — and this was just a few days before its first major lock-up period expired and more than 900mn shares were free to flood the market.

“I think at the time you said in your newsletter that no self-respecting player still owned SpaceX,” says Mikey K, helpfully reminding me. “But over the years I’ve picked up that the market overreacts all the time. So I thought: there’s a chance this could come back.”
And he was right. In the last 48 hours of the competition, SpaceX shares rose more than 23 per cent, giving Mikey K a late surge and allowing him to finish inside the top 10 at number nine.

Some players — and I suspect more than would freely admit to it — used AI to help construct their portfolios. Among them was Nadine Graville. The 56-year-old from north London had never invested before but, inspired by her son, a university student interested in AI and planning to go into finance, she thought: why not?
She used the Perplexity chatbot to help pick her stocks, which included Rolls-Royce, Bunzl and Robinhood. And, frankly, she couldn’t believe what happened next.

Her portfolio shot out of the traps, gaining 18 per cent in the first week. For most of the first month she was in the top 30, and once even got inside the top 10. “When I showed my partner, who works in [finance], we thought it was hysterical,” she says, laughing.
Unfortunately, after a few weeks, the wheels came off. “Obviously,” she says, “my failure was SanDisk.”

Because she had asked the chatbot to select stocks that it thought would perform well over the game’s nine weeks, she chose not to make any changes — something she says she’ll do differently next time. In the last few weeks of the competition, she plummeted, finishing in 2,276th place.

Still, Graville says she can’t wait for the new game to start in October. “I am 100 per cent going to do it again. I’m going to do some different tactics and see if my AI skills will get me a better result next time — and maybe even a prize.”
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.
So who did win? Step forward Swapnil Ingole. The 40-year-old Co-op store manager from Surrey beat 13,000 players to win the game, with a portfolio that grew by more than 36 per cent.

In the article that launched the competition, FT writer — and stock picking game enthusiast — Bryce Elder encouraged players to “gamble like a degenerate” and focus on high-beta (volatile, higher-risk) stocks. He wrote: “Fundamental analysis can’t reliably deliver returns big enough in the window available.”

Ingole chuckles. “I skipped that advice,” he says. “I went into the fundamentals.” His stocks were all low-beta — some with scores less than one, meaning they have lower volatility than the wider market. He bought five stocks (the minimum number under the rules), gave them an equal weighting and made zero changes.
“Jumping in and out [of stocks] is one way to kill your portfolio,” he says. “The other is to overdiversify.”
Originally from India, Ingole moved to the UK in 2008. In 2016, he started day trading after following several “gurus” on YouTube. It did not go well.
“I lost quite a lot of money during those three years,” he says. “And then I realised — I wasn’t investing, I was just gambling.”

So he stopped and read up on what the best investors in the world did. That’s where he came across Warren Buffett. “I wasn’t much of a reader before, but after that I started reading quite a lot. I spend almost four or five hours a day reading now.” He started following Buffett’s principles, he says, investing in proper stocks, in companies whose business he could understand, building a portfolio mostly of small- and microcap UK stocks.
After making some money during the pandemic, he sold some shares and put the deposit down on a house.
For the game, though he was limited to larger-cap stocks, he retained his approach by assessing the fundamentals.

He picked software stocks Adobe and Salesforce. “With everyone moving to AI, they were really good valuations,” he says. Adobe — which he has in his real portfolio — has an 89 per cent gross margin, high free cash flow and strong return on invested capital. When he bought it, it had a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of about 11, roughly 70 per cent lower than its five-year average. The share price was $197. By the end of the game, it had grown to $265.
The other three stocks were Accenture (another he owns in real life), up 38 per cent before the end of the game, Cognizant, up 42 per cent, and Microsoft, up 34 per cent.

Ingole started later than some of the other players and began slowly. But as the rotation out of AI gathered pace, stocks like Adobe, Salesforce and Accenture started recording strong gains; then came the bump from Microsoft.

“Once a stock goes up like that, you are tempted to sell,” he says, but he tried to forget about it. “As with my own portfolio, I try not to log in very often, otherwise you’re tempted to do something silly . . . I learnt that the hard way between 2016 and 2019.”
“Now I just buy it and leave it as it is . . . ” he says, before channelling legendary US investor Peter Lynch, “or until the story changes.”
Registrations for the next season of the game open on September 21.

/content/f37e5176-56f1-48dc-bb52-58c5d85.title: A pioneering voyage up Colombia’s greatest river
articleContent: At the old quay in Cartagena, unconvincing pirate ships are filling with partygoers before heading out for a sunset of pounding salsa and reguetón dance music. A wheelhouse DJ looks up and shouts, “Saluden a los gringos!” (say hi to the foreigners) and we face yells and shaken booties.

I wave back, gently, from the 32-cabin, 223-foot AmaMelodia, an elegant cigar of a boat. The top deck runs from an open prow through a canopy-covered hobnobbing area to an air-conditioned lounge aft. We too slip our cables and steam into the city’s vast bay, the calm as the pirates fall behind a relief.

Edison de Caro, our captain, sets course for the Canal del Dique, a 75-mile cut first built in 1582 that connects the celebrated Caribbean city to the Magdalena, Colombia’s longest river — much of which has been effectively off-limits to all but the most intrepid travellers for most of the past six decades. Ahead lies a journey into a watery world of monkeys and buffalo, kapok and coffee, scattered fishing villages and lots of dancing, all summoning the stories of writer Gabriel García Márquez, naturalist Alexander von Humboldt and South America’s great liberator, Simón Bolívar.

In the early 20th century, passenger steamships paddled the river, but the last great boat, the David Arango (a favourite of García Márquez), was destroyed by fire in 1961. Since then, only big freight barges and pretty pirogues — the local canoes — have plied these waters. Extensive silting and the dangers posed by armed political groups and their associated drug gangs scared off potential tourism operators. But last year, AmaWaterways, a Californian company with boats on the Danube, Nile and Mekong, opened up the route to tourists once more.

A hot tropical darkness falls as we enter the canal and are called down to eat in a cosseted dining room on the middle of the three decks. Here the wild beyond is shielded by silken blinds. The dinner is a surprise, better than expected. Felipe Arango, the chef, turns out excellent sea bass and steak but is also a genius with soups, such as gazpachos and ajiacos.

For the most part, our fellow travellers are Americans, like Wesley and Valerie Lang, taking a break from the kids in Jefferson, Missouri. Valerie is one of nine children from a hill-country family, and has an easy manner to match it. “Normally we’d go to Jamaica,” she says. “But this is turning out great.”
The waiters project happiness that we’ve come to explore Colombia and, although English-speaking, relax happily back into Spanish for chats with my Cuban wife.

It’s all very calm, and afterwards we go down to try out our cabin. It’s sizeable at 22 sq metres and, like all but the four bigger suites, has a queen-sized bed, rattan-faced cupboards and even two sinks in the bathroom. It also has a balcony where I settle with a rum and my friend Michael Jacobs — in the form of his book about the Magdalena, The Robber of Memories.
But rather than read, I find myself watching the waters pass only a foot or so below, speckled with water hyacinth on which herons perch, banks lost to the gluey night.

Michael died in 2014 shortly after finishing this book. When I do open it, it starts with an encounter with García Márquez in Cartagena, the Nobel Prize winner already a bit lost to Alzheimer’s. Hearing of Michael’s plan to travel the Magdalena by barge, he’d said, urgently: “I remember everything about the river.”
We wake with the boat tied to a levee, ficus trees warming in the early sun against vast wetlands beyond. Minivans wait to take us on a first excursion, to San Basilio de Palenque.

I have wanted to visit Palenque for a long time; it feels like an essential piece in the jigsaw of understanding Latin America. Here Benkos Biohó, an escaped slave, established his free settlement in 1603. He was eventually hanged, but the community he founded survived, a rare thing.

Muralists have covered the village in vivid colours. There are painted adverts for elaborate hairstyles, in which we’re told residents traditionally hide their money. Escarli Díaz Valdez greets us, a guide who treats his subject without self-pity. He takes us to a house which shows us the hard old ways, then to the local healer who claims that no one died of Covid under his care, before giving us moonshine.

“We are a close community so there is never too much trouble here,” says Escarli. In Cartagena, I heard people express prejudiced fears about the Palenqueros, just as I suspect they have for more than 400 years, but Escarli says there’s pride enough in the village that the young return, even after getting college educations. He himself is an example.

Back on board, we cruise up the canal. A dredger is spraying silt on to the bank where we meet the Magdalena proper, a steady half a kilometre across, and I think of The General in His Labyrinth, García Márquez’s book about the final journey of Bolívar: “The river had grown vast and solemn, like a swamp with no beginning or end.”

The town of Calamar stands at the junction and we pull into a new dock built by AmaWaterways. A rickshaw tour leads to a cultural centre where Danza San Martin, a local troupe, perform a frenetic, threatening-with-a-smile Afro-Colombian dance. It reaches its conclusion as a storm blows in and we are returned to the boat drenched.

As the AmaMelodia swings away from the dock and begins pushing upriver, the rain is gone as fast as it arrived, the last of the day’s sun cutting through the clouds, like an overwrought vision of heaven.

We sail through the night and in the dawn egrets shine with the brilliance of stars. Clumps of wild cashew, ceiba and balsam pass, in one place tree branches shake with leaping howler monkeys, and pirogues carry fishermen to their hunting grounds.

I drop by the wood-panelled bridge to ask Captain de Coro about his 42 years navigating the ever-shifting waters. A former barge captain for the state Naviera Fluvial, his grandfather and father were captains before him. “There are points where we have very little water underneath,” he says, before adding that like all the crew, he is delighted by “this beautiful project”.

Later I will ask Beno Atan, AmaWaterways’ Colombia director, how hard it was to reopen the route, an almost incomprehensible project given the silting of the river, lack of facilities and Colombia’s history of violence. “There were challenges,” he says. “But we were determined. One of the owners had a spreadsheet with all the rivers in the world. The Magdalena was always top of the list.”

Every now and again, speedboats arrive to take us on excursions, whether to watch fishermen throw their atarrayas (nets) to catch bocachico (the local staple), or to travel through what feels like a vast aviary. We spot kingfishers, tanagers, tyrants, parakeets, woodpeckers, caracaras, hummingbirds, orioles and big-footed jacanas (whose ladies keep male harems).

Finally, we cruise into a narrower channel, and the town of Santa Cruz de Mompox appears. Again, I think of The General in His Labyrinth, of the dying Bolívar arriving in this town he loved: “‘God’s country,’ the general said without opening his eyes.” And then, more famously, “Mompox does not exist. Sometimes we dream about her, but she does not exist.”
I’m with him as we sidle up to the dock — the town arrives as if a mirage. The elegant colonial river frontage wobbles in a heat which, the locals joke, causes the hens to lay fried eggs.

Mompox is where the early Spanish settlers hid their valuables, too far upstream for the pirates of the Caribbean. It is where Von Humboldt stopped to study crocodiles. It is where, in 1812, the Venezuelan-born Bolívar began the liberation of Colombia, recruiting 400 soldiers.
Yet, by the 1900s, the river had silted and boats started using another channel. When Michael Jacobs came through in 2011, “it was a literal backwater, remote and moribund”.

Since then, bridges have been built to connect the island with passing highways. My wife and I take a walk and a cattle farmer down from the Llanos to buy stock stops us to sing the place’s praises. Two shopkeepers from La Guajira to the north tell us the arrival of AmaWaterways has given the town a further shot in the arm.

We stop by the Church of Santa Barbara to climb its tower. It has a balcony that represents Barbara’s imprisonment by her anti-Christian father (who eventually beheaded her — though in a strange reversal of fortunes, it is his severed head that lies at her feet on the church’s golden altar). We look down on a square where we’ll later eat ice cream made with nispero, one of those sweet fruits that are a mystery to people from temperate regions. We continue to the top of the tower and vultures resting in the windows regretfully flap out into the hot sky.

It’s a magnificent town, and we would happily spend days here, but after two nights the AmaMelodia slips its mooring and swings round to head back downstream, towards the coast. The AmaMelodia’s sister boat, the AmaMagdalena, is coming the other way. The company would love to go further inland, as the steamships once did. “We want to,” says Atan. “But there are a lot of different things that need to happen in order to get higher up, not least around general security.”

Even though we still have two days to go, departing Mompox feels like an ending and the river now carries us swiftly. Our ultimate destination is Barranquilla, the industrial town at the northern end of the river delta where we will eventually disembark (to a fiesta of carnival dancers).

But there’s more in between. We stop at Santa Barbara de Pinto, a village that has never hosted tourists, Colombian or otherwise. Argemiro Celestino Méndez, a teacher in a remote school, waits for us on the riverbank. He walks us along a road raised to beat the annual floods, pointing out medicinal rose balsam, guanacaste used for Easter sweets, and bell trees whose shade is loved by both stock and man.

Once, he says, the entire area was in the hands of the Boteros, a family of cattle ranchers whose history in the region goes back to 1719. Argemiro is one of several teachers I notice AmaWaterways using, and he speaks passionately about his calling.

When we reach the riverbank again, townspeople are milling about. A local farmer is demonstrating cigar making, telling an unconvinced American crowd that his cheroots are healthy. Fishermen use local children as quarry in a demonstration of net throwing and a group of frisky twenty-somethings dance cumbia, girls rotating away from their beaux’s proffered kisses.

It’s not a platitude to say AmaWaterways’ boats provoke warmth wherever they go. Another guest, the English composer Michael Hoppé, tells me it’s what has struck him the most: “How these people have overcome the devastation they endured, how they see this boat as part of that.”

A group of schoolgirls approach. Sharith, the most inquisitive, is pushed forwards by the others. “Pleased to meet you,” she says, giggling. They have come down to practise their English. There is no angle, no sale. “Whenever the boats arrive, I bring them,” says their teacher Maria Carolina del Castillo. “It’s the best English laboratory they can have.”

Ruaridh Nicoll was a guest of AmaWaterways (amawaterways.com). A seven-night cruise on the Wonders of Colombia itinerary travelling from Cartagena to Barranquilla starts at £4,309 per person (or £3,879 per person on the Magic of Colombia travelling in the opposite direction), including flights from London, via Bogotá or Miami

/content/fff93467-9a94-46d2-be4b-a746b62.title: FT Magazine. The brilliant trick behind Rome’s Big Four pastas
articleContent: It is early on a warm spring evening and I’m sitting outside a small family restaurant on the edge of the Testaccio neighbourhood in Rome. Everyone at the table orders pasta. This is possibly because the idea was mooted by Anthony Bourdain in one of those shows that everyone now turns to as an itinerary. He didn’t invent the idea, but he single-handedly made sure that nobody can ever visit Rome again without doing The Big Four Pastas: cacio e pepe, alla Gricia, carbonara and all’Amatriciana. You must collect them. It is The Law.

There are dubious origin myths for the dishes. Carbonari were supposedly ancient charcoal burners. An amatrice is an amateur or enthusiast, and grici were said to be “street sellers in Papal Rome” — though these last facts are contested to the point of knife fighting by the villages of Amatrice and Grisciano and the Swiss canton of Grigioni.

All are commonly assumed to go back in the mists of Roman antiquity, though nobody should need reminding that tomatoes didn’t exist in Italy until the Columbian Exchange, and carbonara only appeared on menus in the 1950s. So what connects them? I was desperate to find out.
There were seven of us as we ordered our “primi”, but one of us ventured a pasta with mushrooms, at which the lovely waiter went into a polite panic. We had no Italian and he had little English.
“It is impossible,” he said, unusually insistent. “Four pans,” he gestured to the open kitchen.
And it was here I realised that the Four Pastas have evolved uniquely as a function of the kitchen set-up in a small restaurant or café.

It works like this. There’s a big pot of water in the centre of the range into which, in individual baskets, the pasta is dropped to begin cooking. The boiling water is occasionally topped up, but isn’t usually changed during service.
There are four curve-sided finishing pans. One receives a splash of olive oil, the three others fatty little chunks of guanciale (cured pork jowl) that have been rendered down to produce hot fat.

Eventually, the part-cooked pasta is dumped into the four pans. As the floury water hits the hot metal and steams, it binds with the oil or fat, creating a creamy emulsion. The cook adds a splash more pasta water to each pan to keep the process going. All of the pans receive a heavy grind of black pepper, then one, two and three are granted a handful of pecorino Romano, while the fourth is hit with a ladle of crushed tomato pulp. Finally, an egg is cracked into pan three as the cook pulls it off the heat. All are kept in constant motion with ceaseless stirring, and then, after about two minutes, the pasta is poured on to plates and run to the table.

It’s an astonishing routine. Entirely a function of commercial food prep, a particular batterie of equipment and a mise-en-place established by generations of cooks. Ray Kroc legendarily never stopped tweaking the “line” at McDonald’s, in a life-long search for efficiencies and economies. He never dreamt of anything as perfect as this.

At a stroke, it answers long-standing controversies. Cream in carbonara? Garlic in all’Amatriciana? It would make no sense. Can we par-cook, drain and hold pasta? Should sauce be poured over or stirred in? Isn’t pasta heavy and rich? Is pasta a main? These all become stupid questions.

Pasta made this way explains the architecture of Italian dining. A 100g serving of dressed pasta is the perfect intermezzo between antipasti and “secondi” — and even explains why the main is then served without a carb.

This is the starting point. As the name suggests, it’s just cheese and black pepper. Cacio e pepe is the place to get the emulsification technique exactly right — and once you know you’ve got it cracked, everything else follows.

You’ll need 100g of pasta. Make your own egg pasta if you can, then cut it into noodle-like tagliatelle, maltagliati (irregular shapes badly cut from pasta sheets) or, if you have a chitarra, tonnarelli — in effect square-section spaghetti. You can, if you wish, buy vacuum-packed fresh pasta from the supermarket, but toss it in a couple of tablespoons of semolina flour before dropping it into the water. This whole dish depends on the starches built up in your pasta water. If it’s not the 50th serving of the night, give it a helping hand.

Use a wide pan with curved-up sides. Something that will facilitate fast boiling, evaporation and vigorous tossing. Place it on the hob next to your pasta-boiling pot and put in a modest glug of olive oil. Don’t use an absurdly big pot, it’s not necessary, and don’t bother with all that old toot about salting the water until it tastes like the sea. Modest salting is perfectly adequate.

Make sure you’re in sight of some kind of clock, or prop up your phone where you can see a timer. Pre-grate 60g of pecorino romano on your finest grater and coarse-grind heaps of black pepper into the bottom of the pan, along with a restrained splash of olive oil.

If you’re using shop-bought pasta, make a note of the cooking time. You’ll be pulling it out of the water one minute short. Bring the water to a rolling boil and drop in your floury pasta. If it’s fresh, you’ll need to boil until it floats to the surface.

The finishing pan doesn’t need to be screaming hot, just enough so the water will boil, so turn on the heat beneath it as you start the pasta cooking. It will come gently up to temperature and loosen the aromatic oils in the pepper.

OK. Here goes. Pull out a small ladleful of cloudy pasta water and pour it into the finishing pan, where it should immediately start to steam and bubble. Swap to a pair of kitchen tongs and hoick the pasta out of the water and into the steaming pan. Do not attempt to drain it. Not even a little shake.

Now, add the cheese and stir like a demon. A lot is happening here. The steam is completing the cooking of the pasta. The water is reducing, and the flour is helping to thicken it. The heat, your stirring and the agitation of the bubbling water are helping the melting cheese to emulsify into the liquid without going stringy or grainy. You are effectively making a flour-thickened cheese sauce, but in the pan at high speed and among the pasta you’re going to serve it with.

As you stir (I do it with the tongs) and toss the pasta, occasionally pull it to the side and look at the texture of the liquid sauce. It should be smooth and silky, like thick paint. If it’s runny, keep stirring. If it starts looking thick, add more pasta water. Weirdly, this bit doesn’t feel so rushed. It’s going to take a good minute or so for the pasta to be fully cooked — plenty of time to adjust the sauce.

I realise this will get me immolated in the town square by enraged English Italophiles, but I honestly no longer believe the myth that Italians eat their pasta al dente. I think they cook it al dente, so it’s perfect when it hits the table. Bear that in mind as you plate the pasta and run it to your eager guests.

Once you’ve cracked cacio e pepe, alla Gricia is a logical progression. Here you’re also going to make an emulsion of flavour-packed lipids, but this time, instead of olive oil, we’re going for pork fat. Guanciale, specifically, a kind of by-product of the industrial butchery going on at the Testaccio meat markets. A pig will spend its entire waking life either rooting with its snout or masticating. The muscles in the face are complex and hard-worked, packed with flavour and, if cooked straight away, as tough as hell. To transform them into guanciale, they are buried in salt, seasoned with huge amounts of black pepper, then hung up — not just to dry but also to undergo a kind of lactic fermentation, which breaks down the toughest fibres. The flavour is strong — a little goes a very long way — but possibly more than anything else, it’s the authentic taste of Rome.

Once again, allow 100g of pasta per person, but this time use the dried stuff. Particularly ridged, tubular pasta. If you can get it, bronze die pasta has a rougher surface at a microscopic level, which further increases the maximum surface to which sauce can cling. Arrange your pasta pot and finishing pan in the same way as before.

Cut 60g of guanciale into little sticks, drop them into the pan and put it on a medium heat, stirring occasionally. The fats should begin to clarify and render out. Once this happens, turn up the heat and stir obsessively. When the maximum amount of fat is rendered and the guanciale has crisped beautifully, lift it out with a slotted spoon and set aside.

Now make a cacio e pepe, exactly as you’ve practised. Because the pasta is dried, you’ll need to pull it three minutes short of the recommended time (and you should still make your life a little easier by adding a spoonful of semolina flour to the water).

Keep your eyes on the sauce texture as you finish the pasta. You obviously have a little longer this time, and as you feel you’re approaching the finish, add the bits of guanciale back in to heat through.

This might be the single pasta dish that’s provoked more violent debate than any other. So many bitter skirmishes in an unending war. Can you add onions? Is cream ever forgivable? Pancetta? Smoked or streaky bacon? All questions definitely worth arm wrestling over but, I dare to suggest, once you position carbonara within the framework of the emulsion sauces, all questions melt away. It’s perfectly simple.

Make your carbonara with either dried or fresh pasta: spaghetti, bucatini, tonnarelli or anything long and thin will work. Once again, go for bronze die if you can — but in a carbonara, the sauce is richer and stickier, so no need for ridged tubes.

Now you’re going to make a Gricia, just like you’ve practised. But before you start, add egg to your finely grated cheese. One egg and one yolk per person. Once again, render the guanciale, emulsify the fats with the pasta water. As you finish, put the guanciale back in, then take the pan off the heat and stir through your egg and cheese mixture.

As before, keep your eye on the sauce texture. If it thickens too much, add more pasta water; if you’re worried by runniness, you can slip it back on to a little low heat. Just don’t let the eggs scramble (I watched one chef rest her finishing pan on top of the steaming pasta pot, creating a rudimentary double-boiler. I nearly died of joy.)
All’Amatriciana’s place in the quartet is, at least theoretically, a carbonara with tomatoes replacing the eggs. In practice, the process is nearly reversed.

This time, you should choose a dried pasta. I find the sauce robust, and it feels like it overpowers the subtleties of fresh pasta. In fact — I know this is going to get me stabbed in the neck and dumped in the Tiber — I’m not particularly fussed what shape or type of pasta is used for this. Further, God forgive me, I believe we can stray here into parmesan cheese. Once you start messing with tomatoes, all bets are off.

After you’ve rendered your guanciale and put the meat aside, add half a can of San Marzano tomatoes to the hot fat and stew them down gently. In a restaurant set-up, you might well have prepared a large quantity of this in advance (though that’s not quite in the spirit of the thing, for me).
Lift out your pasta two minutes short of full-time and stir into the sauce. Add the cheese and mix it in, checking the texture regularly, adding pasta water to modify where necessary.

When you eat in Florence, the food celebrates the bucolic riches of the surrounding countryside. It’s about abundance and nature. In Venice, the food reflects the sea, from where wealth came, and the luxuries resulting from conquest and mercantilism. You’d expect the seat of the greatest empire to hark back to the grandeur of emperors, but Roman food is proudly about its poor, its working class, its literal plebs. Pasta is a cheap, manufactured carbohydrate. Small quantities of strongly flavoured trash meat and sparse gratings of redolent cheese are used to enhance. Instead of luxurious cream or butter to enrich, they emulsify the existing fats in water.
It’s almost impossible to think of dishes that make more out of less, or a method of cooking that’s more ingeniously evolved to create them quickly and inexpensively.
Recommended

In researching this piece, it seemed necessary to set up the full rig and cook all four dishes to hit the table at once. I positioned the pans, the pot, the ingredients, planned and drilled and finally, went for it — the process I’d watched a 60-year-old Italian in busted Crocs do, in a kitchen that looked like it had last been modernised when Il Duce tried to ban pasta.

I failed. Messily and spectacularly. Thank God no one was watching me and taking bloody notes. It must take a lifetime of practice to get this right, and none of us has the time. So, don’t try this at home.
Take the individual dishes in order, practise getting them right, then move on. You might never knock them out Roman style, but you’ll eat some terrific pasta as you try.

/content/cd3fcbff-8512-41cf-90eb-f87840c.title: Could AI revive the socialist dream?
articleContent: In all the speculation about what future artificial intelligence is about to usher in for us, everyone seems to agree on one thing. It is generally assumed that if AI will transform our economic system, it will do so in the form of more of the same — a more intense capitalism. Depending on your perspective, that is for better (higher productivity) or worse (more winner-takes-all exploitation), yet the debate is mostly about what sort of remedies, redistribution or regulation are needed in response.

But might all this be a failure of imagination? When we view the technological leaps we are living through in the light of the great century-old disagreement known as “the socialist calculation debate”, a profoundly different possibility suggests itself. If AI fulfils even a portion of the promises made for it, it might herald not a more intense version of the capitalism of the present but a “back to the future” trajectory: it could serve as the handmaid of the socialist planned economy that so many dreamt of in the 20th century but that was never remotely realistic — until now.

1989 marked the political victory of capitalism over socialism. But in technical and intellectual terms, the battle had been fought and concluded long before. The socialist calculation debate, largely forgotten today, raged most fiercely in the interwar years between the thinkers who understood most deeply how the economy functions. And it asked not which social system was more just, egalitarian or free. Rather, it took the more fundamental question to be which was most efficient: whether unrestrained markets or government fiat could most rationally allocate society’s economic resources.

Among the economists lined up on the pro-capitalist side of this debate were luminaries of the Austrian school, such as Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich von Hayek. Against them stood, most famously, Oskar Lange, a Polish economist and diplomat, and Abba Lerner, a brilliant if eccentric British-American economic theorist. The latter pair both argued that state planning could allocate resources as well as (if not better than) markets, and showed how this could be so within the framework of classical economics.
Imagine a super-AI armed with access to all the data we let our devices record . . . such technology would surely bury Hayek

From the late 1800s, theorists had elucidated how, through the mechanism of adjustable prices, free markets can converge on common prices and efficient, stable allocations of resources, pioneering the mathematical modelling of Adam Smith’s “invisible hand”. Pro-planning thinkers, however, used these theories to show how centralised agencies could mimic — and then improve on — the effects of markets. (One idea, for example, was to publish draft production plans and let managers of state-owned companies make bids for supplies and output amounts at centrally given prices — then adjust the plan until all the bids were compatible and matched the planners’ goals).

But to achieve this in practice, a central planner would need massive amounts of information from every little corner of the economy. That was the fundamental insight of Hayek’s 1945 article “The use of knowledge in society”, which set the tone for the half-century that followed. Hayek’s genius was to see market prices not merely as devices to balance supply and demand, but as carriers of information. The knowledge needed to allocate resources well — of who needs what and who can provide what on what conditions — is so local and dispersed that no central planner could ever hope to collect it. But, Hayek argued, the market price, in a single number, conveys just what is needed for local decisions that match the overall efficient market allocation. And this information, much of which just sits in people’s heads, simply does not exist in centralised, communicable form.

Until the end of the last century, this was a winning argument, underlined by the miserable failure of socialist regimes to provide for their populations’ material wellbeing. But if the free-market side won the socialist calculation debate in practice, the socialist side secured a toehold by showing how planning could succeed in theory. The Hayekian conclusion always remained contingent — and only true so long as governments lacked the necessary informational and computational capacity for central planning to outdo free markets.

The question is whether AI changes that. When I studied the socialist calculation debate in the 1990s, the joke was that communism had collapsed just as the computer revolution was making planned economies look less hopelessly unrealistic.

Consider the giant steps already taken in IT in recent decades. In Hayek’s time, information about local prices and quantities could only be collected by human workers armed with clipboards. Today, with so much commerce being done online, prices can be comprehensively “scraped” off the internet. One pioneer was the aptly named “billion prices project”, a Harvard-MIT research initiative launched in 2008 by economists Alberto Cavallo and Roberto Rigobon to collect real-time prices to improve on official statistics. The same goes for quantities: inventories, order books and sales volumes are all digitised and in principle accessible to a government planner.

Add the internet of things, and the amount of information gathered, processed and stored multiplies further. That might have, until recently, been unusable in raw form. But if there is one thing AI can clearly do, it is to organise unstructured information. The upshot is that the practical challenge of collecting, organising and processing data can no longer be seen as a remotely plausible constraint on the efficiency of a planned economy.

That is not all. AI offers the promise of transcending price information altogether by predicting who wants, needs or can produce what at what cost, better than market prices could ever summarise. Behavioural algorithms, notably in advertising, are already doing a decent job of this: we are familiar with the uncanny feeling when search engines and social media serve up an ad that seems just a little too on-the-nose. Judging by the advertising revenues of Big Tech, producers of all kinds of products think that ad-placing algorithms are worth the cost.
Price adjustments do not stabilise the macroeconomy; so we get business cycles, bubbles and busts
Imagine then a super-AI armed with access to all the data we let our devices record for every transaction we enter into, and much more besides. Such an AI would surely bury Hayek.

Indeed, a big motivation for the socialist calculation debate was that market prices get a lot of things wrong. People don’t always know enough to choose the best goods; they get addicted, defrauded or bankrupted. Consumption and production have spillover effects on third parties — “externalities” — that pricing decisions do not capture; so we get pollution, resource depletion and climate damage. Price adjustments do not stabilise the macroeconomy; so we get business cycles, bubbles and busts. These shortcomings of the price mechanism were easy to grasp in the wake of the Great Depression. The same realisation may be gaining strength again, given the disenchantment with capitalism expressed by so many young people in particular.

Against this background, it beggars belief that once a super-AI was asked to advise on the allocation of resources, it would merely follow the outcome of the highest bids in free markets, rather than calculate the most efficient allocations it could find by itself. Why on earth would AI agents abdicate from central planning?

This thought experiment raises more questions than it answers. It hardly proves that AI will bring about socialism. But it does show that AI removes one of the 20th century’s strongest — perhaps the strongest — argument against central planning. And it suggests that to the extent that both public and private sectors adopt AI to guide decision-making — how much to invest; in what; how best to tax for desired policy outcomes? — our economies will look increasingly planned and decreasingly market-shaped.

This raises some huge political questions. Would the current leaders of AI development — almost all hardcore libertarians — support capital allocations being decided by AI-powered planners rather than free financial markets, given how much the latter favour them? Conversely, might the general public, whose AI scepticism is currently rising, be won over by more “rational” economic decision-making that delivers more for them than our existing form of capitalism? Above all, would an economy where AI informs most decisions be able to overcome the conflicts of interest and co-ordination that have always held back productivity in our actually existing economy — all kinds of tragedies of the commons and prisoner’s dilemmas? (Consider, for example, whether a super-AI empowered to allocate resources would tolerate our very slow rate of decarbonisation.)

We don’t know, in other words, whether the superhuman capabilities of AI agents will break free of all-too-human constraints, incentives and interests. Readers will have to judge whether that is a source of disappointment — or relief.
Martin Sandbu is the FT’s European economics commentator

/content/37b1e640-6495-4574-96e3-4934915.title: This 300-year-old Andalusian farmhouse is a truly spiritual getaway
articleContent: Three years ago, Igor Ramírez García-Peralta came across La Sierrazuela – an atmospheric cortijo, built in 1750 as a retreat for Jesuit monks, outside the Andalusian town of Arcos de la Frontera. The sturdy two-storey farmhouse was listed on Idealista (one of Spain’s biggest property websites). It was painted an unappealing mustard yellow and decked out in dated fixtures and fittings, but surrounded by centennial olive groves, the vista beyond dotted with grazing horses and ancient wells. “I gave a great deal of thought to buying it, but had no idea what I was getting myself into,” he says. “I didn’t know that the house was going to become my identity.”

Ramírez García-Peralta trained as a lawyer, has worked as an actor in short films, historical dramas and close to 100 TV commercials, and is the author of two novels. As a contributing editor to HTSI, he has written about cycling around Patagonia and, closer to home, joining the Holy Week celebrations in Cádiz. He directs advertising campaigns for brands such as Tiffany & Co; competes in triathlons; and appeared on Spanish MasterChef earlier this year. He has lived in Spain, Mexico (his father is Spanish; his mother Mexican), Germany, Austria, Italy, the UK and the US. “I grew up very internationally. I went to a place with roots,” he says of his move from Ibiza to Andalusia.

When he opens his windows each morning, “the sun gives out this golden light and I feel embraced by nature”, he says. The grounds are laden with trees: mastic, lime, fig, cypress and palm. The previous owners, members of a mystical Sufi community, designed much of the garden’s current layout, including an inviting series of interconnected spaces and shaded areas around the house. Bougainvillea drapes over the door, dropping blooms that skitter in the wind. Scents of rosemary, lavender, jasmine and laurel fill the air from the main terrace, strung with lights in front of the whitewashed house.

Inside, Ramírez García-Peralta removed partitions to open up the space, preserving the brick steps that date to the 18th century, but also more recent additions, such as the terracotta floor tiles and an Islamic marble niche purchased by the previous owners in Morocco – a feature that is slowly being overtaken by ferns and trailing pothos. In terms of decoration, the intervention has been minimal: little more than a fresh coat of white paint to provide a backdrop for an eclectic mix of art and antiques.

Most of the furniture was acquired in estate sales: a woven damask sofa came from a palatial home in Jerez; a gilt mirror was salvaged from Seville’s Hotel Alfonso XIII. “I bought the dining table from a nearby cortijo and painted it red myself,” he recalls. A large flag hanging in the stairway once sailed with the Spanish navy, while a collection of deer antlers augments the archway into the kitchen; some were stalked by Ramírez García-Peralta in the forests of Chianti and Piedmont, others found at flea markets. In the lounge, one wall is covered with handpainted Andalusian ceramics, purchased at antiques shops and village fairs: “I never pay more than €20 for a plate. I’m not a purist. I like beauty and I like a bargain.”

Today, much of his time is spent working the land: growing and pressing olives, and caring for a growing menagerie of animals. A small flock of endangered Churra Lebrijana sheep – one of Iberia’s oldest breeds – help to prune the trees. Tailless Araucana chickens produce blue-shelled eggs while fluffy-legged Brahma deliver the more traditionally terracotta-coloured variety. A friendly gang of dogs and cats are quick to cover visitors in affection and hair.

Ramírez García-Peralta has also opened up his home for “private rentals and retreats with bespoke experiences”, offering three bedrooms in the main house, as well as a separate one-bedroom apartment with its own lounge – complete with a quirky little bar and a wall of his own brightly coloured paintings. Visitors can enjoy an array of cultural, sporting and dining experiences, from visits to wineries and fighting-bull breeders to horse-riding excursions.

During my stay, dinner by local cook Inmaculada Sañudo was served alfresco: farm-fresh salmorejo – Andalusia’s breadier version of gazpacho, topped with finely chopped jamón and a drizzle of La Sierrazuela olive oil – is followed by higado de cerdo (pork liver), and finished with sweet mulberries picked on the estate. It was accompanied by a full-bodied Arx wine from Tesalia, a local vineyard we visited the next day, where undulating vineyards lead to the Sierra de Grazalema. Founder and owner Richard Golding explains that these mountains are the rainiest spot in Spain. In February, heavy rains wreaked havoc in the area; Ramírez García-Peralta found himself digging out the mud-swamped streets of Arcos de la Frontera – an experience, he says, that cemented bonds with local residents. When we walk through the town, it’s impossible to go 10 paces without someone embracing him or clapping him on the back.

Parts of Arcos de la Frontera, perched atop a cliff, date back to the Roman Empire. Its original name of Arx-Arcis means “elevated fortress”. Under Muslim rule, the natural defensive point of “La Peña” (The Rock) was augmented with an alcazar; it’s now the site of Castillo Ducal de Arcos de la Frontera, home to the Marqués of Tamarón. The castle isn’t open to the public, but it is up for sale (at €7.9mn), looking out over pretty cobbled streets and whitewashed houses. During Holy Week, processions weave through the town, passing by Santa María de la Asunción on the main square. Inside, the perforated ceiling channels rays of light into the Gothic basilica to celestial effect.
Recommended

A sense of spirituality prevails at La Sierrazuela too. A crucifix of Christ is mounted above the doorway to a lounge space, while the cross of the Jesuits is worked into the retreat’s branded “S”. Being here encourages contemplation. After a brief siesta, I spend a few hours working on my novel, before venturing out to the pool. Silver reflections ripple over ripening pomegranates while the land shimmers in the distance. The sun sinks beneath the horizon and the transformative power that Ramírez García-Peralta has found here is palpable.
Private rental of the main house with bespoke experience, from €890pp for a three-night stay, based on double occupancy, and from €250 per night for the apartment; lasierrazuela.com

/content/1a5572de-649e-481b-bf19-8c84c3d.title: Ink vs inc: tattoos in the workplace
articleContent: There’s no risk of any international leader spotting Andy Burnham’s tattoo next time he’s at a global summit, but when he’s out jogging, the one-time Manchester mayor will proudly show off the bee tattoo on his inner right bicep. Burnham isn’t the first prime minister to sport ink but he’s certainly different in displaying it with such bravado; 1970s PM James Callaghan was tattooed during his naval service in the second world war but always covered his arms with long sleeves.

The new prime minister is one of the 26 per cent of British people YouGov reported as sporting a tattoo today — in America, according to Pew Research, the figure is one in three — so little wonder he’s unbothered baring his arms. His attitude underscores how mainstream the idea of body art has become in recent years.
Or has it? Is the professional world, whether a hospital, government department or corporate setting, truly open-minded about inking now?

Friday Jones runs the high-end tattoo parlour Studio Privé on New York’s Upper West Side and says that 90 per cent of her customers have corporate jobs of some kind. “I have a private chef and a DJ currently on roster, but the rest are strictly white-collar pros or retired from that.” As the daughter of a high-ranking Pentagon official whose first career was in corporate America, Jones has carved out a speciality in inking executives, especially women, many of whom hire her for their first design once well established in their fields. “When you get tattooed later in life, you have to expand your own confidence,” she says. “I understand the pressures — you’ve got to think about your future when you’re doing this.”
So how do you square a corporate career with a love for tattooing? We asked four people to share their own first-hand experience of ink vs inc.
Occupation: board-certified plastic and reconstructive surgeon

“Everything is saturated,” says John Brosious, when asked to quantify his tattoos. “Feet, toes, even my armpits — I have Venus flytraps there so when I open my arm up, the little hairs are like whiskers.” He even celebrated the first anniversary of opening his own medical practice, on April 1 2023, with his first face tattoo. “Everyone thought it was an April Fool’s, but then it was still there on April 2.”

He got his first tattoo — a cross on his shoulder, aged 18 — “on a whim” and had to borrow the $180 it cost from the roommate who accompanied him to the parlour. Brosious dabbled in other designs over the next few years. “They were hidden under my scrubs, and no one would ever know I had them on my rotations. The professors grading you were still very old school, and it would have been harmful to my career,” he admits.

It was kismet that he landed a residency in Las Vegas, a place far more permissive and liberal than his own, Pennsylvanian, background. So many people, patients and otherwise, whom he encountered were openly tattooed; it unleashed his urge to ink himself further, but he still made sure he could conceal them if needed. It was a smart move, as his first job after completing school was back in Pittsburgh. “One of the partners did say to me, if they had known when I interviewed that I had a full sleeve, they probably wouldn’t have taken me on. It was still pretty taboo in the field.”

Brosious was soon back in Las Vegas, although as an assistant professor at Nevada university, where he established the gender confirmation clinic as a world-class surgeon in that field. The plastic surgeon considers his tattoos an advantage, helping him find like-minded patients who see his alternative appearance as a marker of his talent. “If I’m able to pull off looking like this, then I must be comfortable in my skills. My patients have been judged every day on their appearance. They’re nonconformists in society, and look at me, and we’re in parallel.”
Occupation: founder of Aaroh Group

Veronica Kohlbecker’s four tattoos are unusual: they’re designed using white or UV-reactive ink. “I fell in love with white tattoos because they were discreet. None of them are completely hidden, but they don’t fall into your face straight away,” she explains. Her designs include an I Ching-inspired tattoo on her lower left arm, from elbow to wrist, and a smaller crow on her neck. She also has a UV-ink tattoo across her back, which will fade in a few years, plus a Balkan cross on her ankle, marking where she was once bitten by a deadly spider.

Kohlbecker prefers these subtle inkings in part because her work takes her around the world from Rwanda to Saudi Arabia; she works on destination development and architectural design. “I did think about being careful, and my tattoos are not there to offend,” she says, noting that she’s never felt the need to conceal them. “It was a big surprise to me how they were greeted with so much positive attention.”

The bigger issue, she admits, was from her family; Kohlbecker was born in what was then the USSR. “My entire family, they’re all doctors and they believed this isn’t a positive thing to put on your body, and in a lot of eastern European countries and the Middle East, people are still quite surprised [by my tattoos]. Everyone does cover them up. But that’s the nice thing with white tattoos because they lead to so many conversations,” she explains of their impact on her professional life. “Every single person asks: what are the lines on your arm?”
Occupation: divorce lawyer
It was a glimpse of what looked like a black felt-tipped pen at James Sexton’s wrist that prompted an older female colleague to smile sympathetically and ask, “Did one of your kids draw on your arm?”

“For the first 15 years of my career, no one knew I had tattoos,” says Sexton. “I would buy a 17.5in rather than 17in shirt so my cuffs were longer, an extra edge so my sleeves [of tattoos] wouldn’t stick out.”

He changed his mind after a photo shoot for a magazine about a decade ago, when the photographer cajoled him into rolling up his shirt sleeves. Sexton’s body art includes a full back piece, two sleeves (“skulls, in black and grey so I look like a serial killer in anything short-sleeved”) plus scattered designs on his stomach, legs, feet and chest.

Sexton’s interest is in parallel to his passion for martial arts. “I’ve always subscribed to the idea: civilise the mind, make savage the body,” he says, adding that every one of his designs has been carefully considered since he started inking as soon as he turned 18. “I was raised very Catholic and then left the faith, so all my tattoos have some spiritual purpose.”

They’re now synonymous with his professional persona. “I have a tenacious courtroom style, and the tattoos are part of it.” He relishes the clash between his swaggering body art and those custom suits. “It’s a Clark Kent-Superman thing — I still look very professional. Part of me is bound by the rules, part of me is a wild card,” he explains. Sexton still recalls the startled look from a “strait-laced” judge whom he chanced on in the locker room of their shared gym; he walked up next to him to say hello. “And he said ‘Oh my god. I would never have imagined you had tattoos.”
Occupation: semi-retired, founded and formerly ran pharma industry research company The Conference Forum

“I think if you speak with people with respect and maturity, and know your industry and to whom you’re speaking, they’ll see your tattoo for about two seconds and then they’re not going to see it anymore,” says entrepreneur Meredith Barbanell Sands. During the past 20 years, she’s slowly increased her assortment of body art to include sleeves on both arms and seven other standalone tattoos, including a heart on her face, picked out in white ink. “I think that was me saying ‘I’m gonna be who I am and not let anybody say you can’t do that’,” she recalls. “But you can’t really see it anymore.”

Barbanell Sands grew up in New York when tattooing was illegal — banned in 1961 to help reduce the spread of hepatitis, it remained outlawed until 1997 due to the Aids crisis. However, she had always wanted a tattoo, and waited until her 40th birthday to get her first one, a small butterfly on her ankle. Barbanell Sands was raised Jewish, which also caused her to hesitate. “My mother had died a year earlier, but my father was still around and he was the most upset of anybody. He thought it was a desecration of my body. But you get addicted.”

During the next few years, she sporadically added to her inking, on a scale of one to 10 from liberal to conservative, the sector “hovers around a seven”, she says. Barbanell Sands knows that some executives might silently judge her but there’s a bonding aspect to tattoos that has helped her with younger clients. Take the time she walked into an exhibit hall during one of the shows she’s organised, inked arms on display. A younger man stopped her, admired them, and then pulled up his own sleeve to compare designs. It quickly morphed into a conversation where he told her he was looking to spend more money with her company. “You have this bonding experience in a corporate setting: it’s like being rebels together, in a little club.”

/content/8f6f99ef-c859-4cdc-ad9c-6b06414.title: Is Star Wars Zero Company a new hope for strategy games?
articleContent: Just before your first mission in Star Wars Zero Company, you see the world from space: an epic fight between fleets of unidentified cruisers and destroyers, laser cannons firing, hulls disintegrating, explosions ballooning. As you zoom in on the desert planet of Serolonis, smaller ships skim the surface, blaster fire trailing after them. And then, even further in, there’s you: a band of just three troops, pinned down in a dusty courtyard, fighting your own little fight against an army of battle droids.

It’s a long way from the first Star Wars movie — Bit Reactor’s new game is set about 20 years before the events of the 1977 film and tens of thousands of light-years from Luke Skywalker’s home planet of Tatooine. But Star Wars has always been about the triumph of the individual in the face of overwhelming odds, and Zero Company is no exception. In this turn-based tactics (TBT) game, it’s you and your tiny force picking your battles, trying to outwit and outfight a foe vastly superior in numbers.

Your fight isn’t with the Empire, which doesn’t even officially exist yet. The gang of mercenaries you’re in charge of, known as Zero Company, is out to make a quick buck, stealing or shooting whatever it can to pay off its substantial debts to the miserly, oversized slug Gorga the Hutt (nephew of the infamous Jabba). And if that means taking on the diseased paramilitary cult the Infinite Coil, a group hell-bent on spreading its plague across the Republic, so be it.

As both an addition to the Star Wars universe and an entry in the genre of TBT games, Zero Company has its work cut out. In the former category, there hasn’t been a great deal to celebrate since the beloved Knights of the Old Republic games in the early 2000s (perhaps with the exception of 2023’s Jedi: Survivor). In the latter, it means going into direct competition with a TBT franchise so cult that it makes the Infinite Coil look like a parish council.

Few games define their genres quite the way that 2012’s XCOM: Enemy Unknown and its 2016 sequel XCOM 2 do. These games take on the timeworn tale of human resistance in the face of an alien invasion of Earth, but apply such a compelling David-and-Goliath gameplay loop that no new release can escape comparison with them.

Like Zero Company, the XCOM titles are games of two halves — strategy and combat: hours and days pass quickly in the organisation’s bases, where you must manage the research and engineering projects that determine your personnel and equipment. Much more staccato are the turn-based missions in which these are put to use fighting the invading aliens.

In these, there is no time limit on each turn. You are free to overthink your approach (unlike real-time strategy games, where you and your opponents must make moves contemporaneously). On harder difficulty levels in particular, where soldiers take longer to replace, perfection is XCOM’s aim: not just avoiding a single loss in combat, but not sustaining a single attack from your AI opponents.

Either you will, though, or your own attacks will fall flat. “That’s XCOM, baby!” is the common refrain among fans to describe the feeling of being roundly screwed over by the gods of random number generation. TBT games are nothing if not an exercise in probability: whether you successfully execute an attack or not tends to be based on a percentage, and you will quickly learn not to be surprised that an 80 per cent chance to hit does indeed mean you’ll miss one in five attempts.

That’s part of the fun, however, because these games thrive on the feeling of responsibility you develop for the people under your control — people you might have unwisely named after your own friends and family.

“The XCOM games give you randomly generated soldiers, let you name them, dress them up, equip them and develop them over dozens of hours,” says Tactical Breach Wizards developer Tom Francis. “You’re so proud of your babies when they ace a tricky mission, and so aghast when an alien psychic mind-controls one of your babies to throw a grenade at the other three.”

Tactical Breach Wizards (2024) follows a team of sorcerers attempting to bring down a private military-contractor-backed conspiracy, and is one of the most critically acclaimed iterations of the turn-based form in recent years. It owes much of its success to clever writing and an easy-to-pick-up but hard-to-master approach.

“Turn-based games are good at allowing you to pull off clever gambits, but they’re so unforgiving that most players get scared into playing it safe,” says Francis. “We let you rewind your turn as many times as you like, trying any crazy plan you want and seeing exactly how it will work out.”

There have been other attempts to replicate the XCOM magic: 2020 brought a pared-back spin-off called XCOM: Chimera Squad, the same year that the Gears of War franchise branched out from its usual third-person perspective with its prequel, Gears Tactics. There was also Phoenix Point, a kind of spiritual successor to XCOM designed by the franchise’s original creator, Julian Gollop. None of them quite scratched the itch, though.

Star Wars Zero Company has a few tricks up its sleeve: third-person platforming segments that let you explore the world in real time; text-based dilemmas that force you to think beyond the next fight; the benefit of a narrative and setting five decades in the making. But the real test lies in its longevity — whether there’s enough replayability to keep you coming back for multiple playthroughs. If not, you’ll find me playing XCOM 2 — and wondering why I named one of my soldiers after my brother.
‘Star Wars Zero Company’ is available on PC, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S from August 27
