/content/69452aea-cee0-47de-be8a-dc790fe.title: Warsh puts Fed on collision course with Trump ahead of midterms
articleContent: Kevin Warsh may be about to hand Donald Trump just the thing he does not want: an interest rate rise weeks before November’s crucial midterm elections.
For years, Trump piled pressure on Warsh’s predecessor as Federal Reserve chair, Jay Powell, to lower rates. Since he appointed Warsh earlier this year, the US president has renewed his calls.

But Warsh made it clear in his speech at the Jackson Hole gathering of economists and central bankers on Friday that “concerning” inflation numbers mean “the Fed’s predominant focus right now should be on prices”.
Any rate rise would put Warsh squarely in Trump’s crosshairs, analysts said.

“Warsh has drawn a clear and vivid line in the sand about his goals and intentions, which will put him directly at odds with Trump’s push for lower rates no matter the data or consequences,” said Eswar Prasad, professor at Cornell University, adding that the Fed chair had “made it abundantly and emphatically clear that he intends to put the Fed’s price stability mandate front and centre”.

Warsh faced a dilemma ahead of his first major speech as Federal Reserve chair: assure his critics on Wall Street and within the US central bank that he is serious about bringing inflation under control — or appease Trump and do little to convince markets that interest rate rises are coming.

His address at Jackson Hole made it clear that he had chosen the first course. He prioritised the demands of markets and his fellow rate-setters, both camps that have criticised him in recent weeks for his failure to spell out how he plans to tackle inflation, which has now exceeded the Fed’s 2 per cent goal for more than five years.
“There was a very strong appetite from investors . . . for him to deliver upon the basic principles of central banking,” said Gregory Daco, economist at EY Parthenon. “And that’s what he did.”

In a taste of what was to come, Warsh began the address at the Kansas City Fed’s symposium with a reference to the “hikes” he had taken at the mountain resort with former Fed vice-chair Don Kohn and Ben Bernanke, his boss during his first stint at the US central bank.

After digesting the whole speech, markets ratcheted up their bets on rate rises, with investors now viewing a quarter-point rise in September as likelier than not after the Fed chair warned there was “work to do” if price rises across the world’s biggest economy did not ease soon.
Warsh’s remarks did what he had set out to do, winning praise from analysts and a strong round of applause from those in the room.
But the prospect of rate rises as soon as September may not be greeted as favourably by a president who has spent much of his second term in the White House calling for aggressive cuts.

Powell fell out of favour with Trump soon after his own tenure started in 2018 over the issue of rate cuts. The relationship reached its nadir after the Department of Justice launched a criminal investigation into the then-Fed chair over his handling of a refurbishment of the central bank’s headquarters.
The investigation has since been dropped. But the Trump administration continues to pursue Fed governor Lisa Cook, calling for her to be fired over allegations of mortgage fraud, which she denies.
Just last week Trump said US borrowing costs — at 3.5-3.75 per cent — were “ridiculous”.
Warsh on Friday dismissed that argument, saying that “on balance, I would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive”.
He also made clear that he was far more concerned about bringing inflation under control than juicing growth in an economy that he said “appears to have strengthened”.

Warsh cited a measure of six-month inflation, which has soared on the back of Trump’s Iran war and voiced fears that, while expectations of future inflation were still well anchored, this could quickly change if the Fed fails to get on top of price pressures.
There is already support among some policymakers for an increase. At the Fed’s July vote, three of the 12 voters on the FOMC backed a quarter-point rate rise.

Warsh supported a hold at that meeting but Robert Sockin, chief US economist at PGIM, said his Jackson Hole speech placed the Fed chair firmly in the hawks’ camp. “[It] reaffirms our view that Warsh is the most hawkish member on the FOMC or, at a minimum, tied for that ranking,” Sockin said.
There was another notable shift evident in Warsh’s remarks on Friday.
After he stepped down as a Fed governor in 2011, he launched frequent attacks on the US central bank which at the time left many of those who were in the crowd at Friday’s symposium disgruntled.

At Jackson Hole he sought to mend bridges with the senior central bankers and economists in the room, saying that it was “a credit to the Fed as an institution — and consistent with the best of the Fed’s traditions — that market prices show confidence that we will deliver price stability”.
“I can assure you, they’re right,” he added.

Some think Warsh, who has closer personal ties with Trump than Powell, will be able to handle any fallout from the White House. Trump has already sought to play down any future rate rises as the result not of the views of the man he picked for the job in January, but a “political” FOMC.
“The administration has framed Warsh’s chairmanship within the context of a potentially hostile FOMC. And that framing gives a little bit more leeway to the chair,” Daco said.
And some think Warsh left enough ambiguity in his remarks that any rise in interest rates — and subsequent ire from the White House — is far from certain.
“He left a lot of room. There’s more data to come,” said Bill English, a professor at Yale.

“I presume [Warsh] intended to send a hawkish signal,” said David Wessel, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution think-tank. “Declaring independence from Trump, though, means raising rates, not just talking tough.”

Your body is not a machine
articleContent: The writer is a systems engineer and author of ‘Wicked Problems: How to Engineer a Better World’

In a hot room, I balance on one foot, lifting the other high on to my opposite thigh, palms pressed together at my chest. Sweat stings my eyes as I lower into a toe stand, caught between faking it and maybe making it.

In corpse pose next, I relax my limbs across the mat and gently stare at the ceiling. “Optimise your breathing,” the instructor says. The word lands like an intruder in a practice far older than our machine metaphors for the body. In stillness, my mind wanders to the work of English physician William Harvey.

Harvey studied medicine when Galen’s ideas still dominated, as they had for 14 centuries. People believed the liver made blood and that arteries carried life-giving “vital spirit”. After years of animal vivisection and human dissection, Harvey published De Motu Cordis in 1628. Blood, he claimed, flowed in a loop, propelled by the heart, which was like a pump.

Harvey still thought in Aristotelian terms, asking what purpose each organ served. His account of circulation, however, gave force to a new mechanical view of the body, like the mechanical clock that was once seen as the model for an orderly universe. And us.

In the 1630s, René Descartes viewed animal bodies as automata. Then, in 1687, Isaac Newton’s Principia described a universe governed by mathematical laws, inviting the idea that it also ran through bones and ligaments. Sixty years later, French physician and philosopher Julien Offray de La Mettrie, sick and on opium, anonymously published L’Homme Machine. Thought and feeling were only matter, he insisted, requiring no soul. Cut a heart open and you see only nerves and valves and nothing of a lifetime of passion and pain.
Taking living things apart has given us vast knowledge. But because such reductionism works profitably, we tend to miss its limits.

In 1911 Frederick Winslow Taylor timed factory workers’ movements with a stopwatch and codified “scientific management” in pursuit of ever-greater productivity. The drive to optimise gradually spread from factory floors into sport, sleep, diet, the gym and the cues of a westernised yoga class.
We invent machine metaphors to understand the body but then start living as if those metaphors were true.

The Yoga Sutras, a collection of aphorisms attributed to the Indian sage Patanjali and widely considered foundational to classical yoga, draw heavily on Samkhya, an ancient Hindu philosophical system. It resists reducing the person to physical processes by distinguishing prakṛti, material nature, including body and mind, from puruṣa, pure consciousness, to free the witness from the witnessed, prizing clarity over accomplishment.

When mending a blocked artery or replacing a worn-out hip, picturing the body as a machine can be useful. Yet as a guiding metaphor, it leads us off course. Randolph Nesse, a pioneer in evolutionary medicine, calls this mistake “tacit creationism”.

We talk and think as if our bodies were engineered from precise parts and partitions when in reality, our bodies depend on complex networks and co-ordination. Gut microbes, for instance, communicate with the nervous and immune systems, but chronic stress can upset both the microbiome and the signals they give out. Inflammation that ought to subside once the threat has passed can instead persist or become dysregulated.
While products can be machined to tight tolerances, natural selection can work only with what it inherits. Bodies make passable compromises across generations, even if they result in oddities.

Take the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. A remnant of our aquatic ancestors, it drops into the chest and hooks under the aortic arch before climbing back to the larynx. Then there is the eye. Light must pass through retinal tissue before reaching the eye’s photoreceptors. Where the optic nerve exits the retina, there are no photoreceptors, leaving a blind spot. Unlike the eye, a modern car partly compensates for a limited field of view with mirrors and sensors. Childbirth is a struggle because a baby’s wide skull and shoulders must pass through a narrow birth canal. Which engineer would approve such designs?

On the yoga mat, the idea of the body as a machine shadows over me. Back in corpse pose, my breath ebbs and flows. The metaphor that once described the body now dictates how we imagine and inhabit it. “Let it go,” the instructor murmurs.

/content/c1c79d47-31c0-4e4e-85b6-57527e3.title: Alex Gerko earned a record £895mn from trading firm XTX in 2025
articleContent: British billionaire Alex Gerko made a record £895mn from the profits of XTX Markets last year, boosting his position as one of the UK’s richest people as his trading group continues to grow.

A pot of £1.7bn from the company’s 2025 trading profits was shared between Gerko and his quantitative traders and top tech developers, Companies House filings show. The 23 other people took home £833mn between them, an average of £36.2mn each.
Gerko’s payout is a 31 per cent increase from the year before, when he earned £683mn, and it marks another record for one of the UK’s richest people and his top team.
XTX Markets declined to comment.

XTX makes money by using vast amounts of computing power and AI processing to identify tiny margins on millions of trades. Gerko founded the London-based firm in 2015 and it has grown into one of the world’s biggest market makers, trading stocks, bonds, commodities and other assets.

Its revenues increased 44 per cent last year to £3.9bn, up from £2.7bn the year before, boosted by turbulent markets. It is building a vast data centre in Finland to manage its growing need for computing power.

The Russia-born mathematician is one of the UK’s biggest taxpayers, according to Sunday Times estimates, and in 2024 set up a family office to manage his growing wealth, named Cromulon Capital after a planet in the sci-fi show Rick and Morty that is shaped like a human head.
In June, he lost a long-running legal battle over £22.5mn-worth of tax on profits that he and other traders made when he worked at hedge fund GSA Capital, before he spun out XTX.
Gerko and his wife have set up a new maths-focused secondary school in north London, which will open in September.
The billionaire and his firm have backed AI start-ups including Anthropic and autonomous vehicle company Wayve.
XTX handles about $250bn-worth of trades a day and employs about 250 people, making it much smaller than its rivals such as Jane Street and Citadel Securities.

/content/25f48fea-ada2-41e1-ba33-07a864a.title: ‘New York loves Canada’: US cities want their Canadian tourists back
articleContent: On one of the most tense weekends in recent US-Canada relations, Rebecca Shapiro felt lucky to have a Canadian passport.

The 33-year-old was on holiday in New York as trade talks between the two countries’ leaders broke down in acrimony, and saved hundreds of dollars on several of the city’s attractions thanks to a marketing promotion that is trying to lure disenchanted Canadians back to the city.
Rattled by the Trump administration’s hostility towards Canada, Shapiro’s sister in Montreal said she would not visit the US. “But I don’t believe in withholding my tourism dollars,” she said.

After a breakdown in relations between the normally close allies that started when Donald Trump returned to office last year and reached a new low this week when he renamed Lake Ontario “Lake America”, US cities and regions have launched a charm offensive to their northern neighbours, scrambling to counter their president’s belligerent rhetoric.

Canadians have borne the brunt of the US administration’s rhetoric for months. Trump has repeatedly threatened to annex Canada as the 51st US state and his administration has upended trade by imposing tariffs on steel and automobiles, with Ottawa in turn promising retaliatory duties.
But in New York, where people know how to hustle for a dollar — or a loonie — the vibe is different.
For three weeks this summer, selected businesses have offered steep discounts on hotels, flights, restaurants and attractions under the “Northern Neighbour Deal”.
They’ve also tried to show their appreciation in other ways. On Canada Day, July 1, landmarks such as the Empire State Building were lit up in red and white to honour the country’s national colours.
New York State’s official tourism website proclaims: “New York loves Canada. We’re lucky to have neighbours like you!”
The charm offensive is not limited to the Big Apple. In Las Vegas, hotels are offering Canadians “Vegas at Par”, a favourable 1:1 exchange rate.

Meanwhile, a ski resort in Vermont on Wednesday addressed Canadians in an open letter. Steve Wright, general manager of Jay Peak Resort, who testified to Congress on the impact of Trump’s tariffs last year, said he understands why Canadians might not want to travel to the US at the moment.

“While we’re not particularly interested in telling anyone what to think about tariffs, trade policy or politics, we do have an opinion about anything that makes good neighbors feel farther apart,” he wrote. “We don’t like it.”
Their efforts were not helped by Trump declaring on Truth Social last week: “WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!”
Tourism operators across the country are not so sure.

Over the past year, the number of Canadians visiting the US has dropped 25 per cent compared with 2024, while the number of US visitors to Canada has gone up. Canadians spent C$3.3bn less in 2025 than the previous year on travel to the US according to the Canadian government.

Varun Deedwaniya, co-founder of Viral Food Tours in New York City, who took Shapiro and her family on a culinary tour, said that 30 to 40 per cent of his clients used to be Canadians. “Recently it’s been closer to 10,” he added.

With the border only a six-hour drive from New York, Canadians have traditionally been the city’s second-largest visitor group after visitors from the United Kingdom. Canadian tourists spent more than $1bn in 2024 according to the New York City Mayor’s office.

Canadian travel to the US had started to recover from its 2025 low in the second quarter of this year, but recent tensions have reignited the “Elbows Up” movement (a national rallying cry and nod to Canada’s national sport ice hockey) that is calling for a boycott of US products and travel.

Julie Coker, CEO of NYC Tourism + Conventions, the organisation promoting discounts for Canadian travellers, is trying to remain upbeat. “There are ebbs and flows in our political relationship,” she said. “We are here when visitors are ready to return as before.”
But businesses are paying the price of the cross-border tensions.
Mark Bello, owner of Pizza School NYC, says he has had just one booking so far through the Northern Neighbor Deal promotion. He said he is offering the discount because he supports its spirit.
“We love Canadians and we’re really hoping to welcome them back,” he said.
On the other side of the border, however, the mood is defiant.

Jared Purdy, a professor at a Toronto community college, has been boycotting the US as a travel destination ever since Trump took office in 2016. The 66-year-old said he returns products to the shelf at the grocery store if they are made in America.
He is not planning to drop his boycott any time soon.
“You want our money, but what are you doing to change what you and your electorate have caused us and the whole world?” he said. “Fix your mess first and then we talk.”
Data visualisation by Michael Taffe

/content/c4c13303-bc80-41de-81fc-65e9a70.title: EU to help tourism hotspots crack down on Airbnb-style holiday rentals
articleContent: The European Commission is readying new legislation to help member states plagued by housing shortages crack down on holiday rentals such as Airbnb.
Short-term lets have become a legal battleground between tourism operators and local administrations seeking to reduce housing pressures, often dragging on for years and with uncertain outcomes.

The upcoming EU law, dubbed the Affordable Housing Act, will set out criteria that cities and regions can use to apply proportionate measures to relieve those pressures, according to people briefed on the discussions.

While short-term rentals only represent 1.2 per cent of total homes across the EU, in some tourist hotspots such as Sorrento in Italy, Dubrovnik in Croatia and Fuerteventura in the Canary Islands, holiday lets can account for as much as 20 per cent of the total housing stock, according to the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre (JRC).
Local authorities claim holiday lets aggravate housing shortages and push up prices for local people, although rental platforms dispute this.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Cities including Amsterdam, Berlin, Brussels, Florence and Paris have responded in recent years by imposing restrictions ranging from limiting the number of tourist lets through a licensing system, to capping the number of nights that any given apartment can be rented out for. Barcelona is aiming to phase out apartment rentals to tourists completely by 2028.
But many measures have been subject to legal action from landlords and tourism operators who argue that they infringe on the freedom to provide services protected under EU law.
“Whatever we do [to curb holiday rentals], an appeal comes,” said Jacopo Vicini, a councillor responsible for tourism in Florence.

The Italian city last year created a licensing system for short-term rentals and placed a moratorium on any new listings in its historic centre but faced a dozen appeals from homeowners and tourism operators. Tuscany’s regional tribunal ruled in favour of Florence’s city council but it is only the first level of judicial review, leaving the city open to more lawsuits. The city has since expanded the moratorium to 44 per cent of its housing stock, and expects fresh legal challenges.

Court rulings across the bloc have been mixed or unclear. In a landmark case in 2020, the EU’s top court upheld local schemes restricting short-term rentals on the grounds of housing shortages and provided that the measures are proportionate.
But what proportionate means is left open for litigation, leaving cities with “recognised competence [but] permanent insecurity”, said Lorène Derhy, a lawyer specialising in property law in France.

That can result in authorities being overly cautious. “Authorities that lack the legal resources to make an ambitious scheme safe hold themselves back. They adopt rules short of what the law would allow them, simply for fear of challenge,” Derhy added.

Vicini of Florence said it was “essential” that the EU “recognises the possibility” for local administrations to impose restrictions on short-term rentals, although he acknowledged that one cannot “make the same regulation for all cities because the cases are very different”.

Across the EU, house prices increased by almost two-thirds between 2015 and 2025, while rents rose by more than a fifth over the same period, according to Eurostat. House prices in many member states have risen faster than household income and priced younger generations out of the housing market.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The main reason is a lag in the supply of the housing stock, which has struggled to keep up with rising demand due to planning constraints, especially in densely populated urban areas. But research by the JRC found a positive correlation between the prevalence of short-term lets and higher housing costs, although the link is stronger for selling prices than for rents over the long-term.
However, platforms such as Airbnb dispute that short-term rentals are to blame for housing shortages and point to the economic boost from tourism.
George Mavros, head of EU government affairs at Airbnb, said “super stringent short-term rentals restrictions are very unlikely to move the needle on housing prices”.
He added: “On the other hand, it has an actual, very concrete economic impact in these cities.”

The European Holiday Home Association, a lobby group, said while short-term rentals “may play a role, there are significantly bigger problems”, pointing to a rate of 20 per cent empty homes on average across the EU.

/content/a1bfac83-5310-4fdb-bbc7-1efb983.title: Claridge’s operator bets on US and UK visitors to offset Middle East
articleContent:
The company behind ultra-luxury London hotel Claridge’s has adjusted its marketing to pull in more customers from the US and Europe as it grapples with a drop in big-spending guests from the Gulf.

Sales teams at Maybourne — which also operates the Connaught, Berkeley and Emory hotels in the UK capital — have “proactively pivoted” to other regions to offset lower bookings from the Middle East since the start of the Iran war in February, said chief executive Marc Socker.

Socker’s comments come as a drop in visitor numbers to the UK from the Middle East has left some of London’s priciest hotels struggling to sell their most expensive rooms, threatening the momentum of a segment that defied a slowdown in the broader luxury sector last year.

VisitBritain said bookings from the Middle East to the UK slumped to about half their “normal” levels in March, immediately after the US-Israel attack on Iran. In July, they were still “well behind” levels from the same month in 2025, the government-backed tourism agency said.

Socker told the FT the push to counter the slowdown from the Middle East included doubling down on the US — its largest source of guests — and winning customers in other markets by emphasising different aspects of its brand while expanding its network of international travel agents.

For US guests, Maybourne was prioritising “the tradition and the heritage” of its hotels in the UK, while seeking to meet domestic customers’ desire to “leave their everyday nonsense behind and get looked after and pampered”, he said.

Maybourne, ultimately owned by Qatari royals Sheikh Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber al-Thani and Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani, had “quite some exposure” to the Middle East, Socker said, without providing specific data.

But it had “luckily” been able to “replace that business with more business from the UK, the US and Europe”, enabling the company to increase revenue in the first half of 2026 compared to a year earlier, he said.

Maybourne this month appointed José Silva, a former chief executive of United Arab Emirates-based luxury hotel group Jumeirah Hotels & Resorts, owner of the Burj Al Arab, to chair its board as it embarks on major international expansion plans.

Socker said the group, which has properties in Beverly Hills and the French Riviera, was working to expand its sources of customers because being “reliant on any single source of business” was “a very dangerous game to play when the world is so volatile”.

The company intends to nearly triple the number of hotels to about 15 by 2035 and is planning to open its first site in Paris next year. It is also targeting properties in cities including New York, Bangkok, Singapore and Tokyo and resort destinations in the Indian Ocean and the Caribbean.
Recommended

Expansion within the UK, where Maybourne properties in Mayfair and Belgravia are facing rising competition amid a flurry of new five-star hotel openings in London, was “not a focus right now”, Socker said.

The Chancery Rosewood opened last year on the site of the former US embassy in Grosvenor Square. The new St Regis London and Waldorf Astoria Admiralty Arch are set to open in 2026.

The competition has put some properties under pressure, with The Stafford in St James’s, ultimately owned by Egypt’s El Sharkawy family, this month being served a winding-up petition by HM Revenue & Customs over unpaid debts.

The company said “the matter is currently being addressed through the appropriate channels.” In its latest accounts last May, The Stafford said London’s luxury hotel market was “increasingly competitive, with a significant expansion in room capacity.”

/content/2c65a745-8169-4192-971a-022bdfc.title: Pharma stocks soar as investors seek AI alternatives
articleContent: Pharmaceutical stocks have had a record year so far with drugmakers hitting fresh highs in August, as investors have sought to diversify away from AI and positive clinical trial data has boosted the sector.

Shares in drugmakers from Johnson & Johnson to Merck have significantly outperformed the market, with the S&P 500 Pharmaceutical index rising 18 per cent in the first eight months of the year. That compares with a 13 per cent rise in the wider S&P 500.
The industry has been on a bull run as a result of deals struck with the Trump administration to lower prices, as well as game-changing clinical trial data that has bolstered biotechs.

Biotech and pharma stocks have had an especially fruitful summer, with shares in the US index soaring 27 and 19 per cent respectively since May. The S&P 500 has risen only 7 per cent during that time.

Drugmakers are expected to receive a further boost on Monday, when Bayer, Takeda, CSL and several mid-size biotechs are expected to announce new pricing deals with the White House, according to two people familiar with the matter.

AstraZeneca, Novo Nordisk, Eli Lilly and other large pharmaceutical companies have already struck similar deals in which they agree to lower prices in exchange for relief from tariffs. Investors have pushed companies to make these deals to provide pricing certainty for drug sales and to stave off harsher pricing regulations.

The White House said details of the agreements “should be regarded as speculation” before they were officially announced, adding that the Trump administration had made progress on lowering drug prices. Bayer, Takeda and CSL declined to comment.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Pharma and biotech valuations were hurt last year after President Donald Trump threatened to force companies to reduce their US prices and potential tariffs threatened to upend the drugmaking industry.
“There were two big unknowns and it felt like most of 2025 was trying to figure out what that all meant,” said Emily Field, head of US biopharma equity research at Barclays.

But after Pfizer agreed a deal with the White House to lower US drug prices, and other large pharma groups followed with similar US-based manufacturing commitments in exchange for tariff exemptions, the industry has been on a bull run.

“You had a lot of concerns about the risks of price controls in the US, in particular, that has dramatically improved over time with the Trump administration,” said Rick Bradt, a portfolio manager at Neuberger’s growth strategies group in New York.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The deals have paved the way for pharma’s record run of dealmaking this year, with the number of biotechs acquired for at least $1bn reaching 37 by July, eclipsing last year’s 35, according to US investment firm Stifel.

There have been several megadeals this year, including AbbVie’s $10.9bn deal for Apogee Therapeutics, GSK’s $10.6bn purchase of Nuvalent and Eli Lilly spending $7bn on cancer biotech Kelonia Therapeutics and $7.8bn on Centessa.
Meanwhile, successful clinical trials have helped biotech stocks to rise 86 per cent in the past 12 months, making them the best-performing component of the US stock market during that period.

Cancer drugmaker Revolution Medicines stunned the market earlier this year when its drug daraxonrasib doubled the survival rate of patients living with advanced pancreatic cancer. The FDA approved the drug last week and Revolution’s share price is up by 168 per cent this year.

Shares in Moderna, which shot to prominence during the Covid-19 pandemic, are up by almost 400 per cent this year after the vaccine maker reported successful clinical trial results for a cancer therapy in development, rising 177 per cent in one day alone in August.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.
Pharma is also proving to be a shield for investors skittish about turbulence in America’s AI-heavy technology sector.

“It’s truly a combination of hunger to diversify beyond this one-way freight train of generative AI since 2024 driving it, as well as the increasing appeal of healthcare,” Bradt said. “We have increased our biotech and pharmaceutical exposure over the last several months.”

“It’s intuitive that pharma and biotech is going to be an AI winner,” Field from Barclays said. “You cannot displace what they do with AI. Whenever there’s freakouts in tech, pharma has always had a defensive halo around it.”

One London-based investor said the positivity surrounding the sector in the US had inflated share prices to the point they were now struggling to find good value for money. This could be good news for European pharma groups, especially “laggards” that are undervalued, such as French drugmaker Sanofi which replaced its chief executive this year following concerns over its pipeline.

“Pharma is getting expensive because of the broadening out of the market,” the investor said. “Now we’re looking out for the laggards . . . European pharma has room to run and there will be a point where they become attractive.”

/content/6fc083c6-1ab2-42e7-b9ff-a654061.title: The search for Air India crash answers
articleContent: Campaigners and groups representing families of the 260 people killed when an Air India plane crashed last year are challenging the theory that pilot action may be to blame as investigators prepare to release their final report into the tragedy.

The Boeing 787 Dreamliner went down in June last year after 32 seconds in the air despite good conditions that day in Ahmedabad, the capital of Gujarat. India’s Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) issued a preliminary report after a month, as required under international air safety agreements, with the full investigation taking more than 12 months.

The idea that a suicidal pilot deliberately starved the aircraft of fuel to crash it appears to have been triggered by the preliminary report’s finding that the fuel switches had “transitioned” from “RUN” to “cutoff” soon after take-off. However, the report also stated that the switches were later found in the debris in the RUN position.
Indian investigators have publicly committed to releasing a final definitive report on the crash by October.

Air safety campaigners and one Indian pilots’ union, along with lawyers for the victims, vociferously contend that a serious electrical failure on the aircraft could be to blame, rather than deliberate pilot action.

“We have been saying right from the word go that there are electrical problems in the aircraft which need to be investigated,” said C S Randhawa, president of the Federation of Indian Pilots and a former Air India pilot who previously worked for India’s civil aviation authority. He told the FT the investigators’ focus on fuel control switches was the “wrong direction” for the probe.

The fuel control switches on the 787 were supplied by US industrial group Honeywell, which, along with Boeing, is facing legal action from victims’ groups over the crash.

Even if an electrical failure is found to have contributed to the crash, “it still opens a whole host of questions”, said Jeff Guzzetti, a former lead accident investigator for the US National Transportation Safety Board and ex-director of the FAA Accident Investigation Division. “It could be a design issue, it could be a maintenance issue, an installation or a manufacturing issue — we just don’t know at this time,” he said.

Campaigners challenging the pilot suicide theory have focused on another aspect of the preliminary report, which found the plane’s emergency power device called the Ram Air Turbine had been deployed “during the initial climb immediately after lift-off”.
Ed Pierson, executive director of the Washington-based Foundation for Aviation Safety and a former manager at Boeing’s 737 factory, said the turbine indicated that “something was not right”.
He added: “The deployment of that device is really under emergency conditions when it detects loss of power or loss of hydraulics — the pilots can’t manually deploy it.”

Lawyers for the victims’ families have written to US Transportation secretary Sean Duffy seeking the results of tests carried out on a Boeing 787 simulator. They argue that the findings suggest the turbine on the Air India plane was deployed “many seconds” before the fuel supply cut out.

“The tests indicate that the [turbine] may be unrelated to fuel system changes and instead may be a symptom of faults occurring prior to any fuel disruption,” the letter from law firm Beasley Allen said.
John Cox, a veteran pilot and aviation safety consultant, cautioned that, while there were “notable questions in the preliminary report, it is not complete — nor should it be”.

He said that determining whether the fuel supply was cut before, or at the same time, that the fuel switches “transitioned” would indicate whether an aircraft fault or pilot action was responsible. Until this information was released, “everything is speculation”, Cox added.

Under international aviation treaty law, Boeing and Air India face restrictions on their ability to comment on matters relating to ongoing accident investigations. The AAIB, Boeing and Air India all declined to respond to detailed questions from the FT pending the final investigation report. Honeywell, a technical adviser to the investigation, also declined to comment.

Boeing said: “Our thoughts remain with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives on Flight 171, and with Air India and everyone affected by this tragedy.”

After suffering huge financial losses and extra regulatory scrutiny over two fatal crashes of the 737 Max jet in 2018-19, caused by flawed sensors and control systems, and a blowout on an Alaska Airlines flight in January 2024, Boeing cannot afford a problem with the Dreamliner — its flagship wide-body jet. The Ahmedabad disaster is the only fatal 787 crash among more than 1,200 aircraft delivered.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.
Air India, owned by India’s Tata conglomerate, is bleeding money as it struggles with issues including high fuel costs and route cancellations due to the Middle East conflict.

Air India, which is part-owned by Singapore Airlines, lost $2.8bn in its most recent financial year and Campbell Wilson resigned as chief executive in April. He will be replaced by Tewolde Gebremariam, who has turned Ethiopian Airlines into Africa’s largest and most profitable carrier.

A parliamentary committee flagged findings in March from a detailed audit of Air India conducted by India’s aviation regulator after the crash. It found about 100 safety lapses on the airline’s planes, including seven of the most serious Level 1 violations requiring immediate action. A Tata-led consortium also insured the aircraft.
Soon after the audit Air India said it acknowledged the findings and restated its commitment to safety and regulatory compliance.

The captain of the doomed plane was Sumeet Sabharwal, 56, who had more than 15,000 hours of flying experience — about half of them on the Dreamliner. He lived in Mumbai with his father Pushkar Raj Sabharwal, a former aviation safety official.

Sabharwal’s father has condemned AAIB investigators for visiting his home two months after the crash “under the pretext of offering condolences” and then insinuating that his son had deliberately moved the switches to cut fuel after take-off.

“Such speculative remarks, made outside the framework of an official report, are procedurally improper and professionally indefensible,” he wrote in an email last September to the pilots’ federation and seen by the FT.
Asked about Sabharwal’s allegations, the AAIB said the final crash report would be published when the investigation had been completed.

The FT has seen a string of 10 automated maintenance alerts sent by the aircraft to Boeing and Air India ground operations centres during its 32 seconds in the air. The pilots’ federation has asked investigators to direct Boeing to interpret the messages, which were first reported by Indian investigative magazine The Caravan.

The federation has also highlighted what it says is a US patent filing for the 787’s fuel control system showing that under certain circumstances the fuel supply to the engines can be automatically shut off without the pilots moving the cockpit switches.

When the aircraft was flying earlier that day from Delhi to Ahmedabad, passenger Akash Vatsa posted a video of what he said were numerous electrical problems with crew call lights, air conditioning and in-flight entertainment screens all out of order.
Vishwashkumar Rajesh, a Briton who was the crash’s sole survivor, has described how the plane’s lights apparently started flickering moments after take-off and recalled hearing a loud bang.
Pierson said: “If this thing was as simple as a pilot issue, they’ve had a year. They should have been able to easily say ‘here’s our evidence’.”
He added: “Our belief is that the plane took off, [then] they had some massive electrical impact.”
Recommended
Whether the AAIB’s findings will satisfy campaigners and the passengers’ families, as well as Boeing and Air India, is impossible to predict.

Investigators may find that deliberate pilot action was to blame. Such an event is not without precedent: in 2015 co-pilot Andreas Lubitz, who had a history of depression, flew a Germanwings plane into the French Alps, killing 150 people.

Randhawa, the pilots’ federation president, trained Sabharwal and knew him personally and professionally and insists: “I am convinced 101 per cent it was electrical failure.”
Additional reporting by Christian Davies in New York

/content/5579f0e8-c19c-46ad-8272-f7678bf.title: CEO of India’s largest private bank to step down
articleContent: HDFC Bank has announced that its chief executive will not seek another term, just months after a rivalry at India’s largest private sector lender resulted in the departure of its chair.

Sashidhar Jagdishan, who has been the bank’s chief since 2020, will not seek a third term, HDFC Bank said in an unexpected exchange filing in Mumbai late on Saturday. He will retire from the bank on October 26.
“Despite persuasion, Mr Jagdishan reiterated his decision not to seek reappointment,” HDFC said.
Jagdishan’s exit comes less than six months after the abrupt resignation of the bank’s chair Atanu Chakraborty, who alluded to “ethical differences” between him and the lender.
The bank, with a market capitalisation of $116bn, will embark on a search for a new chief executive at a time when its shares have also come under pressure, shedding 27 per cent this year.
Jagdishan’s departure marked the second high-profile exit from the top echelons of India’s corporate world announced in recent weeks.

Earlier this month, Tata Sons chair N Chandrasekaran said he would not seek reappointment in February, the culmination of a bitter year-long feud with Noel Tata, the chair of the charitable trusts that control the $280bn conglomerate.

The shake-up of HDFC Bank’s leadership comes as the lender is still adapting to a $40bn merger in 2023 with its parent company, mortgage giant Housing Development Financing Corp. The merger was hailed at the time as one of the largest in the history of corporate India, creating a financial services behemoth with an asset base of $340bn.

While observers have raised concerns about compliance and governance issues at the bank in the past, bankers and shareholders consulted at the time of Chakraborty’s departure said the crux of the issue was a clash of strategy, personality and leadership style with Jagdishan.
Recommended

Tensions came to a head over Jagdishan’s reappointment for a third term, which required regulatory approval. Several people with knowledge of the matter said at the time that Chakraborty, who had been non-executive chair of HDFC Bank since 2021, was opposed to extending Jagdishan’s tenure.
That put him in conflict with most of the board, which backed the 61-year-old CEO who had risen through the ranks at HDFC.

HDFC has also suffered recent regulatory setbacks. Last year, Dubai’s Financial Services Authority restricted a branch of the bank from taking new clients, citing procedural deficiencies stemming from the mis-selling of Credit Suisse AT1 bonds.

/content/38abcff2-241c-4bc1-83a1-8cc135d.title: The companies desperate to hire graduates
articleContent: Like a lot of clean energy start-ups, heat pump installer Heat Geek is growing fast and hiring to match.

The eight roles it opened this summer will increase headcount by more than 25 per cent. Chief operating officer Holly Foster says the entry-level positions in operations, engineering and marketing need to be “filled yesterday” with ambitious graduates ready to get stuck in.

But there is a problem: these hungry young hires are nowhere to be seen. “We’re not doing a good job at finding where these super-grads are,” Foster says. “We know exactly what we want. The struggle is communicating that . . . what we’re looking for is difficult to spot on paper.”

As economic stagnation, the advent of AI and geopolitical upheaval sow uncertainty in UK hiring and threaten entry-level roles, such difficulty in finding good people to work sounds implausible. This month’s Office for National Statistics figures show vacancies have continued to fall over the summer, with smaller businesses and jobs in sectors favoured by younger workers bearing the brunt. Competition for graduate positions recently hit an all-time high of 140 applications per role, as open posts dropped by 8 per cent, according to the Institute of Student Employers.

But as many university leavers struggle with rejections and multinational employers drown in applications, some companies have the opposite complaint. In a June survey by sector body Universities UK, half the employers with open vacancies said graduate posts were tough to fill — the highest of any level. For start-ups, companies in little-known or unglamorous sectors, or smaller businesses, finding skilled, proactive and available graduates is a problem getting in the way of growth.

National workforce data backs up the seemingly contradictory picture. An analysis of government figures by the National Centre for Universities and Business shows that while smaller businesses have shed roles faster than large employers, their rate of so-called skills shortage vacancies — openings that are difficult to fill because workers with specific abilities are hard to find — has remained high, particularly at entry level.

“Overall hiring is down [but] there are companies that struggle to find graduates or people with the right skills,” says Janine Chamberlin, UK country manager at jobs site LinkedIn. “There are lots of opportunities and growth in clean energy, farms, manufacturing, life sciences . . . But those sectors are just not front of mind for graduates.”

In manufacturing, for example, sector body Make UK estimates there are 50,000 vacancies, more than a third of which are hard to fill due to skills shortages. It organises open house days where employers showcase their work environments. Jamie Cater, senior policy manager, says companies are “investing significantly in mental health” and offering more flexible or remote working to attract applicants.

“We as a sector struggle with perceptions of what a manufacturing job is. People think of dank, dirty environments, repetitive manual labour for not very good pay. That’s not the reality,” he says. Increasing automation is shifting demand from production lines to jobs “with higher levels of technical skill” and half of manufacturers plan to increase recruitment in graduate-level roles over the next five years. “We’ve got a bunch of people retiring in the next couple of years in roles we need skilled workers in . . . there will be significant demand.”

Lucy Johnston, founder of UK Innovation Industries, a network for start-ups, says smaller employers can face a “visibility gap” in recruitment. “These innovative companies are often in fields graduates don’t know exist, they’re under the radar,” she says. “Meanwhile, graduates are . . . being told things are extremely difficult, and given lots of traditional advice.”

At fast-growing start-ups it is the urgent need for staff that, paradoxically, makes hiring so tough. “Any time we spend on hiring we’re not spending on building the business,” says Heat Geek’s Foster. Advertising on specialist or larger sites, active recruiting or travelling to graduate events incurs substantial costs for unknown return.

Simon Finley, associate director at Warwick Enterprise, which builds links between universities and entrepreneurs, says career services often default to larger companies. Big firms with “schemes it’s easier to tap into” claim prominent spots at career fairs and invest in getting ads seen, while “regional companies and universities don’t have the relationships that have developed over time”.

Businesses he works with also often complain that students lack the skills — including communication, initiative and organisation — to get stuck in straight away. “In graduate programmes, there’s a lot of training and development . . . in a smaller business it’s not as structured. For a lot of graduates that can be daunting.”
Location is another constraint. “There’s this perception among graduates that you have to go to the big city, but some of the most interesting companies are not in big cities,” says Johnston.

Samantha Fenn arrived as head of HR at Grainger & Worrall, a Shropshire-based manufacturer of aluminium castings, two years ago and was told “categorically that we couldn’t hire graduates — that they wouldn’t stay”, she recalls. She refocused recruitment on local graduates who would see living near home as an advantage. After a period of contraction, the company plans to expand staff from 460 to 500 and is “recruiting like mad”; in this year’s graduate round “we went to market for three, offered five and we’re taking on four”.

One of the company’s graduate hires, Robyn Beaumont, who joined two years ago as a business planning officer while completing an engineering degree, says: “In a larger company you’re often going to get forgotten about; here they nurture and develop you . . . no one’s afraid of speaking to the CEO.”

Steve Welch, who oversees relationships with universities at national agency Innovate UK, says the “paradox” of graduates struggling to find roles and companies struggling to hire is partly a “communication problem, with graduates not knowing how to look in the right places”. But he cites other obstacles, such as smaller companies’ ability to compete on pay. He suggests companies with strong growth potential need to sell “something different . . . than wages”.

At HR culture company FabricShift, founder Johanna Beresford says the chance to advance quickly and try different roles has helped her retain most of the graduates she has hired. “I don’t think employers often talk about . . . how it is such a different working environment for a smaller company.”
But for many smaller firms operating in essential but unglamorous industries, the challenge of being noticed is harder to fix.

“I’m not convinced people are being told about companies like us,” says Ian Goodacre, technical director at Europlaz, an Essex-based medical device manufacturer that employs more than 100 people. The company made several good graduate hires this year but had to work hard to find them, reaching out directly to students.
“We’re offering a fairly decent package, a full-time job, lots of opportunities,” says Goodacre. “But when we put adverts out, it’s surprising how few graduates we get applying.”

/content/952920f9-429d-451a-9913-a360880.title: Grindr bets wealthy gay men will pay more to find the right match
articleContent: Grindr built its business by helping gay men find each other for free. Now its chief executive wants more of its wealthiest users to pay handsomely for the privilege.
The dating app is planning a push into premium services, including a product that could cost $350 a month and a still pricier “luxury” offering pitched as a social club for the modern gay man.

Grindr boss George Arison is betting that charging affluent users more can boost profits at the company, which has grown rapidly over the past decade but has lagged behind rivals in converting them into paying users.

“The targets are people who have significant disposable income and who value their time in a very significant way,” Arison told the FT. He added that Grindr was not yet “anywhere near the premium price points” in terms of “what people will be willing to pay for long-term relationships”.

Grindr had an average of 1.4mn paying users for 15mn monthly active users in the second quarter of 2026, about 9 per cent. Morgan Stanley analysts estimate that the dating app monetises 30 per cent less than its main rivals.

Despite being slower to make money from its users, Grindr has proved an outlier in the dating app sector as it has continually gained users in recent years while peers such as Tinder and Bumble have declined.
Arison has retained the free experience as Grindr’s core product but has set about developing a series of new initiatives to target paying users looking for a tailored offering.

The products include Edge, which began public testing in select cities earlier this year and can cost hundreds of dollars a month depending on user location. It uses AI to suggest profile improvements and compatible partners.
Grindr is also planning a “luxury lifestyle and experiences product”. Arison declined to say how much it would charge for this service, but noted that “it’s going to be expensive.”
The Grindr boss, who joined the company in 2022, said his vision was to “capture more of people’s wallets for more services and products, rather than just dating and connections”.
Recommended

Grindr’s stock has risen by about a third in the past six months, buoyed by the company raising its full-year guidance and being upgraded to “overweight” by analysts at Morgan Stanley. Grindr now forecasts full-year revenue and adjusted earnings guidance of at least $540mn and $232mn respectively.

In a potential warning sign for user growth, Arison said the UK’s Online Safety Act, which requires websites to verify users’ ages before they can access adult content, had deterred some users worried about being outed as gay from using the app, which he thought was “pretty awful.”

“I’ve spoken to members of parliament here who I don’t think understood what the Online Safety Act would do when they passed it from the perspective of the impact that it would have on applications,” he said.
Arison said he had “no desire” for any underage user on the app, but that age verification should take place at an app store level to help users feel more comfortable.

“I cannot overstate how much I don’t want minors to have access to products like Grindr, it’s just that there’s a much better way to do it at the app store level than it is at the application level,” he said.

/content/407f90ed-fe14-4ed5-bfa8-50696b1.title: Nicotine pouch sales jump in UK as companies step up marketing
articleContent: Sales of nicotine pouches in the UK are expected to rise by more than a third this year as Big Tobacco companies push advertising ahead of marketing restrictions coming into force next year.

Sales of the products — small flavoured sachets placed between the lip and gum to deliver nicotine into the bloodstream — hit an estimated £384mn in 2025 and are expected to rise to more than £579mn by the end of 2026, according to figures from market research firm Euromonitor. That would still be a fragment of the £11.7bn spent on cigarettes in the UK in 2025.

The expansion comes as the tobacco companies behind the most popular pouch brands are “really upping” their marketing campaigns, which include everything from physical posters to festival sponsorships, according to Harry Tattan-Birch, a senior research fellow at University College London.

Nordic Spirit, a pouch brand owned by Japan Tobacco, sponsored a stage at Boomtown Festival earlier this month, while Marlboro-maker Philip Morris International, which sells Zyn nicotine pouches, has sponsored a corner shop-themed stage at festivals, including Parklife and Creamfields. British American Tobacco, which makes the Velo nicotine pouches, advertises heavily at UK transport hubs and has a partnership with the McLaren Formula 1 Team.

The campaigns come ahead of a UK-wide ban on advertising and sponsorship for all non-medicinal nicotine products, including nicotine pouches, from next June. The products have surged in popularity in a largely unregulated market, with the sale of nicotine pouches to under-18s still unrestricted until October.
Like smokers, pouch users tend to stick with the same brand, so companies are “doing all they can to get loyal customers now”, said Tattan-Birch.
The government is also consulting on plans to require plain white packaging for nicotine pouches, which it said would “reduce youth appeal without putting off adults who smoke”.

Uptake of nicotine pouches in the UK has been fastest among young men. Researchers at UCL found that 7.5 per cent of male 16- to 24-year-olds in the UK were using the products as of last March, compared with just 1 per cent of the wider adult population.

They typically cost about £5 per can, with most consumers getting through three cans per week, according to specialist nicotine pouch retailer Haypp, making them much cheaper than smoking. The cost is similar to vaping but depends on usage patterns.

Halle Breed, public affairs assistant at the anti-smoking charity ASH, which lobbied for marketing restrictions on nicotine pouches, said adverts for products like Zyn and Velo were “spread far and wide, in plain view of young people and children” on high streets, buses and trains in the UK.
Nicotine pouches are a cornerstone of Big Tobacco’s push to grow beyond cigarettes as smoking rates continue to decline in wealthy countries.

Asli Ertonguc, area director for western Europe at British American Tobacco, said the company was aiming to advertise its Velo nicotine pouches “everywhere relevant” in the UK because the product needed “to be explained to smokers since it’s a relatively new category”.

She added that British American Tobacco had “adjusted our plans to be ready for the [marketing] ban” and was allocating advertising spending “in line with the future changes”. The company “cannot control fully whether teenagers will be interested”, she added, but has guidelines in place to reduce its youth appeal, including a ban on advertising within 200 metres of a school.

Tobacco companies argue that their ability to market products such as vapes and nicotine pouches is crucial to helping smokers switch to safer products. But the World Health Organization has warned that these highly addictive products are increasingly attracting new and younger users rather than ex-smokers.

Nicotine pouches do not contain tobacco and therefore expose users to far fewer toxicants than smoking. But there is evidence that nicotine itself can aggravate cardiovascular conditions, making strokes or heart attacks worse. Some pouch users have also complained of oral lesions and irritated or receding gums.
Tattan-Birch said he expected that new marketing restrictions would reduce the uptake of nicotine pouches from first-time users with “both positive and negative” impacts on public health in the UK.

/content/0a5e4343-2a91-4e76-affd-b6b3692.title: The Dutch city where Europe’s electricity grid crunch hits home
articleContent: In Europe’s summer heat, Utrecht’s libraries face an unusual dilemma: either power their air conditioners or escalators.

Residents, businesses and public services face strict limits on electricity use in the Dutch city, less than 30 miles south of Amsterdam, as the power grid is severely congested. Since July 1, the grid operator has frozen new connections to avoid power cuts.

Utrecht’s mayor Sharon Dijksma fears the crisis could last for several years, with dire economic consequences for the Netherlands’ fastest-growing city. Fewer housing projects can be developed, while plans to electrify local industry and install faster chargers for electric vehicles are on hold.
Utrecht’s predicament could become the norm across the EU unless governments learn from its example and invest heavily in grids to support the bloc’s shift from fossil fuels to cleaner technologies.
“The impact on the economy will be huge,” Dijksma told the FT. “We are at the head of the troop but eventually the rest will face the same problems.”
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

As Europe experiences its second gas and oil price crisis in less than five years, the European Commission recently set out plans to double electricity’s share of energy consumption across the bloc to 46 per cent by 2040. The share has been stuck at 23 per cent for around a decade, with clogged-up grids partly to blame.
The Netherlands’ problems are particularly acute because it has made a big electrification push in recent years.

The EU’s fifth-largest economy has more solar panels and electric charging points per person than any other country in the region. It has successfully cut gas use from 42bn cubic metres per year in 2019 to 30bn in 2025.

But its failure to invest fast enough in pylons, cables and substations to support the transition means the queue of companies waiting for a power connection increased from 12,000 to 15,000 last year. Only 700 companies received a connection in 2025, said Remko Ybema, an adviser on climate and energy at Dutch business association VNO-NCW. “Any business that is successful and wants to grow has problems,” Ybema added.
“The Netherlands is the canary in the coal mine because it’s the earliest to have had these issues,” warned Elisabeth Cremona, an analyst at energy think-tank Ember.

“The majority of European countries are just now heading in that direction because we know grid build cannot keep up with the pace at which you can change your energy system,” Cremona added.

Ember research suggests that in countries such as Austria, Poland, Portugal and Romania, there is enough grid capacity for less than 10 per cent of the renewables projects planned by 2030.
Experts have long criticised the EU’s fractured energy system.

Of the five largest EU economies, only Germany met a 2020 target to install enough cross-border power cables to allow it to import the equivalent of up to 10 per cent of its electricity production capacity from neighbouring countries.

Last year’s huge blackout in Spain and Portugal was a clear warning sign of the fragility of the system. ENTSO-E, a group of grid operators, said the “whole of Europe” needed to modernise its energy infrastructure to prevent a similar fate.

Former European Central Bank governor Mario Draghi’s 2024 landmark report on EU competitiveness estimated that Europe needed to plough up to €600bn into its electricity grids by 2030 to support investments in renewables and cut high energy costs.

The Commission has responded with a grids package designed to bolster the bloc’s resilience to energy crises by expanding cross-border electricity connections. But the proposals have descended into a political fight, with Sweden leading criticism of proposals it saw as a power grab by Brussels and that could lose it revenue operators recoup from grid bottlenecks.

Still, few policymakers dispute that grids have been neglected. “There’s an absolute imperative to improve resilience of the grid across Europe and it’ll stand to us,” Ireland’s energy minister Darragh O’Brien told the FT ahead of his country taking control of the EU’s rotating presidency in July. “We need more copper wires but we can also use the assets we have to better effect.”

In Utrecht, grid challenges are linked to regional distribution of electricity rather than interconnectors with other countries. But the city’s response will be closely scrutinised by policymakers across Europe, who fear they too could face similar problems.
Dutch state-owned grid operator Tennet is planning to spend about €85bn from 2025 to 2034 on improving capacity as it tries to make up for years of under-investment.
Projects will include a new substation north of Utrecht by 2035, but progress was slowed by local opposition to around 10 proposed locations, said Tennet spokesperson Stijn van Woerkom.

It is also encouraging businesses to use more electricity during periods of the day when there is less demand by offering time-dependent contracts. So far this has been less effective in Utrecht than similar initiatives in other parts of the Netherlands because of a relative lack of large industry.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

But Tom Selten, founder of tech start-up Zympler, which helps clients manage electricity to keep within grid connection limits, said more residents and businesses will have to change their habits and avoid using power at peak times.
“Fifty-five per cent of our energy is not used,” he said. For much of the day, “we have no issues with congestion, so we need to design a system that is more tailored to our supply”.

In the meantime, businesses and households will face extra costs. As Tennet’s spending increases, annual electricity costs for Dutch households could rise from more than €1,160 in 2024 to nearly €1,780 in 2040, PwC predicts.

Utrecht’s mayor Dijksma warns that one of the biggest unwanted consequences is a slide back to gas-fired power that risks slowing down the Netherlands’ ambition to cut emissions by 90 per cent by 2040, compared with 1990 levels.

Regional grid operator Stedin is installing backup gas generators around Utrecht to reduce the strain on the grid, while the Dutch government will bring forward new standards from 2029 for hybrid heat pumps that combine electric and gas heating.
“You want to encourage those municipalities that are [transitioning from fossil fuels] really fast instead of making them slow down but that’s what’s happening now,” said Dijksma.

opinion content. 
Women make friends differently from men at work
articleContent: Just after 1pm last Tuesday, I bought a £7.50 chicken salad at the Pret around the corner from my office to test a theory.
It wasn’t the grim little lunch that interested me. It was the other office workers hunkered down over their halloumi wraps and egg pots.
Sure enough, there were more men eating lunch alone than women.
It was the same at the café next door to the Pret, at another lunch spot down the road and also the FT staff canteen.
Sometimes there were more than twice as many single male diners. Sometimes the ratio was smaller. Nowhere did I see more women eating alone than men.

This was just one brief unscientific snapshot of London lunch life. Countless things could have accounted for the preponderance of lone males, not least the possibility that men outnumber women around my office, or have the types of jobs that force a quick bite alone instead of more leisurely lunching.
Still, what I saw gels with new research that sheds a somewhat troubling light on how we relate to one another at work.

Women make friends on the job in different ways from men, according to a study by European and US academics in the Social Networks journal. They form wider, deeper relationships with each other, in part because they are more likely than men to befriend friends of their friends in the office.
Men tend to have more selective one-to-one work friendships, especially if it helps them get ahead.
The study did not go into what happens at lunch, but if men are not as close to their work friends as women, you can see why they might tend to eat solo.

Either way, the implications of the new research are important. Older research shows people with good work relationships are likely to be happier, more engaged, more productive and innovative. They are less likely to be thinking about jumping ship and more likely to know what is going on and what their employer wants them to prioritise.
That’s good news for employers and for women, some of whom do a distinctly better job of making friends at work than men.
Nearly 30 per cent of college-educated American women say they have good friends at work, while only about 20 per cent of college-educated men report the same thing.

Why so? It could be because women have shared experiences of, say, motherhood, and want to be friends with other mothers in the office in the same way that they might gravitate to women with kids outside work.

But the new research suggests the picture is more complicated. The study tracked nearly 140 workers at a US community development group who were aged between 18 and 24. That’s a bit young for parenthood.
Whatever the explanation for women’s tendency to become friends with people they are already connected to, it might not be that helpful.
If you were being strategic about your workmates, you would not necessarily pick people who were friends of friends.

They are unlikely to know much more about what’s going on than your existing friends, says Andrew Parker, a professor of leadership at the UK’s Durham University Business School who co-authored the new research. “As a network, you want somebody in HR, somebody in finance, somebody in marketing, somebody in sales,” he told me, because that’s more useful than if your friends all come from the same department.
It is also sobering to consider the advantages men might get from a more calculated approach to work friendships.
Close to 40 per cent of the gender pay gap at one big commercial bank could have been explained by the social relationships between men and their male managers, a 2019 study estimated.
Ultimately, this speaks to a need to be aware that all is not necessarily as it may seem at work.

Most large organisations have well-established mentoring and sponsorship programmes to advance women and other employee groups. In my experience, they can do a reasonable job of linking junior people with more experienced hands who can offer advice about how things work and who’s who. But both mentor and mentee often come from exactly the same department or division. It might be helpful if they did not.
As for lunch, sometimes it’s nice to eat with others and sometimes it is not. In the world of work today, there are larger things to worry about.
pilita.clark@ft.com

/content/5729b32c-8b7a-42b1-b1e2-b8b0106.title:
opinion content. 
The FT View. Meta’s settlement is a starting point
articleContent: When a blockbuster trial opened this month in California in which four US states representing a broader group sued Meta over allegations that its Facebook and Instagram platforms designed addictive features that harmed children’s mental health, few expected it to be over within a few days. But last week Meta agreed to pay up to $18bn to settle the case, one of the largest settlements ever reached by a US tech company. It also committed to safeguards intended to make its platforms safer for young users. While they don’t yet go far enough, they could be expanded internationally.

Trials are not the best way to resolve public safety issues, but US litigation has again shown its capacity to force changes in corporate behaviour where the country’s legislators and regulators have failed. Even $18bn is, of course, small change for Meta, and well below the $200bn the states had sought. Meta said payment of $5.3bn of the total is contingent on YouTube and TikTok each agreeing matching payments and imposing similar restrictions on teens. For now, the safety commitments apply only to Meta, and only in the US.

But the attempt to bind in YouTube and TikTok is significant: research suggests teens use their platforms more frequently, and both face litigation too. Other governments, moreover, some of which plan to follow Australia by banning minors from social media, now have leverage to demand similar safeguards. Indeed, the settlement could be seen as a starting point for what Meta and others might be made to agree to in return for bans being shelved.

The question for policymakers is whether such steps can be better at keeping teens safe than attempting to block their access to social media. Australia’s pioneering ban has proved distinctly patchy, with many under-16s finding ways to dodge it.

The Meta settlement requires the company to build an age-assurance framework to tighten the age bar on under-13s and distinguish 13 to 17-year-olds from adults, using either third-party or its own technology. There are performance standards with annual third-party testing — though there is no guarantee that Meta can reach these.

Assuming age verification can be made more effective, the strongest parts of the deal are a two-hour limit on use across Facebook and Instagram, a blackout period from midnight to 6am, and a block on push notifications from 10pm to 7am and during school hours. Similarly welcome is hiding “likes” and reaction counts — a big driver of addictive behaviour — by default on posts created by children’s accounts, and banning “beauty” filters that simulate cosmetic enhancements, which can intensify body image anxiety.

There are glaring weaknesses on some of the most addictive features, though. Algorithmic feeds, where Meta continues to serve up content designed to maximise engagement, remain the default even if teenagers have to be offered a “chronological”, non-personalised feed option that parents can set as the default. And “infinite scroll” remains standard, though Meta must impose “productive pauses” — freezing the feed — after 15, 60 and 90 minutes of continuous use.

One of the biggest problems with setting rules for Big Tech, moreover, has proved to be that by the time they are agreed, technology has moved on. How social media works could yet be transformed by AI and other innovations — and new market entrants. If they are to escape more countrywide bans on minors, Meta and other social media platforms will need to agree to work proactively with regulators to adapt safeguards and adopt new ones over time. A “safe by design” approach may be preferable to blunt but patchily observed prohibitions — but it needs to be effective, and constantly evolve.

opinion content. 
Warsh charts a forward-looking path for the Fed at Jackson Hole
articleContent: The writer is the Rene M Kern professor of practice at Wharton School, chief economic adviser at Allianz and chair of Gramercy Funds Management

Kevin Warsh delivered his first speech at the annual Jackson Hole central banking conference as the new chair of the Federal Reserve under the pressure of remarkably high and unusually varied expectations.

Yet in a powerful half-hour presentation, he went a long way towards assuaging doubts by deftly navigating both short- and long-term issues. That’s the good news. Less good is that the immediate media and market focus has been on the less consequential part of his speech.

We should not underestimate the tricky task Warsh faced in the run-up to his Friday speech: striking the right balance in responding to criticisms about the market’s lack of understanding of his so-called “reaction function” — how the Fed would respond to changes in the economy under his watch. At the same time, he had to adhere to the symposium’s original objective (including this year’s focus on innovation) by addressing longer-term issues central to the economic outlook and Fed policy effectiveness.

Despite the considerable volume of Warsh’s writings and congressional testimony, some Wall Street commentators felt not enough was known about his reaction function. They wanted not just details on this but also his current view of the economy and a bit of guidance on future policy. It did not help that, in recent weeks, there has been more focus on inflation.

The criticisms of the reaction function and forward guidance, while misdirected, are understandable. After all, for several years, the market has been conditioned by a Fed that relied on a mantra of “data dependency” for policy decisions, spoke often, and loved to issue forward guidance. The result is something that Warsh and many others, including me, regret: to quote Warsh, “a market regime that looks to the Fed for its next trade” and, as such, plays the referee rather than the ball.

Warsh had other reasons to adhere to Jackson Hole’s original intentions. We are living through a period of historic change driven by innovation-led transformation and the rise of geopolitical factors in economics. Two other considerations have also fuelled the need for thinking about longer-term issues. First, the approach taken by Warsh’s predecessor, Jay Powell, who tended to focus on shorter-term issues in his tenure. Second was the importance of providing a “North Star” vision to help bring together, over time, a highly divided Federal Open Market Committee.

In response to these pressures, Warsh addressed the loud call for his views on the current state of the economy, the balance of risks to the Fed’s dual mandate on employment and price stability, and his commitment to using the Personal Consumption Expenditure index as the central bank’s preferred inflation target. The resulting tone in this section, which has attracted the most media attention, was somewhat hawkish.
Recommended

Warsh also restated his view that forward guidance has “outlived its role” and that it leads to the risk of the “hall of mirrors” phenomenon where the Fed and the market send back the same signals to each other. He referred back to the Fed’s big 2021—22 policy mistake, in which prior incorrect forward guidance slowed the needed response, allowing consumer price inflation to surge to more than 9 per cent. The result was a consequential hit to affordability and the compounded effects are still with us today.

Having said all this, the most important section of his speech pointed to the questions that the current phase of innovation poses for the economy and policy effectiveness, including the role of AI as a “new factor of production”. While it has attracted less media attention, this is the most interesting and important part of his speech, as the issue has massive implications for economic functioning, the evolution of monetary policy and financial stability risks. It is an area where a lot more work is urgently required.

Ultimately, Warsh delivered a masterclass in central bank communication at a pivotal juncture. He addressed immediate market demands for details on his reaction function while, more importantly, putting the broader secular realities of productivity and AI front and centre. If markets can look past the short-term headlines and spend more time on the ongoing strategic shifts, Jackson Hole 2026 may well be remembered as the moment the Federal Reserve began leading the forward-looking economic conversation once again, rather than merely reacting to the latest data.
