opinion content. 
Lex. One fix for UK plc’s underperformance: equity for all
articleContent: The recent spate of FTSE 250 takeovers lends credibility to the idea that UK companies are too cheap or poorly run. Perceptions change only slowly. But much could be addressed by increasing the number of people who own companies’ shares — starting with the board.

Activist investor Cevian Capital has proposed doubling the remuneration of non-executive directors from the FTSE 100 average of £80,000 to £160,000, with the difference paid in stock, on the grounds that a strong board is a good way to increase corporate value. This is a bold call, in that raising pay for business grandees, let alone doubling it, tends to provoke cries of outrage.

But Cevian has a point. In the US, non-execs are paid three times as much as their UK peers. And British companies need the kind of expertise — AI, for starters — that is more easily found on the other side of the Atlantic. Equity is a sensible currency because it links pay to performance, especially when it pays out over a reasonably long period. Only 5 per cent of FTSE 100 groups pay their directors in stock according to new data by Alvarez & Marsal.

Joining a board isn’t purely a monetary question in the UK, where directors face considerable legal risks and public scrutiny. One way to shift the balance of risks and rewards would be to make the job of board director more interesting and engaging, and a good way to do that is to attract more top-flight Chairs.

There, pay compares much more favourably: the UK median for the largest 150 companies is £452,000, according to the Spencer Stuart board index, roughly the same as in the US. Still, that number has grown only half as much as directors’ pay over the past five years. And because it’s almost always in cash, it lacks the performance incentive that stock confers — which is why private equity-backed companies are such potent poachers of UK plc board talent.

Companies considering big share awards may fear a backlash from proxy advisers and investors. They rightly keep an eagle eye out for pay that doesn’t incentivise, or reward, good results. But they often compare compensation packages to local market norms. That’s not particularly helpful when the local market as a whole is falling behind foreign counterparts.

Asset managers are also just following the preferences of their clients, who are steeped in British scepticism of fat-cat incentives. Some of that is justified, but some comes from the relatively low levels of stock ownership in the general population, relative to the US. One thing that can be said in favour of proposals to get more shares into more hands is that they ought to foster a culture that’s more supportive of business and markets, to the broad benefit of UK plc.
camilla.palladino@ft.com

/content/95379ab9-8483-4e0a-a71e-e22b68d.title: Raphaël Glucksmann, the French left’s new hope
articleContent: Most politicians launch their campaigns from a podium. Raphaël Glucksmann began his bid for the French presidency this week by climbing an 80-metre wind turbine. “I’m not afraid, I can’t wait to be at the top,” said the newly declared candidate, clad in a helmet and harness. Back on the ground, he promised a “100-day environmental revolution” if elected in 2027 to fight climate change and wean France off fossil fuels.

After one of France’s hottest summers on record and devastating wildfires, the issue puts him at the forefront of public debates. But his bid for the Élysée faces formidable odds: the French left has not reached a presidential run-off since 2012. With the far right’s Marine Le Pen all but certain to secure one of two places in next May’s run-off, Glucksmann will also be squeezed by Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s radical left, which is gaining in the polls, and Emmanuel Macron’s centrist heirs.

Glucksmann, 46, a writer and activist turned EU parliamentarian who launched his own party Place Publique in 2018, gained national prominence after leading a joint list with the Socialists to come third in European elections two years ago. Though awkward at times — his primetime announcement of his candidacy appeared heavily rehearsed — advocates say his convictions come through.

“I don’t come from the usual political mould,” Glucksmann told TF1 news. “I wasn’t a parliamentary attaché at 20 or an official in a political party, I was standing beside people who had escaped genocide in Rwanda, and opponents of Russian imperialism in Georgia and Ukraine.”

“Many French people no longer believe in politics because it’s not sincere. It’s good to have a fresh start with someone sincere,” said close ally Nicolas Mayer-Rossignol, the Socialist mayor of Rouen. Yet an elite, intellectual background may not always play in his favour, and some positions irk leftist voters, who have accused him of being too pro-Israel, too pro-nuclear power, and not radical enough on the economy.

He forms a power couple with his partner Léa Salamé, one of France’s best-known broadcast journalists, who stepped down from anchoring her primetime news show for the duration of his candidacy. Paris Match splashed photographs of the pair on the beach in Corsica on the cover in August just beneath images of Macron on a jet ski. Glucksmann has a slight “champagne socialist” air that could hurt him, said Daniel Boy of Sciences Po.

Glucksmann was born just outside Paris to activist, intellectual parents. His late father, André Glucksmann, was a well-known philosopher who broke with his early dabblings with communism to become an anti-Maoist leftist for most of his life, like his wife, Françoise, also an activist and a screenwriter. The Glucksmann household played host to a rotating cast of activists and political outcasts. His late mother, whom he called “Fanfan”, has described how a five-year-old Raphaël would lie on the floor with his father discussing the non-existence of God.

Glucksmann’s outspoken critiques of Russia come from formative experiences in Kyiv during the Orange revolution in 2004 and in Georgia, advising then president Mikheil Saakashvili following Russia’s 2008 invasion.

His early warnings to the EU about Russian interference and advocacy for China’s Uyghur minority are examples of his steadfast views, his backers say. “He’s someone who is tenacious, determined. When he takes on a subject — even if it’s not fashionable, even if no one cares — he’ll be right,” said Aurore Lalucq, a member of the European Parliament for Place Publique.

Early polls show that Glucksmann’s campaign has a long road ahead. A survey this week put him fourth at 11 per cent in first-round voting intentions, behind Le Pen, Mélenchon and former Macron prime minister Édouard Philippe. Yet in a hypothetical run-off against Le Pen, he performed substantially better than Mélenchon.

“What is different this time is that the RN doesn’t just have a foot in the door, they have nine-and-a-half toes in at the Élysée,” said Mayer-Rossignol. “The left needs to ask itself if it wants to win. I’m not interested in being the best-looking corpse in the graveyard.”

Glucksmann’s first test will be an October primary against other Socialist candidates for the centre-left nomination. But his biggest task is to close the gap with Mélenchon by persuading leftwing voters that he offers their best chance of reaching the run-off, said Mathieu Gallard of Ipsos. Glucksmann is not yet known as a national politician and his message is less closely aligned with voters’ traditional priorities like cost of living, he added.

At a conference organised by the main business lobby this week, Glucksmann drew applause for his frontal attacks on Le Pen’s bid to clamp down on immigration to cut France’s debt. But he also highlighted his fight against “the religion of free trade” and promised to create a society of “workers not trustafarians and heirs”, notably through a new tax on inheritances over €2mn.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, Glucksmann advocated cancelling Eurozone sovereign debt held by the European Central Bank, although he now opposes Mélenchon’s attempt to revive a similar idea. “There are still some rough edges in his programme,” said one executive.

Glucksmann is determined to beat the odds. “The illusion of the global village, where Europe is the butt of the joke, is over,” he told business leaders on Thursday. “We are a vast country with a gigantic destiny that is not yet over; let us not give in to defeatism.”
adrienne.klasa@ft.com, sarah.white@ft.com

opinion content. 
Zero-sum thinking will fuel resentment and scarcity
articleContent: The age of prepping is upon us. In Sweden, a brochure instructs citizens to keep at least a week’s supply of water and food “in case of crisis or war”. Similar leaflets have been issued to Norwegians, Danes and Finns, and are online in the UK. Even without Russian aggression, cyber attacks and extreme weather mean such precautions are no longer the preserve of doomsday survivalists hoarding baked beans and duct tape. But in such a crisis, social solidarity would also matter. So it’s worrying that we seem increasingly suspicious of one another.

A good deal of public discourse now feels framed as zero sum: the assumption that one group must lose in order for another to gain. It’s common to suggest that immigrants are taking our jobs, the wealthy are getting even richer at others’ expense, or that female workers are hurting employment prospects for men.

It’s as if we are stuck in a game of musical chairs, with too few seats and some players doomed to miss out. The idea that we can expand the circle, that entrepreneurs can spread prosperity, is getting lost. And, worryingly, there is evidence that this kind of thinking undermines willingness to co-operate.

Zero-sum thinking is not new. But it seems to be on the rise, especially among the young. An analysis of English language books finds the use of “zero-sum” terminology has leapt since 1990, pulling far ahead of “positive-sum” descriptions.

Economists Stefanie Stantcheva and Sahil Chinoy have found that American Gen Z and millennials are far more likely than Gen X and baby boomers to imagine the world is a fixed pie, and not just if they’re poor: those making $100,000 a year feel aggrieved, and postgraduates even more so. Residents of big cities displayed the highest tendency for zero-sum thinking: mayor Zohran Mamdani was elected by New Yorkers who see themselves as losing out. Older people tend to have a more expansive mindset — apart from Donald Trump, whose zero-sum tariffs are making US consumers poorer.

Stuttering economic growth since the 2008 crash and anxiety about a precarious world can make the young more likely to see resources as scarce. Researchers suggest this may be down to very real competition in job markets, university admissions and housing.

There is also evidence that beliefs about social mobility can be self-fulfilling. When presented with a fictional company where highly rated employees got bonuses and low-rated ones didn’t, young people in a recent University of Chicago experiment tended to assume the staff were ranked against each other, rather than that everyone could get a high rating if they were good enough.

Such mindsets are not always irrational. The postwar international order was built on the idea that interdependence would boost opportunities for all, and so it did. But, as the century ended, the tide of globalisation was not lifting all boats.

Moreover, across the west, pensions have strained the social contract, charging dwindling numbers of working-age people to support growing numbers of retirees. In big cities where Harvard found the strongest zero-sum mindsets, planning restrictions are a major constraint on housing supply. A reckoning is due, but inequality will not be reduced by penalising success.
If we are not careful, we are heading for a future that is poorer both economically and culturally.

In a study of 37 nations, those who agreed that “if someone gets richer, it means somebody else gets poorer” also tended to be more cynical about institutions and less likely to volunteer. This bodes ill for the social fabric. Inadvertently, this also increases the pressure to expand government. According to Stantcheva and Chinoy, zero-sum thinking is strongly associated with support for government redistribution as well as calls for immigration restrictions: cutting across partisan lines, yet an ever-expanding state is likely to entrench managed decline.

How do we move from a conversation about “who gets the biggest slice” to “how do we increase the pie”? It’s easier for politicians to indulge in the politics of grievance than to build voter confidence that we can grow our way out of this. It’s especially challenging when trust is falling in authorities and employers, belief that leaders lie to us is at an all-time high and large majorities think the wealthy take more than their fair share, according to the Edelman Trust Barometer.

Confidence comes from effective policy. We can build affordable housing that is attractive and doesn’t upset the neighbours. We can tackle climate change while also creating jobs, and welcome entrepreneurs, not drive them abroad.

The Swedish leaflet on emergencies emphasises “we must all help each other”. The British equivalent says to “find out if you are eligible for a priority service register”. There’s nothing wrong with extra help for the vulnerable in a crisis: it was vital in the pandemic. But I can’t help feeling that someone in authority has already given up on us trusting one another.
camilla.cavendish@ft.com

/content/ba4b940e-4a44-473b-9846-eaba943.title:
opinion content. 
Risk of a new age of financial repression is rising
articleContent: In normal person-speak, the grand-sounding term “financial repression” is sometimes translated as like holding a gun to someone’s head and making them buy your bonds. It is not supposed to be taken literally.

And yet a week ago, Donald Trump hinted at precisely that. Asked about Scott Bessent’s recent efforts to support the US government bond markets, the president casually observed that the Treasury secretary’s upsized buybacks are “one type of intervention” and that “the ultimate intervention is our military. And if we have to use that, we will”.

Analysts and investors appear willing to let this wild statement slide — something it would be hard to imagine had it come from the lips of any other president of any country ever. Remember this the next time someone tells you America’s exorbitant privilege is dead or that its role as protector of the world’s premier safe asset and leading reserve currency is a burden. Just like its current president, it simply gets away with stuff in financial markets that no other country could.

But the idea of pushing US government bonds down the throats of otherwise unwilling investors, through coercion, regulation or other means, is being taken increasingly seriously. It is one way to wage a war with the bond market.

Other bond-boosting tactics are struggling. Arguably the slickest is to employ the kind of Jedi mind control trick used by European Central Bank chief Mario Draghi back in 2012. He was able to pull borrowing costs back down in a debt crisis then simply by stating he would do “whatever it takes” to get there. Even now, borrowing costs in, for example, France, are much lower than they might otherwise be thanks to the threat — not the exercise, just the threat — of forceful responses to push them down in a crisis. But this takes rock-solid credibility and in the US at the moment, that is in short supply.

The most durable way to win a bond war is to do the work to fix the underlying economic forces that have created it in the first place. In Turkey, for example, that meant letting the central bank crank up interest rates, despite howls of protest from the country’s president. For the US, it demands a large retrenchment in government spending, or large tax rises, or both to address the real underlying storm sweeping through global debt markets. All the big borrowers are feeling the pain, from Japan to the UK and US. Massive levels of borrowing and huge gaps between what governments collect in taxes and spend at the other end are not new. But in markets, things are fine until they are not, and this is starting to look not so fine. And yet few expect any of the key offenders here to do the work for a proper reset.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Right now, the US is spared the apparent risk of military intervention in markets by another useful resource for winning a bond war: luck. Inflation, the bond market’s traditional foe, has never been the main concern in this latest episode, but the recent fall in oil prices does give the debt markets some breathing room. Bessent also has at the very least succeeded in scaring some speculators out of pushing borrowing costs much higher right now. Yields have stabilised at elevated levels since his Treasury department announced state purchases of long-term debt.

But luck has a habit of running out. If and when it does, the chance of the US reaching for the button marked “financial repression” is rising. It is a dirty phrase in finance circles, encompassing a range of efforts including bank capital requirements and even capital controls to force private sector investors to accept low returns so that countries can keep on spending on the cheap. It’s rather antiquated and very un-American — a refusal to let markets do what they do best: pricing risk.
Recommended

“The primary preoccupation henceforth stands to be financing government expenditure, and with monetary policy being subordinated to this need,” warned David Skilling and John Llewellyn of Independent Economics in a note last week. “Monetary policy support will likely involve financial repression, with lower real interest rates for the US (and others) as yields are capped in various ways and ownership of Treasuries is required or incentivised . . . The US will use economic and geopolitical pressure to attract capital, in increasingly aggressive ways. These capital wars stand to be markedly more consequential than the recent trade wars.”

Any serious moves in this direction would mark a profound shift in the global financial regime. And yet it is already a sufficiently live possibility that money managers are starting to advise clients on what to do if it happens.

“Initiatives that result in financial repression and yields being brought down artificially should be favourable for equities, while gold would be another beneficiary,” was the breezy assessment of UBS Wealth Management in a note this week.
If the past few years have taught us nothing else, it is to imagine the unimaginable. This is the latest example to add to the list.
katie.martin@ft.com

/content/60be9ebd-f1be-4f36-b907-c1a9971.title: ‘SmashCos’: Europe’s oil majors create new generation of independent companies
articleContent: Europe’s oil and gas majors are increasingly turning to joint ventures with their biggest rivals, creating a new generation of independent production companies as the sector tries to balance finding new sources of growth with financial discipline.

This new crop of oil groups includes the biggest independent producer in Europe, Vår Energi, in which Italy’s Eni holds a majority stake, and the two biggest producers in the UK North Sea: Neo Next Plus, in which TotalEnergies and Repsol have stakes, and Adura, a partnership between Shell and Norway’s Equinor.

Over the past decade, BP, Eni, Shell, Equinor and TotalEnergies have bundled together assets and spun them off into standalone companies, giving them names such as Azule, Arcius, Adura, Aker and Vår. One recent deal between Eni and Malaysia’s state oil company Petronas created Searah, which started operations in July.
“We call them SmashCos, because you are basically smashing two companies together,” said Bob Fryklund, vice-president of upstream energy at S&P Global. “There will be more of them for sure.”

These strategic ventures are increasingly important to the sector’s growth prospects. Searah is expected to produce an initial 300,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, while Vår Energi, which announced a deal for Danish producer BlueNord last month, said its daily oil production would be 450,000 boe/d, making it roughly a quarter of the size of Eni.
Joint ventures will account for 28 per cent of BP’s oil and gas spending this year and 31 per cent of Eni’s, according to consultancy Wood Mackenzie.
The trend comes as oil companies navigate their way through the energy transition and seek more flexibility over how to manage assets and maintain the tight fiscal discipline beloved by investors.
“There are a lot of other companies that are studying the model,” said Fryklund, who suggested there could be more tie-ups with national oil companies in the Middle East and Latin America.
While oil and gas companies have always teamed up on specific projects, these new ventures operate independently, raise their own debt and are not consolidated on the balance sheets of their parents.
That has proved useful during a period when shareholders and environmental campaigners were pressing the sector to curb oil and gas spending.

“The shareholders and the lobbyists were pushing the sector not to invest in upstream, so everyone was trying to hide what they were investing in upstream,” said a senior executive at one major oil company.

“If a company announced they were dedicating $15bn for deep-sea Arctic drilling, for example, everyone would freak out. But if they do it in a non-consolidated way, or kind of off-balance sheet, then it is not as public. So you have a lot of it.”
Others said the structures allowed parent companies to develop and scale projects that might not fit into the portfolio of an oil major, and without increasing their parent company’s debt.

“It’s about greater capital efficiency,” said Fraser McKay, head of upstream at Wood Mackenzie. “This isn’t necessarily nefarious, it is more about accounting and unlocking opportunities in the portfolios that in the past they might just have sold, but today they might want to hold on to and harvest production and cash flow from.”

He added that majors were keen to keep a stake in smaller projects, as investors pressed them to demonstrate greater oil and gas reserves. “They’ll want these dividend streams essentially from these smaller companies but want to maintain the booking of the production and reserves”.
There are other rationales for the new wave of companies.

In the UK North Sea, operators have long rolled up assets to achieve scale and cut costs in a mature basin. More recently, forming new companies has had a tax advantage: one partner contributes producing fields, another brings historic tax losses, lowering the combined entity’s bill.
Shell and Equinor’s Adura, which began operating at the end of last year, is one such vehicle.

“It’s really a standalone venture,” said Sinead Gorman, Shell’s chief financial officer, on a results call in February. “You can see them out there looking at raising debt to be able to continue that business. We expect to see considerable dividends coming through.”

Elsewhere, the logic is to create growth. Eni’s recent venture with Malaysia’s Petronas combines fresh discoveries with established cash-generating fields, using today’s revenues to fund tomorrow’s developments.

In Angola, where BP and Eni combined mature portfolios into Azule, there has also been exploration success. The company last month announced it had found a 500mn barrel field. “We’ve got a relatively large base production business and we’ve got a suite of major projects coming towards us in the joint venture,” BP’s head of production Gordon Birrell told the FT.

There has been little need or appetite by US companies to embrace the model. With stronger balance sheets, higher valuations on their share prices and deeper portfolios, the likes of ExxonMobil and Chevron have grown by mergers and acquisitions in recent years.
The new companies also come with drawbacks. For investors, a proliferation of partially owned, independently financed entities makes companies harder to analyse and value.
“It is unclear how they all work out over the longer term as the strategies of the individual equity holders change,” said McKay.

There are other risks, too: they can be hard to manage and struggle to form a distinct corporate culture. Kate Thomson, BP’s chief financial officer, acknowledged the trade-offs on a call with analysts earlier this year.

“Being simple is good, and I think complexity can slow you down,” she said. “But there are times when you can create unique opportunities through a marriage of assets and partners. Where those circumstances exist, then I think it’s appropriate to contemplate stepping into that complexity.”

/content/17c61dd3-fa39-4061-b3a1-2d2333d.title: Incoming Swiss banking chief warns against regulatory over-reach
articleContent: Switzerland risks undermining its position as a global financial centre by imposing excessive regulation on its banks, the incoming head of the country’s banking lobby has warned, as Bern embarks on its biggest overhaul of the sector since the financial crisis.
Giorgio Pradelli, who heads Zurich-based bank EFG International, takes over as chair of the Swiss Bankers Association (SBA) next month.
Speaking in his capacity as EFG chief executive, Pradelli said Switzerland could not assume its pre-eminence in global banking would endure as competing financial centres simplify their rules.

“We cannot take it for granted that Switzerland will always be prominent if we do not apply the right policies, including the regulatory framework,” he told the FT, adding it “had to be proportionate”.
Pradelli’s intervention is a sign of how concerns that Bern risks overcorrecting for the collapse of Credit Suisse stretch across Switzerland’s financial sector.
Although UBS, which took over its rival in a state-sponsored takeover in 2023, is the bank most directly affected by proposed new rules, the reforms reach across the banking system.

A proposed package finalised this month makes individual senior bankers more directly accountable for failures on their watch, tightens bonus and clawback provisions, gives market regulator Finma greater enforcement powers and strengthens crisis planning and access to central bank liquidity.

The debate over how tough its regulatory regime should be comes at a crucial moment for Switzerland’s financial centre. Hong Kong last year overtook Switzerland as the world’s largest hub for offshore wealth, according to BCG.

US regulators are reducing and simplifying some capital requirements, while the UK has delayed parts of its Basel reforms and sought to limit increases in overall capital requirements for competitiveness.
“What we see in the other financial centres is more a trend of simplification,” Pradelli said. “In the US you might even talk about deregulation. So we need to be [on] one level playing field.”
The EFG chief’s warning comes days before a crucial parliamentary committee meeting on the most contentious part of the reforms affecting UBS.

The upper house’s economic affairs committee is due on Monday to resume deliberations on plans that could force the bank to hold about $20bn more common equity, with lawmakers considering alternatives that could soften the government’s proposal.
Asked whether Switzerland had struck the right balance, Pradelli said: “On stability and proportionality, I believe we’re getting there. On competitiveness, we can improve.”
EFG has emerged as one of the beneficiaries of the upheaval in Swiss wealth management following Credit Suisse’s demise. Shares are up nearly 100 per cent since the other bank’s takeover by UBS.

The private bank attracted SFr5.7bn in net new assets in the first half and has recorded positive inflows for 15 consecutive half-years. It hired 140 relationship managers amid the disruption in 2023 — twice its normal annual hiring target of between 50 and 70 — a period Pradelli described as “pivotal” for the bank.

Geopolitical tensions were accelerating the movement of wealth, he said, with rich clients increasingly diversifying their fortunes not only between investments and banks but across countries and financial centres.
“Clients will no longer put all the eggs in one basket, not even in terms of financial centres,” he said.

/content/0d24c0e8-eb65-4009-a236-f2dbf1e.title: Trump deportations take a bite out of an unexpected industry: US fast food
articleContent: The Trump administration’s immigration crackdown is eating into sales at US fast-food restaurants, eroding a source of growth the industry long relied on.

Sales growth at chain restaurants slowed sharply in 2024 and 2025, according to researcher Technomic. McDonald’s said this month it would slow its pace of store openings, while Wendy’s and Subway have closed hundreds of locations over the past year. The shift comes at a difficult time for fast food, with inflation taking a bite out of disposable income.

With the birth rate below replacement level for most of the past 50 years, the US has relied almost exclusively on immigration for population growth. But economists estimate more people left the US than entered it last year for the first time in decades, as the Trump administration curtailed immigration and stepped up deportations. Nearly 3mn people left the US last year through a combination of deportations and self-removal, according to government figures.

The vast majority of those targeted for deportation are from Latin American countries — a crucial segment of the fast-food industry, with 35 per cent of Latino people in the US consuming fast food on any given day, according to a 2018 study by the health department.
Analysts and economists said the sector is sensitive to population decline — and that fewer mouths to feed spells a problem for fast food.

“Population growth is certainly a driver of the [fast-food] industry, because pretty much everyone is a customer, including lower-income consumers,” said Brian Harbour, a restaurant analyst at Morgan Stanley.

The link between population and demand has long been recognised by the food industry. In February, Kofi Bruce, chief financial officer of General Mills, said he expected “lower population growth in the US”, alongside increased uptake of weight-loss drugs, to cost the company 50 basis points of growth in its 2027 fiscal year.

Restaurant executives have also pointed to favourable demographics when explaining expansion. As Tim Hortons expanded in a fast-growing Canada, Joshua Kobza, chief executive of parent company Restaurant Brands International, said in 2025: “If you have 1 per cent population growth, then we should be growing more Tim’s.”
Fast-food chains are now confronting the opposite dynamic.
The US population grew 0.5 per cent between July 2024 and July 2025, according to the US Census Bureau, dramatically slower than in recent years.

Economists at the Brookings Institution estimate net migration turned negative in 2025 for the first time in decades and expect the decline will continue in 2026. Tara Watson, a director at Brookings who worked on the research, attributed the reversal to the second Trump administration’s policies, which have “pretty successfully eliminated most traffic at the border”, she said.
“The fast-food industry, in particular, would likely be feeling the pain there,” said Jon Tower, an analyst at Citi.
Combined with a challenging economy, the population slowdown raises another question, Tower said: “Do we have too many stores in the US?”
Since 2021, the number of chain restaurants in the US has grown between 1 per cent and 2 per cent each year, according to Technomic.

But those stores are attracting less business than they once did. Data from Placer.ai shows foot traffic to fast-food stores grew consistently in 2023, then began to fluctuate in 2024 as inflation-strapped consumers cut back on eating out. In 2025 and 2026, fast-food foot traffic declined almost every month. Analysts say some of the decline reflects the continued rise of food-delivery apps, but not all of it.

The mature US fast-food industry also has limited room left to expand. The sector has “been going in its current form for 30, 40 years, so it’s probably plateauing”, said Peter Backman, a restaurant consultant.

Rapid population growth may have eased some of those pressures during Joe Biden’s administration. Watson’s team estimated net migration of 2.8mn people in 2022 and 3.4mn in 2023, well above the roughly 1mn annual inflow she considers “normal”.
That surge could have given businesses an exaggerated sense of the opportunity for expansion, she said.
“If firms thought that [growth] was likely to continue, they might have over-expanded,” Watson said.

The reversal has shown up in restaurant companies’ results. In 2025, as the White House intensified efforts to deport undocumented immigrants, Jack in the Box and Wingstop said sales were suffering as Latino consumers pulled back.
Recommended
Many fast-food companies reported an improvement in business in the most recent quarter, which executives attributed to lower petrol prices and a stronger consumer economy.
But analysts say the longer-term pressure on growth — and the risk that the US has too many restaurants chasing too few customers — will persist if population growth remains weak.

“If you talk to people in the industry, there’s a sense that this [downturn] is cyclical,” said Harbour, the Morgan Stanley analyst. “I do feel like the ‘over-storing’ piece is a little more structural, and probably something that takes longer to work through.”

/content/bcb35264-a96c-49c0-984f-4b379d0.title: Anglo Teck up against Glencore’s ‘hardball’ negotiators to deliver merger gains
articleContent: Glencore is threatening to frustrate Anglo American’s efforts to reap the benefits of its $50bn merger with Teck Resources as part of negotiations over the integration of mines in the deal to create a copper-mining giant.

Anglo hopes to close the deal as soon as next month but is waiting for Chinese regulatory approval. The deal, announced last September, is the biggest mining merger in years, even as investors around the sector put pressure on boards to find new sources of copper.
The desire to combine copper assets motivated BHP’s rejected takeover bids for Anglo American in 2024 and Rio Tinto and Glencore’s failed merger talks earlier this year.

Talks between Anglo and Glencore are under way to bring some operations together from the Collahuasi mine, in which Anglo and the Swiss company each hold 44 per cent, and Teck’s nearby Quebrada Blanca copper complex.

Combining the mines was key to the deal’s rationale. Anglo chief executive Duncan Wanblad said last year a tie-up agreed by Glencore could add $1.4bn in earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation a year. “The industrial logic of combining Collahuasi and Quebrada Blanca is undeniable,” he said.
But one former Anglo insider said Glencore would “demand a serious price” in talks over the mine’s value compared to Teck’s assets and how it will be run.

The Swiss company “understands there is some real economic value to go after and is likely to play hardball”, said a top Anglo investor. “I don’t expect it to be smooth and easy. Glencore is in the stronger bargaining position.”
Speaking to the FT in July, Wanblad said talks with Glencore were “in progress”.

“Everybody will be looking to make sure we’ve got the right valuations,” he said. “All of us have to get an alignment on that in the first instance and then work out how we distribute the synergy value between us.”
Glencore declined to comment.

Copper is essential to a range of modern industries and is expected to be in short supply in the coming decades, with diversified miners looking to increase their exposure to the metal. Copper miners are valued more highly than companies with broader commodities exposure.
The red metal climbed close to its record high in August after several mine interruptions and continued to flow in huge quantities into the US in anticipation of possible import tariffs.
Anglo has emerged as a key player in the race to mine more of the red metal, when not long ago the miner faced a sinking share price and mounting questions about its sprawling portfolio.

There was a marked downturn in Anglo’s sales and earnings from 2022 to 2024, in part on the falling price of platinum and diamonds. But BHP’s failed bid catalysed a radical turnaround plan, designed to streamline the group and focus on copper, iron ore and crop nutrients.

With its platinum business now spun off and buyers found for its coal and nickel units, Anglo’s sales and earnings from its continuing operations — which exclude those segments — were higher in the first six months of 2026 than in the same periods in 2024 and 2025 on a pro forma basis.

Copper accounted for almost three quarters of those earnings this year — though that was largely the result of higher prices, not added production. In the first half of 2023, by contrast, copper accounted for under a third of Anglo’s earnings.

The performance over the past two years is a “vindication for the board and also for Duncan . . . He got put in a tough spot. But I think Duncan is in a far strengthened position,” said Adam Matthews, chief responsible investment officer at the Church of England Pensions Board, a shareholder.
“The unknown is Glencore,” said George Cheveley, portfolio manager at Ninety One, an Anglo shareholder. “There’s a negotiation to be had.”
Talks will see the groups thrash out the changes at the two mines, how much additional value that will create and how to share out the benefits between the partners.
One Anglo investor said they expected that “not all the economic value that would rationally be ascribed to the Anglo Teck side will be ascribed to them”.

Investors have continued to speculate about whether BHP — which said earlier this month that copper had overtaken iron ore as its primary profit driver for the first time — could return with a buyout offer for the combined Anglo Teck.
BHP’s new chief executive Brandon Craig said the company’s focus was its “major organic growth programme”.
Anglo investors said they would be reluctant to back any new bid for the company. “I think you would see strong resistance,” said Matthews.

/content/4822389d-5bb2-4e31-a627-bcda849.title: Swiss wealth managers urge delay to ownership register after Liechtenstein hack
articleContent: Swiss wealth managers are urging the government to halt the launch of a vast new register of company owners after hackers stole similar data on thousands of people from neighbouring Liechtenstein.

The Swiss Association of Wealth Managers has asked Bern to pause the October 1 rollout of its new “transparency register”, which will be accessible by designated authorities and financial institutions subject to anti-money laundering rules but not directly by the public.

The association warned the government that concentrating information on the ultimate owners of more than 500,000 companies and other legal entities in one place would create an attractive target for cyber criminals.

The Swiss Bankers Association has separately raised concerns over cyber security and data protection relating to the register, which has been under development for three years in a country known as a haven for often secretive wealth.

The financiers’ intervention follows a major breach of Liechtenstein’s equivalent register in late July, in which unknown hackers stole beneficial ownership data relating to about 31,000 companies, foundations and trusts. Authorities have yet to identify the attackers or establish their motive.

Switzerland is creating the register as part of efforts to strengthen its defences against money laundering and meet international standards ahead of a review by the Paris-based Financial Action Task Force next year.

From October, companies and other legal entities will be required to report the individuals who ultimately control them to the central federal database. As well as names, the register is due to include data on dates of birth, nationalities, postcodes and places of residence.
The stakes are particularly high for Switzerland, whose financial sector accounts for about 9 per cent of GDP and remains one of the world’s biggest centres for cross-border private wealth.

In a letter to Swiss justice minister Beat Jans seen by the FT, the wealth managers’ association warned this week that Switzerland was creating an “extremely attractive target for cyber criminals” by collecting highly sensitive ownership information in a central database.

Vivien Jain, the association’s chief executive, told the FT the new register should be paused for an official security assessment following the attack in Liechtenstein. “The reputation of our financial centre is at stake,” she added.
The SBA had similarly expressed concerns about the register’s safety, said multiple people familiar with the situation.

“Transparency registers contain highly sensitive information and therefore require particularly strong safeguards . . . it will be crucial that the highest standards of data protection and cyber security are maintained,” the SBA said.

The government said the law mandating the register “will enter into force on October 1, 2026”, adding that “the incident in Liechtenstein demonstrates once again the importance of the planned measures to ensure IT security”.
The Federal Office of Justice, part of the justice ministry, said it was “taking this security incident seriously and is in contact with the Liechtenstein authorities”.

The pushback is likely to draw scrutiny given Switzerland’s history as a haven for secretive wealth. Although Bern has dismantled much of its traditional bank secrecy regime under international pressure, campaigners have long argued that greater transparency over who ultimately controls companies is essential to combat money laundering and other financial crime.

“Delaying implementation would not mean abandoning transparency. It would mean ensuring that transparency is pursued without creating disproportionate risks,” said Fabio Poma, managing director of wealth manager WMM Group and vice-president of the Swiss Association of Wealth Managers.

Switzerland is tightening its regime just as the US is moving in the opposite direction. On August 11, less than two weeks after the Liechtenstein breach, the US Treasury made permanent an earlier retreat from ownership reporting, exempting domestic companies and US persons and saying it would delete information on Americans already collected.

“If even the US has reconsidered its model, it is legitimate to ask why Bern, particularly following the warning signal from Liechtenstein, should necessarily proceed with TranspaReg as early as October 1,” Poma added.
Jamie Vrijhof, managing partner of Zurich-based wealth manager WHVP, said the developments in Liechtenstein and the US strengthened the case for Switzerland to hold off.
“For me, the benefits are very close to zero, and the risks are potentially extremely high,” she said.
One option suggested by wealth managers could be to allow viewers to retrieve only certain information rather than accessing the entire database.

But Patrick Humbert-Verri, chief operating officer of Swiss wealth manager Probus Pleion, was sceptical that restricting access would eliminate the underlying risk. “The access will not be public, but the information will be somewhere,” he said. “If there is a big leak, it will be exactly the same story, but this time in Switzerland.”

/content/359d4ea5-59b6-425f-ac66-c9836ce.title: Glencore threatened with $1.4bn lawsuit from embattled trader Radiant
articleContent: Embattled iron ore trader Radiant World is threatening legal action against Glencore, alleging that its larger rival is responsible for over $1.4bn of losses as part of a wider dispute between the two groups.
Singapore-based Radiant, which grew rapidly from relative obscurity to become one of the largest iron ore traders in the world, has been battling a liquidity squeeze in recent weeks.

Banks and trading firms including Glencore cut the group off over alleged inconsistencies in the documentation underpinning its trades. Japanese lender Mizuho — which was one of dozens of global banks that lent money to the business over the years — on Friday brought a legal challenge to Radiant World in Singapore’s Supreme Court.
Singapore’s police also confirmed to the FT that they were carrying out an investigation into Radiant — which is headquartered in the city state — after receiving complaints about the business.

Radiant, which has denied any wrongdoing, sent a legal letter to Glencore on Thursday seeking to recover more than $800mn that Radiant and another entity, Sapphire Minmetals, claim they had already paid to the Anglo-Swiss metals and mining group in recent years, as well as losses from “the destruction of the value” of its business.

“These claims are meritless and Glencore will vigorously contest them,” Glencore told the FT, adding that it “has incurred losses and been exposed to risks by Radiant’s actions and will take appropriate action”.
Glencore said this month that it had stopped doing business with Radiant and had taken a provision relating to its contracts with the trader.

Radiant’s letter describes a complex trading and financing relationship with the London-listed commodities trading giant stretching back years that came to a head in 2021, when Glencore allegedly decided to close out derivatives positions and demanded repayment of almost $1.2bn in exposure it said Radiant and Sapphire had racked up under the derivatives contract.

Radiant previously owned a stake in Sapphire but disposed of its shares in the group in 2015, according to Hong Kong corporate records. Radiant described Sapphire as a “separate legal entity” in its letter to Glencore, while Sapphire stated in response to a Bloomberg News article earlier this month that a “historical shareholding does not imply operational or financial co-relation today”.

Radiant has alleged that the parties reached an agreement over the derivatives exposure, which allowed them to gradually pay it down while Glencore assisted the Singapore-based trading firm in raising outside financing and investment.
In its letter, Radiant cited a WhatsApp message allegedly sent by senior Glencore executive Peter Hill in 2024 outlining the support it had offered the iron ore trader.

“Remember — we are the guys that you were allowed to build up $1.2bio [sic] exposure to and basically bank rolled your entire existence for the last few years,” Hill’s alleged WhatsApp message states. “So give me a break and relax, we will always support you as we have done and continue to do so.. we will do so to the extent it makes sense for us.”
Hill declined to comment.

Radiant also alleged that its relationship with Glencore went beyond that of a counterparty and described the commodities group as “a senior partner in the relationship”. It claims that Glencore reviewed and approved the qualifications of potential hires, advised the company on fundraising, and suggested the price at which it should enter into trades.

The letter also alleged that Glencore struck a deal under which it subscribed to a 4.995 per cent equity warrant in Radiant and subsequently communicated that it would “assist in bringing hedge funds and other investors” to finance the group. Glencore allegedly forecast that Radiant’s valuation could reach around $5bn through this additional investment.

Radiant claimed that Glencore recently served a termination notice to the Singapore firm and Sapphire, alleging that they owed the London-listed group $951mn, set off against $471mn that Glencore owed back to the two firms.

“The exposure on our books [to Radiant] is not material and well below our threshold of $500mn,” Glencore said earlier this month. That figure takes into account the provisions Glencore has already booked.

A person familiar with the matter said that Glencore’s net exposure to Radiant had always been under $1bn, and on average over the past decade Radiant had accounted for less than 10 per cent of Glencore’s iron ore business in volume terms.

/content/8eaa49a6-6722-46fc-be4c-cce25ed.title: James Cleverly steps down from shadow cabinet to run for London mayor
articleContent: Conservative MP Sir James Cleverly has stepped down from the shadow cabinet to prepare a bid to become London mayor, arguing the UK capital is being treated as a “cash cow” by Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Cleverly said he wanted to challenge incumbent mayor Sadiq Khan and fight what he described as Burnham’s plans for London to be “taxed, regulated, raided and blamed”.
The former Foreign and Home Secretary in the last Conservative government has held the position of shadow housing secretary under Tory leader Kemi Badenoch since July 2025.

“Burnham treats London as a cash cow: somewhere to be taxed, regulated, raided and blamed,” Cleverly said in a statement. “Londoners are crying out for a mayor who will take the lead out of the saddle, the rocks out of the rucksack and the drag anchor off our economy.”

The MP for Braintree in Essex, who still needs to win the Conservative nomination for the contest, added that he believed Labour’s Khan, who has been Mayor of London for a decade, had let London’s reputation “slip at home and abroad” while “too many of its problems have been left to fester”.

Cleverly’s move comes as the Conservatives are languishing in the polls behind Labour and the populist, anti-immigration Reform Party, though Badenoch’s personal approval ratings have risen in recent months.

Nigel Farage, leader of Reform UK, suggested on X that Cleverly “will not be the first Tory MP to give up any hope of winning their seat in Essex” at the next general election. “They are done for,” he said.
Cleverly, who lost out to Badenoch in the race to become Conservative leader in 2024, has long been rumoured to be considering running for mayor. The vote in the capital is due to be held in 2028.

Cleverly told the Sunday Times he saw London as key to sparking a revival for the Conservatives. “Our route to getting Kemi in No 10 has got to be through success in London,” he said. “It’s a business city, entrepreneurialism, arts, culture. I don’t buy the lazy idea that London is a Labour city. It represents the philosophical heart of the Conservative Party.”
Boris Johnson, the former Conservative prime minister, served as mayor of London from 2008 to 2016.
Cleverly said Badenoch had taken his decision to step down from the shadow cabinet “very well”, describing her as “gracious”.
Badenoch is expected to undertake a shadow cabinet reshuffle in the coming weeks. The Conservative Party annual conference is due to be held in early October.

Burnham, previously mayor of Greater Manchester, took over from Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister in July and has since established a “Number 10 North” that his government argues will help spread power and decision-making outside London.

In the past Burnham has supported scrapping council tax and stamp duty, replacing them with a land tax on a property’s value. If ever introduced, such a policy would be likely to disproportionately affect homeowners in London and the south-east of England.

/content/c0687fe3-a984-4082-927d-e614eb7.title: Bayeux deal could pave way for Parthenon marbles loan, says British Museum head
articleContent: The deal that brought the Bayeux Tapestry to the UK could pave the way for a loan of the Parthenon Sculptures to Greece, the director of the British Museum has said, reviving the prospect that one of the world’s thorniest arts disputes could finally be resolved.

Nicholas Cullinan told the FT that the return of the near-1,000-year-old embroidery, which will go on display on September 10 after a deal between Britain and France, was “a very compelling example of international partnership” that pointed to the success of “reciprocal exchange”.
“Every example of a relationship or cultural history is different, so there isn’t a cookie-cutter template,” Cullinan said in an interview.
“That said, you would hope the fact that it took several goes to pull off the Bayeux Tapestry loan might provide a glimmer of possibility to move forward [on the sculptures].”
“I would hope that some tangible progress can happen,” he added, of the 2,500-year-old carvings. “It would be a wonderful thing.”
The sculptures, often known as the Elgin Marbles after the Scottish aristocrat who brought them to Britain from the Acropolis in Athens in the early 19th century, have long been contested.

Greece made its first formal request for the permanent return of the sculptures in 1983, and talks picked up after former Conservative chancellor George Osborne became chair of the British Museum in 2021.

As prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer made clear he would not block a loan accord, under which parts of the frieze would be shipped to Athens for specific periods while significant Greek antiquities were shown in London, if the two sides could reach agreement. But Greece has insisted on ownership.

His successor Andy Burnham told the FT this week that the future of the sculptures was a matter for the British Museum, despite previously calling for the artefacts to be returned to Greece permanently.

Approximately 1,630 other objects from the museum’s 8mn-strong collection were on long-term loan nationally last year, and Cullinan said the museum would “always remain open for dialogue” around the sculptures, acquired in 1816.

But the former head of the National Portrait Gallery and Tate curator warned of “unintended consequences” if the British Museum Act 1963 were amended to allow artefacts in its possession to be removed.
“As a museum person, I think you’re always thinking about being a temporary custodian of these objects . . . you never know how future generations will perceive what you’ve done,” he said.
“I’m glad that, when the pandemic began in 2020, museums couldn’t begin a fire sale of their collections, because that definitely would have happened if the law had not prevented de-accession.”
Three years ago, revelations of the theft of about 2,000 items including ancient semi-precious stones rocked the museum’s reputation and prompted the exit of its previous chief.
Now Cullinan, 48, and his team see the Bayeux Tapestry as a coup of cultural diplomacy that should draw positive international attention.

The display of the 70-metre fabric depiction of the Norman Conquest, thought to have been made by nuns in England in the 11th century, will be the biggest and most expensive exhibition in the institution’s 273-year history.
Running until next July, the show will coincide with the transfer of treasures from the Sutton Hoo burial ship and the Lewis Chessmen to France.

Before his death in June, the painter David Hockney accused the museum of “vanity” in moving the tapestry from Bayeux, echoing concerns voiced by some in the French art establishment about its fragility.

Cullinan said the tapestry was in “fantastic condition” and would not have travelled — via the Channel Tunnel last month, under police escort — if “people with intimate knowledge and expertise” had “raised a flag”.
Other critics have hit out at entry prices to the exhibition, which is being sponsored by hedge fund billionaire Igor Tulchinsky in a deal valued at £5mn.
A standard adult ticket costs £33, while under-16s go free. The first allocation sold out in just over a day last month, yielding more than £2.5mn.
Cullinan said the museum had “thought long and hard” about prices and hoped to turn a profit on the exhibition.
Recommended
“We could probably have tried to accommodate more visitors, but quality has been as important as quantity,” he said.

The institution, which this month celebrated the 20th anniversary of its international training programme for cultural heritage professionals, welcomed 6.5mn visitors last year, most from overseas. It hopes to draw more with a new entrance pavilion and garden from next spring.
Asked about ministers’ proposal to charge overseas tourists to access venues such as his, Cullinan said ending the policy of free admission was “not something to be done lightly”.

The museum raised £2.5mn through its inaugural ball last October. It is now stepping up efforts to attract donors to its £1bn redevelopment of the Western Range galleries, which is set to last about a decade.

During the renovation, some artefacts housed in the complex network of 10 separate buildings, which include the Parthenon Sculptures, “may be loaned as part of our commitment to increase national and international loans”, the museum has said.
Recommended

Detailed designs for the project, led by Beirut-born architect Lina Ghotmeh, would become public by 2028, Cullinan said, with a bigger “master plan” aiming to create space for “entire sections of the collection, like south-east Asia and the Caribbean” never exhibited before.

A major gift towards the renovation would be announced in the autumn, and “conversations are happening” about donations in the region of £150mn, which would match record-breaking sums secured by the National Gallery in 2025, he added.
“The transformation of this building is a generational change, and it brings huge potential to get more of the collection out in the world and rethink the role of a universal museum,” Cullinan said.
“It’s a big, collective endeavour, and it’s not an overnight thing. We’re in the limbering-up phase.”

/content/d3924170-6978-4b0a-8357-a621c0d.title: English wine reaps rewards of heatwave but extreme weather brings risk
articleContent: England’s wine industry is celebrating a successful harvest, with the year’s hot weather raising hopes of a potential expansion of red wine production. But there are also fears about the impact of more extreme weather in future.
In a year which has seen temperatures rise as high as 38.1C and the majority of England in drought, winemakers say the quality of their grapes has been enhanced.
Yet, keenly aware of the risks that heavy rainfall may pose, many are reluctant to focus all their efforts on preparing for heatwaves.

Alastair Benham, head of wine operations at Kent-based producer Gusbourne, said the heat had had a “really positive impact” on the vineyard, with the fruit harvested so far in “exceptional condition”.
But Benham notes that just two years ago “we had quite a cool, wet vintage”.
“I think it’s [about] allowing ourselves to be nimble and . . . [using] techniques to try and mitigate the impact of those extreme events,” he said.
Ian Beecher-Jones, owner of JoJo’s Vineyard in Henley-on-Thames, Oxford, said: “It’s gearing up to be a good year . . . from a grape point of view.”
He suggested that producers should not limit themselves to preparing for hot weather.

“Whilst it’s easy to focus on higher temperatures . . . we may well be looking at greater rainfall and how we manage the soils,” Beecher-Jones said, adding: “As farmers we’re having to look at either end of the spectrum.”
He said it would be too early to go down the “drastic route” of considering new grape varieties solely to account for the heat.

Beecher-Jones added they should instead consider “more affordable, cost-effective” tools that protect against various weather events, such as “cover crops”, which are planted off-season to preserve and enrich the soil.
Sam Lindo, who runs Camel Valley vineyard in Bodmin, Cornwall, said the grapes were looking “really good”.

However, sparkling wine would be “slightly different” and it would be necessary to “minimise” the yield’s flavour through whole-bunch pressing, a much lengthier process by which entire bunches of grapes are put into a press rather than being crushed and de-stemmed first.

“For the traditional method of sparkling wine that we make here . . . the wine that you start with before the second fermentation is one of minimal character because the bubbles are going to exaggerate any character you have . . . That’s why the best sparkling wines are not made in really hot places,” Lindo explained.
“To carry on making traditional method sparkling we need to make sure there is not too much flavour in the base wine . . . It was an easy job that was done by nature until this year,” he added.

Although Lindo said it was “too early to start ripping up some of the varieties that are grown in the UK”, he believes that for others, their days are “numbered”. Varieties such as Schönburger and Siegerrebe were ripe far too early this year with “extremely low acid” levels.

Wine expert and business consultant Kent Barker said that continued hot weather could improve English winemakers’ chances of producing high-quality red wine, which is often associated with France and Spain.
“One of the things we can’t do that well . . . at the moment is red wine. That’s certainly changing,” he said.
“At the moment we produce wonderful sparkling wine and our white wine is gaining ground, but our red wine has always lagged,” Barker added.

Christopher Walkey, co-founder of wine consultancy Clerissa, also thinks the warmer weather could lead to more winemakers in England. “New producers are up, production is up and sales internationally are up. These positive figures intrigue and attract business individuals.”

Cherie Spriggs, head winemaker at Nyetimber, which has 11 vineyards in West Sussex, Kent and Hampshire, said it was difficult to know how to prepare for future harvests “because it’s not a straightforward scenario”.
“We’ve had years in very recent history . . . where frankly the growing season was the opposite [to this one], quite cool or quite wet,” she said.
“The only way we can continue to work is how we have already been working, which is to be prepared for both scenarios. And that’s very hard,” Spriggs added.

Changing grape variety is one option for Denbies Wine Estate in Surrey. Chief executive Chris White said that, if hot summers persist, they may turn to grapes which “ripen slightly earlier on in the season” such as the Pinot Noir and Chardonnay varieties.
But if wet periods become more frequent, Denbies may move towards hybrid varieties which are “slightly more disease resistant”.
Galia Pike, creative director at Westwell Wine Estates in Kent, said the business would experience an “amazing harvest” this year.
However, she said that just because some years were “really exceptional”, like this one, “that’s not to say that next year’s going to be anything like it”.
This article has been amended after publication to correct the location of Denbies Wine Estate

/content/fc925436-4bcb-444c-b929-83014f6.title: Healey to shelve his own defence spending target of 3% of GDP by 2030
articleContent: Chancellor John Healey will shelve his own target of spending 3 per cent of Britain’s GDP on defence by 2030 when he presents his first Budget in October, with tough decisions on how to fund the military pushed down the track.

Healey resigned as defence secretary in June over what he saw as inadequate ambition for military spending by Sir Keir Starmer’s government, but since arriving at the Treasury has had to grapple with financial constraints.
Healey’s previous insistence that Britain should spend 3 per cent of its GDP on defence by 2030 — as a milestone to reaching a Nato target of 3.5 per cent by 2035 — is now up in the air.

Government insiders told the FT that Healey’s Budget would focus on filling a defence equipment funding gap of nearly £5bn left behind by former prime minister Keir Starmer, amounting to about £1.2bn a year.
Recommended
But much bigger decisions on an uplift in defence spending will be delayed until a Treasury spending review next year.
One government figure said: “The immediate priority is to fund the defence investment plan that was published by Keir Starmer and the chancellor will set out more details on that at the Budget.”

“Beyond that, at the spending review we’ll set out a clear path to meet our 3.5 per cent Nato target in 2035 and set a target date for us to hit 3 per cent on that path. The spending review is the right place to set a target date,” they added.
Bee Boileau, a researcher at the Institute for Fiscal Studies think-tank, said raising spending to 3 per cent in 2030 would cost an extra £10bn a year in today’s terms.
Boosting spending further to 3.5 per cent of GDP would cost £25bn compared with existing levels.
Defence spending is currently set to reach 2.7 per cent of GDP by 2030.

Boileau said lifting defence spending to 3 per cent of GDP in 2030 would provide a “sensible waypoint” if the government were to increase outlays in a linear way on its route to the ultimate Nato target, but that the increase could be backloaded.
The chancellor was previously adamant that Britain must increase defence spending to 3 per cent by 2030, notably to address a growing threat from Russia.

In his resignation letter to Starmer in June, the former defence secretary said: “As we have regularly discussed, I am certain that a headmark date for 3 per cent of GDP on defence in 2030 is what Britain must set.”
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has refused to commit to hitting a 3 per cent of GDP target by 2030. He said this week that the fiscal backdrop to the Budget was “challenging”.
Wes Streeting, defence secretary, has also declined to commit to such a target, but said: “I certainly feel like we have a firm friend in His Majesty’s Treasury.”
A government spokesperson said: “The first duty of government is to keep its citizens safe. The prime minister and chancellor are committed to fully funding the Defence Investment Plan.”
“At the spending review we will set out a pathway to meet our Nato commitment of 3.5 per cent of GDP on defence by 2035 and will set a target date to hit 3 per cent on that path.”
James Cartlidge MP, Shadow defence secretary, said it was “extraordinary that [Healey] is backtracking on the very pledge which sealed the fate of the last PM”.
He urged the government to meet the 3 per cent target, adding: “Russia doesn’t work to Treasury timetables, and we can’t wait for a spending review to keep Britain safe.”

In an interview with Sky News broadcast on Friday, Healey said that “fiscal discipline” was the “first priority” for any chancellor, adding that a Burnham government “simply can’t deal with the problems we face as a country by maxing out the country’s credit card”.

When asked about the 3 per cent defence spending target, he said: “Fiscal discipline has been the bedrock of the government that I was part of for the first couple of years, as a Labour government since July 2024.”
“We build on that but it is not easy. It is not easy in a world in which you see global conflict, increasing dangers,” Healey added.
Robert Jenrick, Reform UK’s Treasury spokesperson, said that Healey’s comments “confirmed what the rest of us already knew”.
“Andy Burnham isn’t a fresh start — he’s just continuity Labour with a new face,” Jenrick said.
Additional reporting by David Sheppard and Rachel Rees

/content/157eedfa-fe64-4494-840a-b4a60e5.title: UK Science Museum drops BP as a sponsor
articleContent: The UK Science Museum has dropped BP as a sponsor, ending a partnership with the British oil and gas major that stretched back a quarter of a century but was long criticised by environmentalists.

The London museum said on Friday that BP’s sponsorship of its “academy”, which offers training programmes to teachers and science industry professionals, would expire “at the end of its agreed term” next Monday.
The institution is a major tourist attraction in the UK capital and welcomed 2.64mn visitors last year.

But the Science Museum has faced repeated criticism from climate activists over its longstanding ties to BP, which last year ditched former chief executive Bernard Looney’s strategy of seeking to turn the company into an energy-transition leader.
More recently it has come under fire for accepting money from Adani Group, which is India’s largest renewable energy producer but also one of the biggest coal-mining and trading groups in the world.

Environmental campaigners have accused BP and Adani Group of greenwashing and the museum’s 2021 deal with the Indian conglomerate’s renewable power arm to sponsor a green energy wing — which was worth £4mn, according to UK government documents — prompted two trustees to resign.

The National Education Union, Britain’s biggest teaching union, last year endorsed a boycott of the museum over BP’s sponsorship of its academy, which was set up in 2018 to provide “training and resources” to teachers and other educators. The museum has not disclosed the value of the BP sponsorship.

Culture Unstained, an anti-fossil fuel sponsorship campaign group, said on Friday the museum had “finally come to its senses . . . after years of campaigning and growing pressure from educators and schools pledging to boycott trips”.
“But today represents only a partial victory — the museum . . . must now bring to an end its indefensible sponsorship deal with Adani,” it added.
BP has sponsored the museum’s academy since its launch, but ties between the FTSE 100 company and the institution stretch back to the early 2000s.

Sir Ian Blatchford, Science Museum director, has strongly defended sponsorship from oil and gas companies in the past. He told the FT in 2022: “Business and finance is so complex and intertwined. There’s a danger that if the arts world is not careful, it will be eaten alive by its own piety.”
However, much of the cultural sector has backed away from fossil-fuel sponsorship in recent years, following pressure from artists, patrons and campaigners.
In 2016, BP announced an end to its near 30-year sponsorship of the Tate network of art galleries, and in 2022 the National Portrait Gallery cut ties with the company after more than three decades.
But in a break with the sector-wide trend, the British Museum in 2023 agreed a fresh £50mn sponsorship deal with BP, sparking claims by Greenpeace of “brazen greenwashing”.
Blatchford said in a statement on Friday: “The Science Museum Group Academy’s partnership with BP has drawn to a close at the end of the current contract term.

“BP’s generous contributions helped us to inspire more than 11,000 education, museum and science professionals through research-informed science engagement training, supporting vital work to spark curiosity and bring science to life for more than a million young people across the country,” he added.
The Science Museum did not comment on Culture Unstained’s call for it to end its sponsorship deal with Adani Group.
BP said in a statement: “BP and the Science Museum Group Academy’s partnership will draw to a close on Monday 31 August at the end of its agreed term.”

/content/6249139a-6ca6-4888-86e2-f2f381e.title: Football clubs’ race for data creates bright spot in Britain labour market
articleContent: Professional football clubs’ share of UK hiring has tripled over the past five years, with a jump in demand for data experts as Britain’s top teams use their growing financial strength to expand their off-field operations.

The clubs have emerged as a bright spot in an otherwise sluggish British jobs market, now accounting for more than seven in every 10,000 roles advertised, up from 2.4 per 10,000 in 2020, according to data from recruitment website Indeed.
Data and analytics make up 5 per cent of the roles advertised by Premier League teams this year, according to job analytics firm Lightcast. This is double the share two years ago.

The hiring boom has been fuelled by the deep pockets of Premier League clubs, which have seen revenues soar off the back of strong performances in European competitions and lucrative new commercial deals.

“Data and analytics is an area where clubs have increased their focus to try to find an edge on rival clubs in areas like player recruitment and opposition analysis,” said Jack Kennedy, senior economist at Indeed.

Brighton and Hove Albion, Newcastle United and Manchester United have increased hiring for data and analysis roles the most over the past five years, according to analysis of job postings by Lightcast.

Current openings include a scouting insights analyst at Tottenham Hotspur, described as “a key role in shaping the club’s player recruitment strategy through data-driven analysis and insight”, and a position in Brentford’s insights and strategy department.
Kennedy said Brentford and Brighton, both promoted in the past decade, “really punch above their weight” as they tend to be more effective at using data.
“Both of those club owners made their money as professional gamblers so they’ve always been very data-driven and applied that to owning football clubs,” he added.
“The legacy clubs can almost buy their way out of trouble so if they make a signing that doesn’t work out, they can just spend £100mn on another player. Smaller clubs cannot do that.”
Premier League clubs are set to break the record for transfer spending this summer, with Chelsea and Tottenham Hotspur topping the charts as the September 1 deadline nears.

Joris Bekkers, a football analytics and tech strategy consultant at UnravelSports, said the rise in hiring was probably down to a combination of factors, including expanding budgets, the buzz around AI, younger and more innovative decision makers and clubs recognising that the workload has become too great for a one-person data department.
“Teams no longer have just a single data scientist, but they might have multiple and they might have data engineers and a whole separate data department,” he added.

The growth in football recruitment is at odds with the wider UK labour market, with Indeed’s mid-year report showing an 11 per cent decline in postings since the start of the year, leaving figures down a third on the pre-pandemic baseline.

/content/aa929cd9-b4b4-4858-9160-4d6f885.title: Middlesbrough crisis highlights challenges for small UK police forces
articleContent: When a car carrying five young men smashed head-on into a police vehicle on August 22 near Middlesbrough in north-east England, the incident at first looked like a horrific but isolated event.

Blame for the crash on the A66, which killed all five in the car and two police officers, initially focused on a social media craze for young men to post videos of themselves driving the wrong way on busy roads.

But the latest information and subsequent violent incidents have suggested the Cleveland Police are grappling with a series of tit-for-tat attacks that have strained the capacity of a relatively small force. It has arrested 24 people since August 22 — including seven on Friday — on suspicion of involvement in serious and organised crime.

The force is also dealing with an alleged arson attack in the early hours of Wednesday on a house, near the scene of the August 22 crash, that killed a 34-year-old woman and her seven-year-old niece. Cleveland Police said they were not currently linking that incident — for which two people have been arrested on suspicion of murder — to the crash.
Cleveland Police’s assistant chief constable Dave Sutherland on Friday acknowledged the attention that the incidents had drawn.
He said: “Since these tragic incidents, the reality of policing in Cleveland, and the levels of violence suffered in our communities, have come under the spotlight on a national level.”

Helen King, a former assistant commissioner of London’s Metropolitan Police, now principal of St Anne’s College, Oxford, pointed out that Cleveland Police currently had only about 1,500 officers, some 250 fewer than in 2009.

The force — the 13th smallest by officer numbers of the 43 in England and Wales — has had to call in 200 officers from the National Crime Agency and other police forces to help it cope with the crisis.

“They’ve got all the complexity and intensity of crime issues that are normal levels in forces like Merseyside or West Midlands or Manchester that have got a much larger infrastructure and resource pool to call on,” King said.
Alec Brown, Labour leader of Redcar and Cleveland Council, said the “unprecedented” events had left people in the area concerned for their safety.
“People feel . . . unsupported and forgotten,” he said.

The factors underlying this week’s events have not been fully explained. Police have said that in the hours before the August 22 crash, two cars were seen being driven dangerously in the Middlesbrough area, with one — a Volvo XC60 — ramming into properties. The other vehicle involved — a Volkswagen Passat — was later involved in the head-on crash on the A66. Police have said that four of the five killed in the Passat — who were aged between 17 and 23 — had previous criminal records.
Brown said police had asked him not to speculate on what was behind the various incidents.
King said the challenge of incidents involving organised crime groups was that members felt “reputation-dependent”.
“When a gang or any individual has been subject to some attack or slight, they have to have some kind of public retribution,” she said.

She added that, in a situation where large numbers of people from one group had died or otherwise been taken out of action, it would create “instability” as survivors worried about issues such as where any illegal drugs, firearms or money might be.
King said that, as well as seeking to arrest those responsible, police could mount visible patrols in the affected areas to reassure residents.
The police force was coping with the crisis while members were mourning the two colleagues who had died, she pointed out. “It’s a very difficult situation all round.”
Brown insisted that overall numbers of calls to the police were down for the time of year. “It’s my job as council leader to try to give people reassurance.”
However, Brown also pointed to wider problems. As well as the cuts to policing, his area had suffered cuts to wider public services, including mental health provision, in the past 15 years, he said.

Cleveland Police’s most recent inspection report by HM Inspectorate of Constabulary said the force had the highest levels of deprivation in any police force in England and Wales and the highest number of recorded incidents per head of population. Incidents include reports of crime and other complaints, such as antisocial behaviour, that may not qualify as a crime.
Cleveland Police’s Sutherland on Friday said the force would remain “unwavering” in its efforts to tackle criminals.

King, meanwhile, said the week had shown the continued importance of reforming policing in England and Wales. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood in January announced plans to cut from 43 the number of police forces in England and Wales.
Lord Bernard Hogan-Howe, leader of a review charged with devising plans for force mergers, has been asked to revisit his conclusions to fit in with the prime minister’s thinking on devolution.
King said that, without reform, forces such as Cleveland would struggle to develop the specialist capabilities needed to tackle organised crime.
“Cleveland has the size of a small or medium county force, but with all the problems of an inner-city area,” she said.

/content/73507be3-f4c9-420f-9476-9418330.title: Balvenie’s 88-year-old whisky is the oldest. Is it any good?
articleContent: Next week, The Balvenie will set a new record for the oldest single malt Scotch whisky ever released. Its 88-year-old bottling breaks the previous record (an 85-year-old Glenlivet bottled by Gordon & MacPhail) by three years.
