This superannuated dram was distilled at The Balvenie in Speyside in 1931 from barley grown on the distillery’s estate. It was malted at Balvenie’s own home floor maltings facility, which, unusually, continues to operate to this day. The whisky was then placed in a single sherry butt that lay undisturbed in Dufftown until 2019, when the contents was decanted into glass. It is field-to-bottle in a way that modern grande marque malts rarely are. (There are whiskies in circulation that were distilled prior to 1931 – what makes this one record-breaking is the amount of time spent in the cask.)

The whisky world loves a superlative – so I’m prone to be cynical. I’ve tasted a lot of antiquated spirits, and if it’s taught me anything it’s that older is not necessarily better. There are very mature whiskies with incredible flavour, but plenty more just taste as tannic, woody and lifeless as a creaky antique. Knowing how far you can push is a real skill. But simply seeking deliciousness is perhaps missing the point. Part of the thrill of tasting old whisky is that each sip is a step back in time. And the lineage of this particular whisky is unusually distinct: just before I tasted it, I was shown a black-and-white photo of the distillery team, which includes the malt men (and one distillery dog) who malted the barley for the liquid I was about to sip.

The deep amber spirit is lively and concentrated on the nose, with some of the tropical aromas – passionfruit, mango – that often characterise malts of a great age. There are also maturer, umami-ish notes of Worcester sauce, coffee, tea and tobacco. The palate skews more savoury with a tannin that’s quite brittle at first before softening into a long finish with notes of juniper, bitter orange, dried apricot and fig leaf. It splices charm with gravitas.

Each of the 17 bottles is housed in a patinated bronze-and-wood case designed by Daniel Arsham, an American artist known for works that explore the passage of time. He’ll also direct a live piece inspired by his visits to The Balvenie distillery when the bottles are unveiled at Frieze Seoul. The whisky is only available via private sale, and Balvenie won’t disclose the price. (For context, the RRP for the Gordon & MacPhail Glenlivet 85-year-old, released in 2025, was £125,000.) The estimates I sought from rare whisky specialists were mostly around £200,000-£250,000, though one well-placed source considered even £200,000 “aggressive”. Alongside the 88-year-old will also be a pair of more affordable 12-year-old (£80) and 15-year-old (£150) single malts that have been made using similar heirloom techniques.

It’s only really in the past 20 years that ultra-aged whiskies (with correspondingly “ultra” packaging) have become a phenomenon – a movement spurred by a surge in whisky collecting and investment. Now barely a year goes by without a record being broken. “There is a status intrinsic to a whisky aged 50 years old or more,” says Sotheby’s head of whisky, Jonny Fowle, who sees the trend echoed in the secondary market. “It’s impressive. It’s expensive. The time taken to produce these whiskies is awe-inspiring. Whether or not old whiskies are your thing.”

Everyone is now waiting for the world’s first 100-year-old malt. But how much older can whisky get? One important limiting factor is a whisky’s abv, which falls over time, in cask, due to evaporation (what’s known as the “angel’s share”). In Scotland, freshly distilled spirit (or new make) goes into the cask at around 63.5 per cent abv, and then declines in strength by an average of 0.5 per cent a year. It must be bottled before the strength dips below 40 per cent abv or it can no longer be legally called Scotch malt whisky. (It’s striking how many deluxe whiskies are about to cross this threshold when it is decided they have reached their peak.)
Recommended

Thanks to variations in warehouse microclimates and wood types, some whiskies survive in cask longer than this. And distillers are constantly exploring ways to artificially recreate these conditions – adjusting the temperature or humidity of the maturation warehouse, for example, or even wrapping casks in plastic to reduce evaporation. These may be innovative but they often come with risks: most methods are scalable, they might interfere with other important stages in flavour formation, or even contravening Scotch Whisky Association (SWA) rules.

A 100-year-old malt, then, might be a little way off. And there are plenty of whisky aficionados who prefer bottles even a fraction of that age. Says Fowle: “I would choose a Springbank Samaroli 12-year-old over any 50-year-old whisky.” Perhaps, in this case, it’s a question of beauty before age.
@alicelascelles

/content/6075123e-42f3-4231-ac29-56dc7b1.title: Rugged Americana’s age of innocence
articleContent: “Where Have All the Cowboys Gone?”, Paula Cole sang in her 1996 hit song — but this autumn you’ll know where to find them. A whole army is taking up residence in Paris’s Palais Royal, at Acne Paper gallery: line upon line of pictures of American men posing backstage at rodeos from the 1940s through to the 1970s.

Some smile happily at the camera. Others look pensively away. Some sit casually on a fence or the floor, while a fair few lean back, a little awkward and unsure. All are in the same uniform: shirt and jeans, cowboy boots and hat, occasionally a gleaming belt, with everything just so — except for one guy whose shirt is completely undone, revealing his ruggedly hairy chest. Did he know who was photographing him?

Bruce Bellas (1909-74), aka Bruce of Los Angeles, has been described as “the grandfather of physique photography”; in other words, he’s the daddy of gay picture-making. A former chemistry teacher from Alliance, Nebraska, he gained a cult following with his sexy, cheery images of men in various degrees of the buff, which appeared first in mail-order magazines that were ostensibly fitness-orientated, but had a large illicit gay fan base, and then, from 1956, his own publication Male Figure, which likewise claimed to speak to aspiring artists.

A standard Bellas image is witty, graphic and cheekily artful. The cowboy pictures are a bit of an anomaly, and not just because the men are fully clothed. If Bruce’s fascination with male beauty remains obvious, the effect is softer, sweeter, almost romantic, with no need for the hard sell. They are “modest”, yet sensual, “without having any sense of the men showing off or being obviously ‘sexy’,” says the curator and photography critic Vince Aletti, who owns this cache of images.

Aletti is the author of two photobooks that explore themes of male eroticism: The Drawer (2022) and Physique (2025). He came across the pictures in Physique Memorabilia, a “sort of private salon in a loft” selling all kinds of vintage gay imagery, near his home in New York’s East Village. It turns out that Bellas shot these as he went to see rodeos in Wyoming, Colorado or Canada, mostly for pleasure, not work. Eventually, though, he did include them as an option in Male Figure, a kind of mail-order catalogue for male hotness. “They were clearly, to me, very private,” says Aletti.

Ever since the cowboy rode into North American consciousness in the late 19th century, a descendant of the Spanish Colonies’ vaqueros, he (and eventually she) has had a hold on our imagination. Cowboys very much still exist, working on ranches across the continent, but mostly we appreciate them as an exercise in style. Most of the items of clothing the men in the pictures are wearing have become everyday staples; whenever you put on a shirt and jeans, you are lightly cosplaying the cowboy look. It’s one reason why the lonesome figure keeps coming back into fashion — be it on screen (Yellowstone), on the catwalk (Louis Vuitton’s autumn/winter 2024 menswear show) or in music (Beyoncé’s Cowboy Carter album).

And ultimately, however much we may wonder whether the macho, monosyllabic cowboy is dated — and however much Cole’s song was, in fact, a satire on the romance of it all, bemoaning how her wannabe John Wayne leaves her at home with the dishes — we seem to love it. Impassive and impressive, the cowboy reminds us that there’s still no getting away from America or its impact on our desires.

The pictures in Rodeo do, however, speak to a sunny American optimism that is surely past. There is an innocence to the subjects, and actually to the act of photographing itself, that seems quaint. Yes, these men are posing, but with an artlessness that is essentially now extinct.

“It just feels like it is harder to get unselfconscious, handsome men today,” says Aletti. “They’re all very conscious now of how they look and how they’re dressed. These guys, I’m sure, were very careful about how they looked for the rodeo, because most of them were performing in some way or another, so they were doing something public. But at the same time, it wasn’t showy.”

The art of representing manhood is, now, a much more complicated and self-conscious affair; it is also big business. Compare this long gallery of similar men to the long gallery of similar men who might crop up on anyone’s Instagram feed. Such images are now, by definition, tweaked, curated and captioned to high heaven; the men themselves will be primped, pumped, and — God forbid — even “looksmaxxed”. If these poor cowboys went on social media today, they might discover Reels telling them how exactly to tuck in that shirt, and how best to train your legs so you can ride the horse perfectly. They would be reminded always to wear sunscreen. By contrast, back in the day, the only nutrition advice they’d have sworn by was the virtue of a good bloody steak.

It’s not as though they weren’t performing back then. And it’s not as though the codes of masculinity weren’t any less restrictive. It’s just that the contract was probably simpler, and the pleasure too. Aletti likes the idea of Bellas wandering around backstage at the rodeos, just going up to someone and asking to take a picture, and them acquiescing unthinkingly in the moment. He didn’t even cajole them to strip; the act of being photographed was, crazy as it may seem, enough. “They were just waiting for something to happen,” says Aletti simply.
As for Bellas, he died at a rodeo, of a heart attack, in 1974. The show, says Aletti, is a fitting memorial. It’s also a memorial for a certain way of being.

September 3-October 7, acnestudios.com;
‘Rodeo: Bruce of Los Angeles’, edited by Vince Aletti’is published by Acne Studios
Louis Wise is deputy editor of HTSI

opinion content. 
How finance redeemed itself
articleContent: Only twice in my life have I thought that Britain could succumb to the mob. One was after the death of Diana, when it became unwise and perhaps unhealthy to suggest that people were overdoing the grief. The other was in 2012, when, as a delayed response to the financial crash, bankers were so vilified that some I knew felt unsafe.

I should send them the latest Gallup World Poll. Across the 25 countries that were worst-hit by the crash, trust in financial institutions sank to a low of 37 per cent in, sure enough, 2012. It is now 63 per cent. For context, that is higher than it was pre-crash. Finance has overtaken national government and the judiciary in public esteem. It is even closing in on the military. The HBO/BBC show Industry, with its neutral-to-glamorising portrait of finance, would have been unthinkable a while back.
Tech is the black sheep now. Look at the court settlements. Look at the clamour for regulation. What might the sector learn from finance about how to pull off a redemption?
A certain mathsy naiveté might be inevitable in tech. But the sterile separateness of its home region reinforces it

For one thing, get out of Palo Alto. I don’t just mean travel more, I mean relocate. Financial centres are in big cities, near to other professions and therefore other points of view. In London and New York, the banks if not the funds back on to bohemian districts. The client-facing side of the business also forces people to be out and about. The result? Feedback from the outside world is constant. Public sentiment is unmistakable. Palo Alto, in contrast, is a disastrous place from which to view the world: too cloistered and monocultural. Hence the endless bewilderment of tech bosses that people don’t take their good intentions on faith.

A certain mathsy naiveté might be inevitable in tech. But the sterile separateness of its home region — Nvidia’s HQ could be a Gulf airport — reinforces it. The incomprehension goes both ways. The public’s unease, the sense of “What are they doing over there?”, might soften if the industry were not such a world unto itself.

Besides geography, finance could teach tech another lesson. Give more money away, or rather give it more conspicuously. One sponsor of the upcoming Renoir and Love show at the National Gallery is the hedge fund boss Kenneth Griffin. Another is Rothschild & Co. Frida Kahlo at Tate Modern? Bank of America. You might prefer an outing to the Barclays-emblazoned Lord’s Cricket Ground. You can get there on a red Santander bike.

Finance brands insinuate themselves into the fun or soft areas of national life. As a result, people are disarmed without quite knowing it. (In England, a laddish colloquialism for Premier League football is “Barclays”, as in “What a weekend of Barclays”.) In retrospect, societies let their anti-bank sentiment lapse after the crash in part because it was unaffordable. Much of cultural and sporting life would be at risk without the sector. No doubt, tech is also munificent, and perhaps more rigorously so, given its zeal for measuring inputs and outputs. But effective altruism has to be visible altruism to defang the public.
If relocation is impractical, and high-profile charity too crass, there is much simpler PR advice that finance could offer:
Shut up.

Finance bosses tend not to muse on the course of civilisation, on aesthetics, on what is to be done about this foreign nation or that foreign planet. With exceptions, such as Bill Ackman, their obiter dicta are confined to macroeconomics, and communicated with institutional dryness. This keep-quiet-and-take-the-money approach minimises offence.

For what it’s worth, I think the reputational switch-around of tech and finance is unfair. The former has received no public bailout, at least none of meaningful scale. Its products allow access to the sum of human knowledge for zero marginal cost. The range of social problems for which tech is blamed has become literally incredible. But one stray remark about birth rates on the Dwarkesh Patel podcast and I want to roll out the tumbril.

“Will AI break the world?” has no good answer. “Must we always hear from these people?” clearly does. Strategic silence: I can’t decide if the tech world will find it the easiest advice to implement, or by miles the hardest.
janan.ganesh@ft.com

/content/d767e54e-f1af-4b36-acc4-e3a1e2d.title: Surfin’ Bird — a divisive earworm that has delighted and irritated generations
articleContent: In 1964, a US TV broadcast changed the course of music. No, not The Beatles singing “She Loves You” on The Ed Sullivan Show. For some young viewers, it was an entirely different kind of performance that had a profound effect: one by a besuited Steve Wahrer, lead singer of The Trashmen, performing an awkward chicken dance while barking nonsensical lyrics about birds on American Bandstand, in a moment that proved to be a watershed. (Wahrer was the only member of the group to appear, as they couldn’t afford plane tickets for all of them.)

The song was “Surfin’ Bird”, and the performance has been called the “defining moment” of 1964 by Alfred Yankovic, better known as “Weird Al”. It was “loud, dumb and pointless . . . absolutely everything that was great about rock ’n’ roll distilled into one song,” he told NPR in 2009.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

With its goofy lyrics, “Surfin’ Bird” might never have surpassed the status of novelty hit, but its cultural impact hasn’t faded in the past six decades. New generations of bands, filmmakers and TV writers have confirmed The Trashmen’s claim that “the bird is the word”.

At first listen, the song sounds flimsy, consisting of a three-chord structure, lasting little more than two minutes and garnished with Wahrer’s demented ramblings. But the driving drum patterns and guitar sound inspired by surf music gave the song a rough edge that would later become common in garage rock, and then punk rock.

The bird — originally released in 1963 — had a contested pedigree. The band said that Wahrer had come up with “Surfin’ Bird” as he goofed around backstage at a gig, having heard another local band singing the absurd lyrics. A local DJ, Bill “the Wizard of Wax” Diehl, was in the audience that night as the band were urged to play the experimental “Surfin’ Bird” repeatedly. He encouraged them to record it immediately.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Lawyers soon got involved. “Surfin’ Bird” seemed to be a fusion of parts of two separate songs, “The Bird’s the Word” and “Papa-Oom-Mow-Mow”, both of which had already been released the previous year by a doo-wop group called The Rivingtons. The gentle strains and slow speed of the little-known LA singers may have been a long way from Wahrer’s delivery, but parts of the songs are clearly the same. The Trashmen said they had not heard those recordings, but still opted to credit The Rivingtons as the writers of “Surfin’ Bird”. Meanwhile, the song became a hit, spending more than three months on the charts and reaching number four in 1964.

In 1977, it was revived by The Ramones on their Rocket to Russia album in a sparky, fuzzed-up version. They also discovered first-hand how divisive the song could be when they supported Black Sabbath in San Bernardino in 1978. According to Joey Ramone, “Surfin’ Bird” got the heavy metal crowd agitated, and the band were forced to dodge carburettors, spark plugs and whiskey bottles, eventually exiting the stage when an ice pick landed at their feet.

The bird found a more natural home in the hands of psychobilly pioneers The Cramps, who included a cover on their debut EP in 1978. Their version descends into mayhem as fluttering squawks give way to a reverb-heavy guitar freak-out from Poison Ivy Rorschach. Few frontmen could be trusted to plump up the bird’s feathers with such panache as Cramps singer Lux Interior — one exception being Iggy Pop, who in 2016 was filmed crooning “Surfin’ Bird” to his Moluccan cockatoo Biggy Pop.

Others to take the song on include Australian grunge rockers Silverchair, who sped it up for an ocean tribute album, and a thrash metal version by Germany’s Sodom that proves to be one-note in tone. The Replacements, who like The Trashmen hailed from Minneapolis, chose it for a 2014 reunion show, in homage to the homegrown garage rock pioneers.

The hyperactive song has also been incorporated many times by filmmakers, most notably in an unforgettably bizarre scene in John Waters’s Pink Flamingos. Stanley Kubrick also used the raucous song to capture what the director called “post-combat euphoria” in his Vietnam war epic Full Metal Jacket.

But it was the cartoon Family Guy that really gave “Surfin’ Bird” a new set of wings and rammed home its status as the divisive king of earworms. The song was the basis for a 2008 episode in which the character Peter Griffin’s obsession with singing and dancing to the song at every juncture is countered by other characters trying to destroy all copies of it. It went on to become a recurring joke in the long-running series. That triggered an unexpected renaissance for “Surfin’ Bird” in the UK when the song entered the charts in 2009, and again in 2010 when it rose to number 3, after an unsuccessful push by fans to block an X Factor winner from obtaining the Christmas number one.
The appeal of a then-47-year-old novelty hit to a new generation proved that, to this day, the bird is indeed the word.
Let us know your memories of ‘Surfin’ Bird’ in the comments section below. More at ft.com/lifeofasong

/content/560f77c6-c970-492e-9664-37028b3.title: Sarah Creal makes make-up for 40-plus skin. Everyone wants in
articleContent: “There couldn’t be a better fucking example of what I’m talking about than this,” says an amused and exasperated Sarah Creal as we battle to hear each other in the lounge of a central London hotel. The 56-year-old beauty entrepreneur is trying to tell me about all the male investors who “didn’t get why women over 40 needed more representation”, but is barely able to make herself heard over a group of loud baseball-capped young men at a nearby table.

Creal, as tall, glamorous and self-assured an adoptive New Yorker as you’ll find, is not the sort of woman to be drowned out by the sound of louder men. She has enjoyed a three-decade career as a product formulator and developer for other people. Much of it was spent at Estée Lauder, where she masterminded product development for the high-profile beauty collaborations of both Tom Ford and Victoria Beckham, which spawned their blockbusting standalone brands. In 2024 she launched her own: a collection of make-up, skincare and brushes. Created to suit 40-plus women, Sarah Creal Beauty will finally be distributed in the UK next month from its website and from Space NK.

She also had to counter arguments that other brands were already speaking to the demographic she was targeting. “You’re telling me that women of 40-plus only deserve two brands when Gen Z gets 20,000? That’s kind of the problem right there,” Creal says. She may appear NYC ice-queen but her personality is anything but. She’s sharp, funny and relentlessly upbeat. A girl’s girl, she tells anecdotes that centre around conversations with her friends, sisters, life with teenage daughters (her ex-husband lives in the same building; their daughters ride the lift between him on the 16th floor and her on the 29th).

She canvassed the opinions of 2,000 women before launching the brand. Now she’s on a mission to ensure that those “shockingly under-served” make-up customers get what they deserve. “No one wants to be told they look good ‘for their age’. But equally we want make-up that works well for our age,” she says.

As a formulator, she found that most of the frustrations older women experience with make-up – creasing, smudging, settling into fine lines – arrive because products are traditionally formulated for twentysomething skin. A younger person’s skin is “like working with a rubber mat. It’s bouncy. It’s smooth. It’s uniform. It can take anything,” she says. From around 40, skin gets noticeably thinner. “It’s more like tissue paper. You need even better performance because of fine lines and sagging eyelids. It’s about working with things like film-formers that are going to set but not be brittle, flex when the skin flexes.” Creal believes unconscious ageism is an issue in the way beauty products are tested. “I was part of that problem for a long time and I didn’t even know it,” she says. Now she tests her products exclusively on 40-plus skin.

The standouts in her collection are the ones that offer solutions. Through research she realised how many 40-plus women were “quiet quitting” mascara and eyeliner because their drooping eyelids were causing products to smudge. She formulated Victoria Beckham’s much-loved Satin Kajal liner, but made her own Eyes Up liner so that it was “creamy but does not move”.

Likewise the Face Flex concealer, which offers fairly comprehensive coverage in a tiny application – good for older women who are less comfortable wearing an entire “face” of foundation. “It has a great creamy texture, blends in super well, stays put, no creasing into fine lines and lasts all day,” says British make-up artist Val Garland. The Complexion Brush, which is somehow soft but sturdy, makes concealer application look much smoother. The pHLip liner changes colour so you get a perfect lip match.

“Sarah is known for creating the most epic liner in the industry [Victoria Beckham’s Kajal], then levelling it up to work on specifically mature eyes,” says American make-up artist Erica Taylor, who shares advice and recommendations on 40-plus make-up with her 1.9mn Instagram followers. “She creates colours and formulas that are so real-life wearable and usable. She makes the 40-plus club one you want to be in.”
Recommended

There are other global brands championing a more grown-up approach to make-up. Minimalist brand Merit – which was created around a no-nonsense “five-minute morning” philosophy – reached around $200mn in retail sales in its fifth year. While it won’t share latest figures, Bobbi Brown’s Jones Road Beauty, launched in 2020, was on track to generate more than $150mn in 2024. But Sarah Creal is the first to be so committed to her audience that she’s printed “For Babes 40+” on every box. It’s a characteristically bold move in a market where brands are reluctant to skew so specifically to a certain demographic for fear of, as Creal says, “leaving money on the table”. But it’s also part of the appeal. “It’s highly considered and quietly confident,” says Shannon Monteith, make-up and fragrance director at Space NK. “Sarah brings a rare clarity to the positioning of the brand.”
Face Flex Concealer & Complexion Enhancer, £44. BUY
Eyes Up Creamy Kajal longwear liner, £28. BUY
pHLip liner, £25. BUY
Just Like Paradise 12H Peptide Sculpting bronzer, £40. BUY
Recommended

Retail presence was key to Creal’s early success. She opened in 22 Sephora stores just three months after launching, and will have 102 by the end of this year. She reported $10mn in turnover after her first full year and is on course for triple-digit growth by the end of 2026. The UK is the brand’s first international outpost, and she thinks that it will resonate here. “So much of this brand is about having a sense of joy, because honestly, I’m sick of brands being like, ‘You’re getting older, oh poor you.’”

The “Babes 40+” label may be “divisive”, she shrugs. “But it’s not an objectification. It’s how I see myself, my friends. My fight isn’t about whether [our customer] should be using make-up. My fight is to make her feel fabulous and seen in a landscape that is making her feel less seen.”
